e: Forum of Caesar (Forum Iulium)
54–46 BC; rebuilt by Trajan, AD 113
Forum of Caesar
Dedication
46 BC, together with the Temple of Venus Genetrix
Site
according to Suetonius it cost more than 100 million sesterces
Suetonius, Iul. 26
Caesar began building his forum from the spoils of war; the price of the land alone exceeded one hundred million sesterces.
Cassius Dio 43.22
In 46 BC, after his triumphs, Caesar dedicated the forum named after him and the Temple of Venus Genetrix.

The first in the series of imperial fora: a long square lined with porticoes, with the Temple of Venus Genetrix at its end. The remains visible today date largely from Trajan's rebuilding of AD 113. Most of the square was excavated in the 1930s, during the construction of the Via dell'Impero (today Via dei Fori Imperiali), and further parts after 1998.

Lanciani's map was made before the excavation: on the Lanciani layer the temple and the square appear c. 35 m further to the southeast, in a conjectural position. A good example of how much the 20th-century excavation changed the picture.
Forum of Augustus (Forum Augustum)
vowed 42 BC; dedicated 2 BC
Forum of Augustus
Exedrae
two semicircular halls on the two sides of the square, with galleries of statues
Firewall
toward the Subura it was closed off by a high stone wall; one of its gates is today the Arco dei Pantani
Res Gestae 21
“On my own land, from the spoils of war, I built the Temple of Mars Ultor and the Forum of Augustus.”
Suetonius, Aug. 29
He built it because the two existing fora could no longer cope with the crowds and the lawsuits; he had vowed the temple at the battle of Philippi, to avenge his father.
Suetonius, Aug. 31
In the two porticoes he set up statues of the great generals of the Roman people in triumphal dress.
Pliny, Nat. hist. 36.102
He ranks it among the most beautiful buildings in the world.

In the middle of the exedrae stood the statues of Aeneas and Romulus, and around them the statues of the great Romans with short biographical inscriptions (elogia); fragments of these have been found. Toward the Subura the end of the square was closed off by a high stone wall that also served as a firewall and still stands today.
Its outline and the exedrae come from the OpenStreetMap survey.
Forum of Nerva (Forum Transitorium)
begun by Domitian; dedicated by Nerva, AD 97
Forum of Nerva
Shape
a long, narrow square on the line of the Argiletum
Suetonius, Dom. 5
Among Domitian's building works he mentions the forum “which is now called the Forum of Nerva.”

A narrow forum laid out on the site of the old Argiletum street, between the Basilica Aemilia, the Forum of Caesar and the Forum of Augustus on one side and the Temple of Peace on the other; it got the name Transitorium from its character as a passageway. The walls were decorated with closely spaced columns, because the narrow space did not allow a portico.
Temple of Peace (Templum Pacis)
AD 71–75; rebuilt by Septimius Severus after the fire of 192
Temple of Peace
Function
sanctuary, garden square, library and art collection
Region
Region IV (according to the Notitia)
Josephus, Jewish War 7.158–162
Vespasian built it after the victory at Jerusalem, and placed here the golden vessels of the temple of Jerusalem.
Together with the Forum of Augustus and the Basilica Paulli, he ranks it among the most beautiful buildings in the world.
Notitia, Region IV
“templum Pacis”: the region took its name from it.

A large garden surrounded by a portico, with the sanctuary and halls on its southern side. The Marble City Plan (Forma Urbis Severiana) hung on the wall of one of the halls: this hall is today part of the church of Santi Cosma e Damiano, and the fixing holes can still be seen in its wall. The excavations of 1998–2000 also uncovered the rows of the garden's planting beds.
Its outline is from the OpenStreetMap survey; part of the area today lies under the Via dei Fori Imperiali.
Forum of Trajan (Forum Traiani)
Forum of Trajan
Architect
Apollodorus of Damascus (Cassius Dio 69.4)
Pausanias 5.12.6
He singles out Trajan's building among the sights of Rome for its general beauty and above all for its bronze roof.
Aulus Gellius 13.25.1
On the roofs of the forum's halls stood gilded statues and inscriptions reading “ex manubiis” (from the spoils of war).
Ammianus Marcellinus 16.10.15–16
On his visit in AD 357, Constantius II stood in the forum in amazement; according to the Persian Hormisdas, one would first have to build a stable like this for such a horse.

The largest and last imperial forum, built from the spoils of the Dacian wars. A spur of the Quirinal hill was cut away for its sake. Its layout: an ornate entrance, a large square with the equestrian statue of Trajan, behind it the Basilica Ulpia, and then the column between the two libraries. Whether the Temple of Trajan stood at the northern end of the square is disputed in the light of recent excavations.
Trajan's Markets (Mercati di Traiano)
Trajan's Markets
Ancient name
not known; the name “market” is modern

A multi-story, semicircular brick complex cut into the slope of the Quirinal, behind the eastern exedra of the forum. It probably contained shops, offices and warehouses. Today it houses the Museum of the Imperial Fora.
Tabularium
78 BC
Tabularium
state archive (according to the traditional identification)
Builder
Q. Lutatius Catulus
CIL VI 1314
According to the building inscription, the consul Q. Lutatius Catulus had the substructio and the tabularium built and approved them, in 78 BC.

The huge substructure closing off the slope of the Capitol is today the foundation of the Palazzo Senatorio; its corridor can be visited from the Capitoline Museums. Its arcade faced the Forum, as a backdrop to the temples of Vespasian and Concordia.
Its outline is taken from the FORTVNA map (Häuber–Schütz 2014); previously only a schematic rectangle was shown here.
Temple of Vespasian and Titus
after AD 79
Vespasian
Front
6 Corinthian columns
Today
3 standing columns
Notitia, Region VIII
The catalog mentions it next to the Temple of Saturn: “templum Saturni et Vespasiani et Titi.”
Inscription
According to the fragmentary inscription on the architrave, it was restored by Septimius Severus and Caracalla.

Titus began it in honor of his father, Vespasian; Domitian completed it and dedicated it to his brother as well. Because of the narrow site, the staircase led up between the columns, cut into the podium. Its three corner columns have stood since Valadier's restoration in the early 19th century.
Temple of Concordia
367 BC (vow); 121 BC; AD 10
Concordia
Ground plan
wider than it is long: cella c. 45 × 24 m
Plutarch, Camillus 42
In 367 BC Camillus vowed a temple to Concordia on the reconciliation of the patricians and the plebeians.
Appian, Civil Wars 1.26
In 121 BC L. Opimius rebuilt it, after the killing of Gaius Gracchus.
Sallust, Cat. 46
In December 63 BC the Senate met here on the case of Catiline's associates.
Cassius Dio 56.25
Tiberius had it rebuilt; it was dedicated in AD 10.

The unusual ground plan (the long side of the cella faces the Forum) results from the narrowness of the site. Tiberius's temple also served as a museum: Pliny mentions numerous Greek statues and paintings in it.
Carcer – Tullianum
regal period (tradition); the facade 1st century AD
Carcer
beneath the church of San Giuseppe dei Falegnami
Livy 1.33.8
King Ancus Marcius had the first prison built above the Forum.
Sallust, Cat. 55
In the chamber called the Tullianum, sunk 12 feet below the ground, Catiline's associates were strangled in 63 BC.

Two chambers, one above the other; the lower, round room was built of tufa. The inscription on the facade is that of the consuls C. Vibius Rufinus and M. Cocceius Nerva (early 1st century AD). Medieval tradition venerated it as the prison of St Peter.
Porticus Deorum Consentium
present form AD 367
Dei Consentes
the city prefect Vettius Agorius Praetextatus had the statues of the gods restored in AD 367 (CIL VI 102)
Gods
the gilded statues of the twelve chief gods (Dei Consentes) stood here
Varro, De re rustica 1.1.4
In the Forum stand the gilded statues of the twelve “gods who take counsel together,” six male and six female.
Inscription, AD 367
Restored by the city prefect Vettius Agorius Praetextatus: one of the last pagan building projects in Rome.
A portico bent at an angle, with small rooms, at the foot of the Tabularium. Its columns were re-erected in 1858.
Temple of Saturn
497 BC; 42 BC; 4th century AD
Saturn
8 standing columns (6 in front, 2 at the sides)
Podium
22.50 m wide, c. 40 m long
Order
Ionic, hexastyle prostyle: 6 columns in front, and 2 on each side in addition to the corner columns
On the map
the 8 standing columns surveyed in OSM, and, as dashed circles, the one missing side column on each side, at the spacing of the standing columns
Livy 2.21
It was dedicated in 497 BC.
Plutarch, Poplicola 12
Publicola made the Temple of Saturn the seat of the state treasury (aerarium).
In the time of Augustus, Munatius Plancus had it rebuilt.
“Senatus populusque Romanus incendio consumptum restituit”: after a fire it was restored by the Senate and the people.

The survey shows clearly that the row of columns standing today is at the northeastern end of the podium, the end facing the Forum and the Clivus Capitolinus: the facade of the temple therefore faced the Forum. The row of columns standing today belongs to a 4th-century restoration: the columns consist of reused pieces of various origins, and one was even put in place upside down. The aerarium was inside the podium. The Saturnalia began here every December.
Arch of Septimius Severus
AD 203
Arch of Severus
Size
c. 23 × 11 m, 21 m high
Openings
Inscription (CIL VI 1033)

The Senate and the people erected it to Septimius Severus and his sons for the victories over the Parthians. Geta's name was chiseled out after Caracalla murdered his brother in AD 212, and its place was filled with new text.
The reliefs show the two Parthian campaigns. Because a church and houses were built up against it in the Middle Ages, it survived almost intact. Next to it were the Umbilicus and the old Volcanal.
Curia Iulia – the Senate house
44–29 BC; rebuilt by Diocletian after AD 283
Curia
The hall
Seating
three broad steps on each side, for c. 300 senators; at the end, two low steps form the platform of the presiding magistrate
Middle Ages
church of Sant'Adriano (AD 630)
Cassius Dio 44.5
Caesar was commissioned to build the new Senate house, which bore his name.
Res Gestae 19
Augustus lists the Curia and the Chalcidicum among his own buildings.
“senatum” – still the Senate's building in the 4th century.

The brick building standing today is Diocletian's (after the fire of 283). It survived because in 630 Pope Honorius I converted it into a church; the church was dismantled in 1930–37. Its original bronze doors have been in the Lateran basilica since the 17th century. Inside, the marble floor and the steps for the senators' seats can be seen.
Comitium
regal period – until Caesar's rebuilding
Comitium
Purpose
the place of the popular assembly and of the administration of justice in the Republican period
Varro, De lingua Latina 5.155
The Comitium got its name from the verb “coire” (to come together): here the curiae came together for the popular assembly and for trials.
The Republican-period assembly space in front of the Curia; only its paving layers and fragments have survived. Its location is certain, its shape disputed.

The map follows the reconstruction of the Carandini–Carafa atlas (Tab. 21, 117–52 BC): an irregular quadrilateral, with the Republican Rostra on its southern edge. The older reconstruction drew a round, stepped space on the model of the comitia excavated at Paestum and Cosa.
Volcanal – Shrine of Vulcan
the excavated phases are 4th–1st century BC
Volcanal?
Identification
according to SITAR, the shrine around the Lapis Niger
Dionysius of Halicarnassus 2.50
Romulus and Titus Tatius held council at the shrine of Vulcan above the Comitium.
Pliny, Nat. hist. 16.236
In the precinct of the shrine of Vulcan stood a lotus tree which, according to tradition, was planted by Romulus.

The SITAR database identifies the sacred area around the Lapis Niger with the shrine of Vulcan, following the interpretation of F. Coarelli; its excavated phases run from the 4th century BC to the early 1st century BC, when the late Republican black marble paving covered it. The identification is disputed, which is why it is shown with a dashed line. Its outline is from SITAR (CC BY-SA 4.0).
House of the rex sacrorum
508 BC – 27 BC
house of the rex sacrorum
The office
in the Republican period the religious duties of the kings were carried on by the rex sacrorum (king of sacrifices)

The SITAR database (on the basis of the excavations of Carandini and his colleagues) identifies the Republican-period building excavated along the Sacra Via, east of the House of the Vestal Virgins, with the house of the rex sacrorum; it was in use between 508 and 27 BC. Its outline is from SITAR (CC BY-SA 4.0); the identification is the excavators' interpretation.
Lapis Niger
inscription c. 570–550 BC
Lapis Niger
one of the earliest known Latin texts, with the word RECEI (rex = king)
Festus, “niger lapis”
In the Comitium the black stone marks an ill-omened spot; according to some, the place of Romulus's death, according to others the tomb of Faustulus or of Hostus Hostilius.

In 1899 Giacomo Boni found beneath the black marble paving an altar, the stump of a column and a stone pillar (cippus) with a boustrophedon inscription. The inscription appears to be a sacral regulation addressed to a king.
Underground shrine of Romulus (2020)
6th century BC
Shrine of Romulus?
Find
a 1.4 m tufa sarcophagus and a round altar(?)
Presented
February 2020
Festus, Dionysius 1.87
Several ancient authors place the tomb or memorial of Romulus in the area of the Comitium, behind the rostra.

The Parco archeologico del Colosseo presented it in 2020, beneath the 1930s staircase of the Curia: Boni had already seen it once, but attached no importance to it. The sarcophagus is not a tomb: according to the archaeologists it may have been a symbolic memorial, deliberately preserved even after the Curia was built.
Rostra (speakers' platform of the Augustan period)
44–42 BC; extended c. AD 470
Rostra
c. 24 m wide, 3 m high
Name
after the ships' prows (rostra)
Livy 8.14
In 338 BC the bronze prows of the ships of Antium were nailed to the speakers' platform of the Comitium, which is why it was called the Rostra.
Cassius Dio 43.49
Caesar moved the old platform to its present position, at the western end of the Forum.
“rostra III”: in the 4th century there were three rostra.

The present remains are the platform of Caesar and Augustus, with the fixing holes for the ships' prows on its facade; at its northern end it was given a brick extension in the 5th century AD (Rostra Vandalica). The other two rostra stood in front of the Temple of Divus Iulius and perhaps in the Comitium.
Umbilicus Urbis
Severan period
Umbilicus
Meaning
“the navel of the City”: the symbolic center of Rome
“umbilicum Romae”: the navel of Rome, the symbolic center of the city.
The round brick core standing next to the Arch of Severus is, according to the traditional identification, the remains of the Umbilicus.
Milliarium Aureum – the golden milestone
20 BC
Milliarium?
Set up by
Augustus, as chief superintendent of the roads (Cassius Dio 54.8)
a column covered in gilded bronze, the symbolic starting point of the roads of the empire
Cassius Dio 54.8
In 20 BC Augustus, as superintendent of the roads, set up a gilded milestone near the Temple of Saturn.
Pliny, Nat. hist. 3.66
The distances of the roads were measured from the gilded column standing at the head of the Forum.
Its location cannot be identified with certainty; it is placed between the southern end of the Rostra and the Temple of Saturn. Fragments of its marble base were found nearby.
Arch of Tiberius
AD 16
Arch of Tiberius
Occasion
the recovery, during the campaigns of Germanicus, of the military standards lost in Varus's defeat (Tacitus, Annales 2.41)
Tacitus, Ann. 2.41
In AD 16 an arch was erected beside the Temple of Saturn for the recovery of the military standards lost in the battle of Varus.
Only its foundations were found, at the northwestern corner of the Basilica Iulia; it is depicted on one of the reliefs of the Arch of Constantine.
Basilica Iulia
54–46 BC, completed by Augustus; rebuilt after AD 283
Basilica Iulia
the court of the centumviri
Livy 44.16
The Basilica Sempronia (169 BC) previously stood on its site.
Res Gestae 20
Augustus completed the basilica begun by his father, and when it burned down he rebuilt it on a larger scale in the name of his sons, Gaius and Lucius.
Pliny the Younger, Letters 6.33
At the court of the centumviri, sitting in four panels, there was such a crowd that people listened to the trial even from the upper galleries.

Today only its floor and the foundations of the piers can be seen, but it is also depicted on fragments of the Marble City Plan. The game boards scratched into the steps and the floor are traces of the people who passed the time here during breaks in the hearings.
Basilica Aemilia (Paulli)
179 BC; rebuilt 55–34 BC
Basilica Aemilia
a row of shops (tabernae) and the Portico of Gaius and Lucius
Livy 40.51
In 179 BC the censors M. Aemilius Lepidus and M. Fulvius Nobilior had it built behind the fish market.
He ranks the Basilica of Paullus, with its columns of Phrygian marble, among the most beautiful buildings of the city.
“basilicam Pauli” – in the 4th century it was counted as part of Region IV.

In AD 410, during the sack by Alaric's Goths, it burned down: the bronze coins melted into the floor can still be seen today. The row of shops facing the Forum square (tabernae novae) was the place of the money changers of the Republican period.
Shrine of Venus Cloacina
of archaic origin
Cloacina
Goddess
Cloacina, the goddess of the Cloaca Maxima, who was identified with Venus
Livy 3.48
Near the shrine of Cloacina, by the tabernae, Verginius killed his daughter to save her from Appius Claudius.
Pliny, Nat. hist. 15.119
The Romans and the Sabines purified themselves here with myrtle branches after the war.

The outline of the shrine's base is from the OpenStreetMap survey (“Sacello di Venere Cloacina”). Its round marble base has survived in front of the steps of the Basilica Aemilia; a denarius depicts it with two statues of goddesses. This is where the Cloaca Maxima entered the Forum.
Column of Phocas
AD 608 (the column is 2nd-century)
Column of Phocas
Height
Smaragdus, exarch of Ravenna, set it up in honor of the Byzantine emperor Phocas in AD 608.
The last ancient monument of the Forum. The column was taken from an earlier building; the stepped base was excavated in the 1810s.
Lacus Curtius
legendary origin; paving 1st century BC
Lacus Curtius
Legends

three origin legends were told about it: the horse of the Sabine Mettius Curtius sank into the marsh here; the knight Marcus Curtius threw himself into the chasm that had opened here; the consul C. Curtius fenced off the spot struck by lightning (Livy 1.12–13 and 7.6; Varro)
Varro, De lingua Latina 5.148–150

Gives three explanations for the name: the horse of the Sabine warrior Mettius Curtius sank into the marsh here; the young Marcus Curtius leaped into the chasm that had opened here; or the consul C. Curtius fenced off a spot struck by lightning.
Livy 7.6
In 362 BC Marcus Curtius, on horseback and in arms, threw himself into the chasm that had opened in the middle of the Forum.
An irregular depression in the paving of the square, bordered by stone slabs. The original of the Mettius Curtius relief (a copy) was found in 1553.
Equestrian statue of Domitian
AD 91
Equus Domitiani / Doliola?
Other name
Doliola (Carandini–Carafa, VIII 413)
Statius, Silvae 1.1
A long poem about the huge bronze equestrian statue standing in the middle of the Forum.
Boni excavated the concrete foundation in the middle of the square; the statue was removed after Domitian's death in AD 96 and the condemnation of his memory (damnatio memoriae).

Another interpretation: the Carandini–Carafa atlas marks the same spot as “Doliola” (VIII 413) and keeps it on the map from the 8th-century BC phase onward. Varro (De lingua Latina 5.157) describes the Doliola as a place beside the Cloaca Maxima where spitting is forbidden. OpenStreetMap also uses this name. The map indicates both interpretations.
Temple of Divus Iulius
decree 42 BC, dedicated August 18, 29 BC
Divus Iulius
speaker's platform (rostra aedis Divi Iulii) with a semicircular niche
Appian, Civil Wars 2.148
The people built a pyre for Caesar's body in the Forum, near the Regia, and burned it there; later an altar, then a temple, was erected on the spot.
Cassius Dio 47.18
In 42 BC the triumvirs decided to build a temple of Caesar on the site of the cremation.
Augustus lists it among his own building works.

The concrete core of the podium survives, along with the semicircular niche in front of the facade containing the base of a round altar: according to tradition this is the site of Caesar's cremation. Flowers are still often laid on it today.
Arch of Augustus
29 or 19 BC
Arch of Augustus
Cassius Dio 51.19, 54.8
The Senate voted Augustus an arch for the victory at Actium, and later for the military standards recovered from the Parthians.
The foundations of a three-bay arch were found between the Temple of Divus Iulius and the Temple of Castor; whether they belong to the Actian or the Parthian arch is disputed.
Temple of Castor and Pollux
484 BC; 117 BC; AD 6
Castor and Pollux
32 × 49.5 m, 7 m high
Corinthian, octastyle peripteral: 8 × 11 columns, with a double row of columns on either side of the pronaos
Pronaos
Cella
3 columns on the east side: 12.50 m high, 1.45 m in diameter
Vowed by the dictator A. Postumius at the battle of Lake Regillus (496 BC); dedicated by his son in 484 BC.
Dionysius 6.13
After the battle two young horsemen appeared in the Forum, watered their horses at the spring of Juturna, announced the victory and vanished: the Dioscuri.
Suetonius, Tib. 20
Tiberius rebuilt it in his own name and that of his younger brother Drusus (AD 6).

The three standing columns belong to Tiberius's temple and are one of the symbols of the Forum. The building was excavated and published by a Scandinavian academic mission between 1983 and 1989. The podium housed the standard weights and measures of the office of verification and chambers for strongboxes.
Spring of Juturna
5th century BC; marble facing in the imperial period
Iuturna
Legend
after the battle of Lake Regillus the Dioscuri watered their horses here and announced the victory here
Ovid, Fasti 1.705–708
The shrine of the nymph Juturna beside the temple of the Dioscuri.
Here the Dioscuri watered their horses when they brought news of the victory at Regillus.

In 1900 Boni excavated the rectangular basin with the pedestal standing in its center; fragments of the marble statues of the Dioscuri were also found in the basin. Beside it stand a small shrine of Juturna and an altar.
Temple of Vesta
by tradition Numa; present form after AD 191
Vesta
Foundation
circular, 15.05 m in diameter
Columns
20 Corinthian; shaft diameter 0.51 m, height c. 4.45 m
inner diameter c. 8.6 m, wall 0.6 m
dashed circle: the foundation; the radius of the ring of columns is calculated from the published dimensions (±0.3 m)
Inside
the eternal fire; there was no statue
Ovid, Fasti 6.257–282
The temple is round because Vesta is the Earth itself; there is no statue of the goddess in it, only the ever-burning fire.
Plutarch, Numa 11
Numa built a round temple for Vesta, in the image of the universe.
Cassius Dio 73.24
It burned down in AD 191; the empress Julia Domna had it rebuilt.

In 1930 a section was partially re-erected on its round podium. Inside the temple a secret storage place (penus) held the sacred objects brought to Rome, among them, according to tradition, the Palladium.
Regia
late 7th century BC; rebuilt 36 BC
Regia
the office of the pontifex maximus
Plutarch, Numa 14
Numa lived in the Regia, near the Temple of Vesta.
Cassius Dio 48.42
Cn. Domitius Calvinus rebuilt it in marble in 36 BC.

An irregular, trapezoidal building; Boni and later the American excavations uncovered its superimposed phases from the late 7th century BC onward. The sacred shields of Mars (ancilia) and the annals of the pontiffs were kept here; the lists of the Fasti consulares and triumphales stood on its marble walls.
Atrium Vestae – the House of the Vestal Virgins
present form after AD 64
Atrium Vestae
Courtyard
c. 69 × 24 m, with pools
Residents
six Vestal Virgins
“Vestam” – the Temple of Vesta and the house of the Virgins were still standing at the end of the 4th century.
Symmachus, Letters
At the end of the 4th century he was still corresponding with the chief Vestal (virgo Vestalis maxima).

A multistory residence built after the fire of AD 64 and later enlarged several times, arranged around a colonnaded courtyard with two pools. In the courtyard stand the statues of the chief Vestals on their pedestals; the name has been chiseled off one of the pedestals (probably Claudia, who became a Christian). Beneath it are the remains of the Domus Publica.
Domus Publica
Republic; the excavated phase c. 125–100 BC
Domus Publica?
Resident
the official house of the pontifex maximus; Caesar lived here from 63 BC until his death (Suetonius, Caesar 46)
Fate
Augustus gave it to the Vestal Virgins in 12 BC (Cassius Dio 54.27)
Suetonius, Iul. 46
As pontifex maximus, Caesar lived in the state house beside the Sacra Via.

The more recent excavations (Carandini and colleagues) uncovered a large Republican-period house with a peristyle beneath the eastern part of the imperial-period House of the Vestal Virgins, beside the Summa Sacra via; this is identified with the Domus Publica. The outline on the map comes from Tab. 15 and Tab. 18 of the Carandini–Carafa atlas; the accuracy of the fit here, at the edge of the sheet, is c. ±3–4 m.
Formerly the remains beneath the western part of the House of the Vestal Virgins were taken to be the Domus Publica; the identification is still not beyond dispute.
Temple of Antoninus and Faustina
AD 141; church: San Lorenzo in Miranda
Antoninus and Faustina
10 monolithic cipollino columns, 17 m high, 1.45 m in diameter at the base
Corinthian, hexastyle prostyle, with 2 further columns on each side of the pronaos
DIVO ANTONINO ET DIVAE FAUSTINAE EX S C
On the architrave: to the divine Antoninus and the divine Faustina, by decree of the Senate. The second line was added after the death of Antoninus (161).
“templum Faustinae”.

It survived because it was converted into a church in the 11th century. The deep grooves on the columns are the traces of a medieval attempt at demolition. In front of it the ancient level of the Sacra Via was uncovered gradually between 1546 and 1876, which is why the church door now hovers above the steps.
Iron Age cemetery (sepulcretum)
10th–8th century BC
Iron Age graves
Graves
cremation and inhumation burials, hut-shaped urns

In 1902, in the deep excavation beside the Temple of Antoninus and Faustina, Boni found the earliest cemetery of the Forum valley. Since the Romans did not bury their dead inside the city, this shows that the area was not yet inhabited. The valley was paved as a public square only after it had been drained by the Cloaca Maxima.
“Temple of Romulus”
early 4th century AD; vestibule of Santi Cosma e Damiano
“Temple of Romulus”
Door
original bronze door, with a lock that still works today
Coins
The commemorative coins that Maxentius struck for his son Romulus, who died in 309, show a round, domed building.

A round, domed brick building with two apsed side halls; its original 4th-century bronze door is still in place today. Whether it was really dedicated to Romulus is disputed: some scholars take it to be the shrine of Jupiter Stator or of the Penates, others the vestibule of the Urban Prefecture. Since 527 it has belonged to the church of Santi Cosma e Damiano.
Basilica of Maxentius (Basilica Nova)
AD 308–312, completed by Constantine
Basilica of Maxentius
c. 100 × 65 m, the vault of the nave 35 m high
Aurelius Victor 40.26
Everything that Maxentius had built in the city, including the basilica, the Senate dedicated to the merits of Constantine.
“basilicam Constantinianam”.

The largest vaulted hall of ancient Rome; the three giant barrel vaults of the north aisle still stand today. The pieces of the colossus of Constantine found in the west apse in 1487 (the head, the hand, the foot) are in the Capitoline Museums.
Arch of Titus
after AD 81
Arch of Titus
13.5 m wide, 15.4 m high
Inscription (CIL VI 945)
“The Senate and the Roman people to the divine Titus, son of the divine Vespasian” – erected after the death of Titus.

Its inner reliefs show the treasures of the Temple in Jerusalem (the seven-branched menorah) in the triumph of AD 71. In the Middle Ages it was built into the Frangipani fortress; in 1821 Valadier completed it in travertine, so the restored parts can still be clearly distinguished today.
Horrea Agrippiana
Augustan period
Horrea Agrippiana
named by an inscription found in the courtyard of the warehouse, set up to the genius of the warehouse (Horrea Agrippiana)
“horrea Germaniciana et Agrippiana”.

Agrippa's three-story warehouse building along the Vicus Tuscus, with rooms around a courtyard; it has been partly excavated, and part of it lies beneath the buildings at the foot of the Palatine. Its extent here is approximate.
Santa Maria Antiqua
mid-6th century AD
S. Maria Antiqua
Frescoes
6th–8th century, one of the richest ensembles of early medieval painting

A church installed in a Domitianic vestibule leading toward the Palatine; it was buried by an earthquake in 847, which is why its frescoes survived in exceptional condition. It was excavated in 1900 and has been open to visitors since 2016.
Temple of Divus Augustus
after AD 14, completed by Caligula
Divus Augustus?
Location
unknown; two main hypotheses (see below)
Ionic (based on coin images)
Suetonius, Cal. 21; Tib. 47
Begun by Tiberius, completed by Caligula; Caligula also had a bridge thrown across from it to the Palatine.

The temple itself has never been found, and its size and exact location are unknown; according to the coin images it was of the Ionic order. Most current scholarship places it behind the Basilica Iulia, in the unexcavated area: the map follows this hypothesis, and the position and size are estimates.

Another hypothesis: Lanciani took the large Domitianic brick hall behind the Temple of Castor to be the temple of Augustus; the Lanciani layer carries the label “T. Divi Augusti” there, and OpenStreetMap also puts its “Tempio di Augusto” point at this spot.

The 4th-century AD city map of the Carandini–Carafa atlas (sheet 19) follows the first hypothesis: it writes the label “Templum novum divi Augusti?” in the block behind the Basilica Iulia, between the Vicus Tuscus and the Vicus Iugarius, and marks the large Domitianic hall as “Templum Minervae”.

This hall is part of the Domitianic building complex around Santa Maria Antiqua. According to the on-site panel, its identification with the temple of Augustus is still strongly disputed; according to M. Heinzelmann (2011), for example, it may have been Domitian's unfinished new Senate building.
Basilica Porcia
184 BC
Basilica Porcia?
Built by
M. Porcius Cato as censor (Livy 39.44)
Destruction
burned down together with the Curia in 52 BC, in the fire of Clodius's funeral pyre
Livy 39.44
In 184 BC Cato the censor bought up private houses beside the Lautumiae and had a basilica built there.
Asconius, In Milonianam
In 52 BC it burned down together with the Curia, set alight by the pyre of Clodius's body.
The first basilica in Rome, but no remains of it are known.
Its location and outline are the reconstruction of the Carandini–Carafa atlas (Tab. 21): west of the Curia Hostilia, beside the Clivus leading toward the Carcer. The accuracy of the fit is c. ±3 m.
Rostra (Republican speaker's platform)
from 338 BC; until Caesar moved it
Rostra (Republ.)
on the southern edge of the Comitium
In 338 BC the bronze prows of the ships of Antium were nailed to the speaker's platform of the Comitium.
Caesar moved the platform to the western end of the Forum, its present location.
Its outline is the reconstruction of the Carandini–Carafa atlas (Tab. 21, 117–52 BC), beside the Lapis Niger; the accuracy of the fit is c. ±3 m.
Porticus and Tabernae veteres
from the Archaic period until the construction of the Basilica Iulia
Tabernae veteres
the Basilica Iulia stands on its site
In 169 BC Ti. Sempronius Gracchus had the Basilica Sempronia built on the site of the houses behind the old shops (tabernae veteres).
Varro, De lingua Latina 6.59
The name of the old shops (veteres) as opposed to the new ones (novae).

A row of shops and columns running along the south side of the Forum, the place of the money changers (argentarii); it disappeared when the Basilica Iulia was built. Its outline is the reconstruction of the Carandini–Carafa atlas (Tab. 21); the accuracy of the fit is c. ±3 m. Behind it stood the Basilica Sempronia, whose extent cannot be read in full from the photographed sheet, so I have not drawn it in.
Honorary columns of the Sacra Via
turn of the 3rd–4th century AD
honorary columns
Pedestals
7, at intervals of c. 10–11 m in front of the Basilica Iulia
two columns have been re-erected
Atlas
Carandini–Carafa: VIII 17–23

Seven brick-cored pedestals line the Sacra Via, in front of the steps of the Basilica Iulia; they are part of the late imperial embellishment, and statues once stood on their columns. The position of the pedestals comes from the OpenStreetMap survey; their number and alignment are given in the same way by the 4th-century city map of the Carandini–Carafa atlas (sheet 19, VIII 17–23).
Pedestal of the equestrian statue of Constantius II
mid-4th century AD
Pedestal of Constantius II
the equestrian statue of Constantius II was set up by the urban prefect Neratius Cerealis in AD 352–353 (CIL VI 1158)

A late antique pedestal for an equestrian statue between the Arch of Severus and the Curia; its location and identification are OpenStreetMap data (“Base di Costanzo II”). The Carandini–Carafa atlas also marks an equestrian statue of Constantine in this area (Equus Constantini, VIII 168); whether the two are the same cannot be decided from the photograph.
Curia Hostilia
regal period
Curia Hostilia?
according to tradition built by King Tullus Hostilius (Varro, De lingua Latina 5.155)
Livy 1.30
King Tullus Hostilius built it for the Senate, and it bore his name.
Sulla enlarged it; it burned down in 52 BC. Its remains have not been securely identified.
Its location and outline are the reconstruction of the Carandini–Carafa atlas (Tab. 21): north of the Comitium, west of the present Curia Iulia. The accuracy of the fit is c. ±3 m.
Ianus Geminus
by tradition Numa
Ianus?
Custom
its gates were closed in peacetime and stood open in war (Livy 1.19)
Augustus
closed three times during his reign (Res Gestae 13)
Livy 1.19
Numa built the shrine of Janus at the foot of the Argiletum as a sign of peace and war: open in war, closed in peace.
Res Gestae 13
Before Augustus it had been closed only twice since the foundation of Rome; under his principate, three times.
It was a small bronze gateway shrine, known to us only from coins; its site is to be sought at the beginning of the road between the Curia and the Basilica Aemilia, but no trace of it has been found.
Temple of Venus Genetrix
46 BC; rebuilt by Trajan, AD 113
Venus Genetrix
3 re-erected columns (1930s)
Appian, Civil Wars 2.102
Caesar built the Temple of Venus Genetrix in fulfillment of the vow he made before Pharsalus, and had a beautiful statue of Cleopatra set up beside the goddess.
Pliny, Nat. hist. 35.156
The statue of the goddess was made by the sculptor Arcesilaus, in such haste that he had not even finished it by the dedication.
The temple of the ancestral mother of the Julian clan at the end of the forum, on a high podium. The podium and the three columns can still be seen today.
Basilica Argentaria
Trajanic period
Basilica Argentaria
Graffiti
inscriptions scratched by schoolboys survive on its walls, among them lines of Virgil
“basilicam argentariam”.
The hall between the Forum of Caesar and the slope of the Capitol; it took its name from the money changers (argentarii). Its outline is from the OpenStreetMap survey.
Temple of Mars Ultor
Mars Ultor
Corinthian, eight-column facade
the podium and 3 columns
Res Gestae 29
He placed the military standards recovered from the Parthians in the inner shrine of the Temple of Mars Ultor.
Ovid, Fasti 5.549–598
Describes the temple: weapons on the walls, statues of Aeneas and Romulus in the porticoes, the name of Augustus on the facade.
Cassius Dio 55.10
The Senate deliberated here on war and triumph; victorious generals laid down their insignia here.

It stood at the northeastern end of the forum, backed against the firewall, with its facade toward the square. I assembled its outline from the podium sections surveyed in OpenStreetMap, so its accuracy is c. ±2 m.
Hall of the Colossus
Augustan period
Hall of the Colossus
Statue
judging by the pedestal it may have been c. 11–12 m high; marble fragments of it survive
A hall in the northern corner of the forum, with the pedestal of a colossal statue at its rear wall. Whom the statue represented (perhaps the genius of Augustus) is disputed.
Temple of Minerva
AD 97
Minerva
begun by Domitian, inaugurated by Nerva in AD 97
Martial 1.2.8
The bookseller's shop is behind the Temple of Peace and the forum of Pallas (Minerva).

The temple of Domitian's favorite goddess at the northern end of the Forum of Nerva. It stood in good condition until the early 17th century; Pope Paul V had it demolished in 1606, and its stones were used for the monumental fountain of the Acqua Paola. Today only the core of the podium is visible.
Le Colonnacce
Colonnacce
Italian for “ugly big columns”: the popular name for the columns, which were long half-buried in the ground

The only standing section of the decorative wall of the Forum of Nerva, with two Corinthian columns. The frieze shows the myth of Minerva and Arachne, the weaving contest; the attic shows the figure of Minerva.
Basilica Ulpia
AD 112
Basilica Ulpia
c. 170 × 60 m, with five aisles
Apollodorus of Damascus
Among the sights of the region it lists the imperial forums.

The largest basilica in Rome, named after Trajan's family name. It had an apse at each end, and a double row of columns ran around the interior. Today some of the gray granite columns of the nave stand again.
Trajan's Column
AD 113
Trajan's Column
the column shaft is 100 Roman feet (c. 29.8 m); with the pedestal c. 35 m
Inside
spiral staircase; the Notitia records 185 steps and 45 windows
Inscription (CIL VI 960)
Set up by the Senate and the people to show how high the hill and the ground were that were cleared away for these great works.
Cassius Dio 68.16
The column was made both as a tomb marker and as a memorial of the building of the forum.
Eutropius 8.5
Trajan's ashes were placed under the column in a golden urn.

The relief band, more than 200 m long and winding upward in a spiral, depicts the two Dacian wars (101–102, 105–106). A statue of Trajan originally stood on its top; since 1587, one of St Peter. The Notitia's list for Region VIII also mentions it by name (“columnam cochlidem”).
Foundation of the equestrian statue of Trajan
c. AD 112
Equus Traiani
Source
according to Ammianus Marcellinus (16.10), Constantius II admired the equestrian statue standing in the middle of the square in 357
Constantius II admired the equestrian statue standing in the middle of the forum and wanted to have a similar one made.
A large foundation excavated in the middle of the square, identified with the equestrian statue of Trajan. Its location is from the OpenStreetMap survey.
Auditoria of Hadrian (Athenaeum?)
age of Hadrian (2nd century AD)
Auditoria of Hadrian
Discovery
2008–2009, during the construction of Metro Line C
Aurelius Victor 14.3
Hadrian founded a school for the liberal arts, which was called the Athenaeum.
Under Piazza Venezia three large halls came to light with stepped seating, for lectures and readings. The identification with the Athenaeum is a hypothesis.
Tomb of C. Poplicius Bibulus
1st century BC
Tomb of Bibulus
the Senate and the people granted a burial place at public expense to the aedile C. Poplicius Bibulus and his descendants for his merits (CIL VI 1319)
Inscription (CIL VI 1319)
He received the burial place by resolution of the Senate and decree of the people for his merits, for himself and his descendants.
It stood at the northern foot of the Capitol, at the start of the Via Flaminia, outside the city boundary; part of its facade is still visible today.
Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus
509 BC (according to tradition)
Jupiter Optimus Maximus
Deities
Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, in three cellae
Burned down
83 BC, AD 69 and AD 80, rebuilt each time afterward
Foundation on the map
c. 52 × 73 m (according to the FORTVNA drawing)
Tarquinius Superbus built the temple vowed by his father, Tarquinius Priscus, with craftsmen summoned from Etruria.
Livy 2.8
It was dedicated by the consul M. Horatius Pulvillus in the first year of the Republic.
Dionysius of Halicarnassus 4.61

It stood on a high substructure, its perimeter eight plethra; its sides were nearly 200 feet, and its length exceeded its width by barely 15 feet. It had three parallel cellae: Jupiter's in the middle, those of Juno and Minerva on either side.
Tacitus, Historiae 3.72
In December AD 69 it burned down during the fighting between the supporters of Vitellius and Vespasian; Tacitus calls this the most lamentable and most shameful disaster since the founding of Rome.

The most important temple of Rome stood on the southern summit of the Capitol, on the western side of the hill. The walls of its foundation, built of cappellaccio tufa, can be seen today in the Capitoline Museums (in the Marcus Aurelius Hall of the Palazzo dei Conservatori) and along the Via del Tempio di Giove.

The map shows the outline from FORTVNA (Häuber–Schütz 2014). The author deliberately does not reconstruct the ground plan, because too little of it survives and the scholars do not agree either: according to F. P. Arata the large foundation supported not the temple itself but the sacred precinct around it (area Capitolina).
Temple of Jupiter Tonans (?)
22 BC
Jupiter Tonans?
Suetonius, Augustus 29
Augustus built it because, during a night march on the Cantabrian campaign, lightning struck beside his litter and killed the slave carrying a torch in front of him.
Cassius Dio 54.4
He dedicated it on the Capitol in 22 BC.
Augustus, Res gestae 19
He lists it among the works he built.

Its exact location is not known. The FORTVNA map follows the hypothesis of G. Mazzei, who attributes the concrete platform south of the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus to this temple; the map too marks it with a question mark.
Temple of Veiovis
192 BC
Veiovis
Position
“between the two groves” (inter duos lucos), in the saddle of the Capitol
Livy 35.41
In 192 BC two temples of Jupiter were dedicated on the Capitol; L. Furius Purpureo had vowed them. One of them is generally identified with the Temple of Veiovis.
Ovid, Fasti 3.429–430
The Temple of Veiovis stands in front of the two groves.
Vitruvius 4.8.4
He mentions as an example the “Temple of Veiovis between the two groves,” whose layout differs from the usual.

It came to light in 1939 behind the Palazzo Senatorio, at the corner of the Tabularium. The cella is wider than it is deep. On the podium the Apollo-like marble statue of the god was also found, which can be seen today in the Capitoline Museums. Its outline is from the FORTVNA map.
Temple of Jupiter Custos (?) and fortifications
age of Domitian (AD 81–96)
Jupiter Custos?
Origin
built by Domitian in memory of his escape during the siege of the Capitol in AD 69 (Tacitus, Historiae 3.74; Suetonius, Domitianus 5)
Tacitus, Historiae 3.74

In AD 69, during the siege of the Capitol, the young Domitian hid in the lodging of the temple attendant. During his father's reign he built a small chapel there to Jupiter Conservator; as emperor he dedicated a huge temple to Jupiter Custos, with his own statue in the god's lap.
Suetonius, Domitianus 5
He had a new temple built on the Capitol to Jupiter Custos.
The FORTVNA map marks the remains of fortifications at this spot and suggests, with a question mark, that the Temple of Jupiter Custos may have stood here.
The Ara Coeli apartment block (Insula dell'Ara Coeli)
early 2nd century AD
Insula
Type
multistory apartment block with shops on its ground floor
in the 1920s–30s, when the surrounding houses were demolished
Juvenal 3.190–202
On Roman apartment blocks in general: they are prone to collapse and fire, and the tenant on the top floor is the last to escape.

One of the best-preserved Roman apartment blocks; several of its stories stand on the northern slope of the Capitol, beside the staircase of the Vittoriano. In the Middle Ages a small church (San Biagio de Mercato) was built into it; its bell tower and fresco are still visible today.
Its outline is from OpenStreetMap; the drawing on the FORTVNA map agrees with it.
Temple of Juno Moneta (location ?)
344 BC
Juno Moneta?
Vow
L. Furius Camillus, in the war against the Aurunci
Livy 7.28
The dictator Camillus vowed the temple in the war against the Aurunci. It was built on the Arx, on the site of the house of M. Manlius Capitolinus, and was dedicated a year later.
Cicero, De divinatione 1.101
Before an earthquake a warning voice spoke from the Temple of Juno; according to Cicero this is how the goddess got the name Moneta (“the warner”).

Its exact location is not known; it is sought on top of the Arx, in the area of today's Santa Maria in Aracoeli. The FORTVNA map marks its possible site with a question mark. The Roman mint operated beside the temple; this is the origin of the word “moneta” (money).
Auguraculum – the observation post of the augurs (location ?)
very early, exact date unknown
Auguraculum?
from here the augurs watched the sky for taking the auspices from birds
Livy 1.18
At his inauguration as king, Numa was led to the Arx. He sat on a stone, and beside him the augur, with his head covered, watched for the signs in the sky.
Festus (Paulus) 17 L
The ancients called auguraculum the place that we now call the arx, because the augurs took the official auspices there.
It must have been on top of the Arx; no archaeological trace of it is known. FORTVNA marks its possible site with a question mark beside Santa Maria in Aracoeli.
Shrine of Isis Capitolina (?)
1st century BC (the cult)
Isis Capitolina?
inscriptions mention the priests of Isis Capitolina
Tertullian, Apologeticum 6.8
According to him the consuls Piso and Gabinius banned Serapis, Isis and Harpocrates from the Capitol and destroyed their altars.
Cassius Dio 40.47
In 53 BC the Senate ordered the demolition of the shrines of Serapis and Isis built by private individuals.
The location of the shrine of Isis on the Capitol is unknown. The FORTVNA map marks it with a question mark on the site of today's church of Santa Maria in Aracoeli.
Asylum – the place of refuge
according to tradition, the age of Romulus
Asylum
Romulus opened a place of refuge here for fugitives in order to populate the city (Livy 1.8)
Livy 1.8

To populate the city, Romulus opened a place of refuge at the spot which today, as one goes up, can be seen enclosed between the two groves. All sorts of people from the neighboring peoples fled here.

It is sought in the saddle between the two summits of the Capitol, the Capitolium and the Arx, on the site of today's Piazza del Campidoglio. No archaeological trace of it is known; on the map it follows the FORTVNA marking.
Temple of Jupiter Feretrius (?)
according to tradition, the age of Romulus; restored by Augustus
Jupiter Feretrius?
Spolia opima
the armor taken with one's own hands from the enemy commander was offered here; first, according to legend, by Romulus (Livy 1.10)
Livy 1.10

After defeating the king of Caenina, Romulus carried the captured armor (spolia opima) to the Capitol and marked out the site of the Temple of Jupiter Feretrius. According to Livy this was the first temple of Rome.
He mentions it among the temples he built on the Capitol.
It was a small, very ancient shrine; its exact location is not known. The FORTVNA map adopts the uncertain identification of G. Mazzei, with a question mark.
Porta Stercoraria (?)
unknown
Porta Stercoraria?
according to Festus, the refuse of the Temple of Vesta was carried out here every year on June 15
Varro, De lingua Latina 6.32
On June 15 the refuse swept out of the Temple of Vesta was carried by way of the Clivus Capitolinus to a designated place.
Festus 466 L
The refuse was carried into a narrow alley about halfway up the Clivus Capitolinus, which was closed off by the Porta Stercoraria.
There is no archaeological trace of it. According to FORTVNA the gate may have stood above the Clivus Capitolinus, in this area.
Tarpeian Rock (Saxum Tarpeium)
according to tradition, a place of execution from the regal period
Saxum Tarpeium?
Punishment
traitors were thrown down from here
Livy 6.20
In 384 BC M. Manlius Capitolinus, who had once defended the Capitol against the Gauls, was thrown down from the Tarpeian Rock.
Dionysius of Halicarnassus 7.35
The rock rises above the Forum; those condemned to death are customarily thrown down from here.

Its exact location is disputed: some look for it on the southwestern side of the Capitol, others on the eastern side facing the Forum. FORTVNA marks it near the Gradus Monetae, above the Forum; this is the place I show here.
Porta Fontinalis
gate of the Servian Wall
Porta Fontinalis
in 193 BC a portico was built from here to the altar of Mars in the Campus Martius (Livy 35.10)
Livy 35.10
In 193 BC the aediles had a portico built from the Porta Fontinalis to the altar of Mars in the Campus Martius.

It opened in the saddle between the Capitol and the Quirinal, where the city wall crossed the valley. FORTVNA marks it at the break in the wall; the saddle was later cut away when the Forum of Trajan was built.
The Servian Wall
after 378 BC (tradition attributes it to Servius Tullius)
Servian Wall
Material
squared blocks of Grotta Oscura tufa
Livy 1.44
Servius Tullius surrounded the city with a rampart, a ditch and a wall.
Livy 6.32
In 378 BC the censors let a contract for a wall to be built of squared stone.

The map shows the wall line from FORTVNA (Häuber–Schütz 2014). On the Capitol it ran along the northern side of the Arx and the western edge of the hill. The section crossing the saddle between the Capitol and the Quirinal was demolished when the Forum of Trajan was built.

On the Caelian Hill the map shows the line of FORTVNA Map 3 (2014) from the Porta Capena via the Porta Caelimontana (Arch of Dolabella) to the Porta Querquetulana; on this section the wall is largely only hypothetical.

In the southern part of the Aventine (Region XII) the map shows the line of FORTVNA Map 7: from the Porta Capena south along the eastern foot of the Murcus minor to S. Balbina, and from there west via the Porta Naevia toward the Porta Raudusculana. SITAR (following Coarelli 2008) assumes a different course: it also brings the Little Aventine (S. Saba) inside the wall, and places the Porta Naevia south of S. Balbina, at the end of the Via di S. Balbina. This version and the assumed sites of the two gates can be seen on the SITAR layer.

Around the Aventine (Region XIII), the line of FORTVNA Fig. 58 (Häuber 2022): from the Porta Carmentalis along the Tiber via the Porta Flumentana and the Porta Trigemina, then along the western edge of the Aventine to the Porta Lavernalis and from there east to the Porta Raudusculana. That map is at a small scale, so on this section the line is accurate only to c. ±10–20 m.

On the Esquiline (Region V) the wall was a large earthen rampart (agger) with a ditch. Here the map shows the line of FORTVNA Map 3 (2014) from the Porta Querquetulana via the Porta Esquilina (Arch of Gallienus) northward; connected to it are the wall sections still visible today in front of Termini station and beside the Piazza Manfredo Fanti (OpenStreetMap).

Around the Quirinal and the Viminal (Region VI) the map shows the line of FORTVNA Fig. 58 (Häuber 2022) from the southwestern corner of the Quirinal via the Porta Quirinalis and the Porta Collina to the Porta Viminalis, where it joins the rampart of the Esquiline (±10–20 m). The wall sections still visible today beside the Via Salandra and the Largo di Santa Susanna are from OpenStreetMap.
Huts of Romulus (Casa Romuli)
Iron Age huts (10th–8th century BC)
Casa Romuli
the postholes and trenches cut into the tufa show the ground plans of three huts
Dionysius of Halicarnassus 1.79

On the side of the Palatine facing the Circus there still stood in his own day a hut made of wood and reeds, which was called the house of Romulus. Its keepers added nothing to it, and if it was damaged they restored it in its original form.
Notitia, Region X
The first monument of the region: “casam Romuli”.

In 1948 S. M. Puglisi excavated the traces of three huts on the southwestern edge of the hill, on the Germalus. The best-preserved, hut “A”, measured c. 18 m², with seven postholes along the walls and one in the center, and a hearth in the middle. A model of it made in 1950 can be seen in the Palatine Museum.
The exact location of the “hut of Romulus” maintained in antiquity is not known. The FORTVNA map places the label “Casa Romuli” slightly south of the excavated huts.
Temple of Magna Mater (Cybele)
191 BC; rebuilt by Augustus
Magna Mater
Cult image
the sacred black stone brought from Pessinus
Festival
Megalesia, with plays held in the square in front of the temple
Livy 29.14

In 204 BC the sacred stone brought from Pessinus was received at Ostia by P. Scipio Nasica; the Roman matrons carried it to the Palatine, passing it from hand to hand, and placed it in the Temple of Victoria.
Livy 36.36
In 191 BC M. Iunius Brutus dedicated the temple; the first plays at the Megalesia were held in honor of the dedication.
He mentions the Temple of Magna Mater among the temples he built on the Palatine.

The concrete core of the podium still stands today in the southwestern corner of the Palatine. In front of it lay the stepped square where the plays of the Megalesia were held. In the excavations many terracotta figurines of the goddess and of Attis came to light.
Temple of Victoria
294 BC
Victoria
L. Postumius Megellus
Livy 10.33
In 294 BC the consul L. Postumius Megellus dedicated the temple, which he had begun to build as aedile from the money from fines.
Livy 35.9
In 193 BC M. Porcius Cato dedicated a small shrine to Victoria Virgo beside the Temple of Victoria.
The sacred stone of Magna Mater was kept here until her own temple was completed.

The large podium lying northeast of the Temple of Magna Mater has generally been identified with the Temple of Victoria since the excavations of P. Pensabene. Its outline is from the FORTVNA map (Häuber–Schütz 2014, Map 7).
Auguratorium (?)
mentioned by the Notitia (4th century)
Auguratorium?
the 4th-century regionary catalog lists it in Region X
Livy 1.6
At the founding of the city Romulus chose the Palatine and Remus the Aventine as the place for taking the auspices.
It lists it among the buildings of the region: “auguratorium”.
It was the augurs' place of augury on the Palatine. The small building beside the Temple of Magna Mater was given this name by the excavators; the identification is uncertain.
House of Livia
second half of the 1st century BC
House of Livia
Naming
based on the stamp IVLIAE AVG(ustae) on lead pipes (CIL XV 7264)
Inscription on the lead pipe of the house
IVLIAE AVG(ustae) – that is, “to Iulia Augusta,” the name Livia bore after the death of Augustus. The connection of the building with Livia rests on this.

It came to light in the 19th century, during the excavations of P. Rosa. A house with an atrium, with excellent wall paintings of the Second Pompeian Style (Io and Argus, Polyphemus and Galatea, garden landscapes). It may have belonged to the House of Augustus; it received Livia's name on the basis of the inscription, but this is not certain proof. The FORTVNA map also suggests, with a question mark, the curia of the Salian priests (Curia Saliorum).
House of Augustus
House of Augustus
the Room of the Masks and the Room of the Pine Garlands can be visited
Suetonius, Augustus 72

He lived first near the Forum, then on the Palatine, in the modest house of Hortensius: its short porticoes were of Alban stone, and its rooms had no marble or ornate floors. For more than forty years he slept in the same bedroom, winter and summer.
Augustus, Res gestae 34
By resolution of the Senate the doorposts of his house were decorated with laurel, and an oak wreath (corona civica) was fixed above his door.

It was excavated by G. Carettoni from the 1960s onward. The Second Style wall paintings of its rooms are excellently preserved. The house stood directly beside the Temple of Apollo, to which it was connected by a ramp.
Temple of Apollo Palatinus
