Its exact location is disputed; the highest point of the Sacra Via, the area of the Velia, is the most likely. The FORTVNA map suggests several places with a question mark (beside the “Temple of Romulus” and near the Arch of Titus); here I show the one toward the Velia.
Temple of Portunus
the temple standing today: early 1st century BC
Portunus
Ionic pseudoperipteral temple with a four-column facade
church of Santa Maria Egiziaca (from the 9th century)
Varro, De lingua Latina 6.19
The festival of the Portunalia was named after Portunus, to whom a temple was dedicated on this day at the Tiber harbor.

It stands in the Forum Boarium, beside the old Tiber harbor (Portus Tiberinus). Because it was converted into a church in the 9th century, it survived almost intact. It used to be known as the “Temple of Fortuna Virilis”. Its outline is from OpenStreetMap; on the SITAR layer the details examined during the restorations can also be seen.
Round Temple of Hercules (Hercules Victor / Olivarius)
second half of the 2nd century BC
Hercules
Pentelic (Greek) marble; the oldest surviving marble temple in Rome
20 Corinthian columns around the round cella
Notitia, Region XI
“Herculem olivarium”: the Hercules of the oil merchants; many scholars identify it with this temple.

A temple of circular ground plan in the Forum Boarium on the bank of the Tiber. To whom it was dedicated is disputed: Hercules Victor or Hercules Olivarius; SITAR records it under the name “Aedes Herculis Olivarii”. According to SITAR, the stepped foundation built of Grotta Oscura tufa is dated to the end of the 2nd century BC. In the Middle Ages it was converted into a church (Santa Maria del Sole), which is why it survived. Its outline is from OpenStreetMap.
Ianus Quadrifrons – the four-way arch
4th century AD
Ianus Quadrifrons
c. 12 m wide and 16 m high
“arcum divi Constantini”: many scholars identify it with this four-way arch.

A marble-faced brick structure standing in the Velabrum, opening with one archway on each of its four sides; statues once stood in its niches. In the Middle Ages the Frangipane family turned it into a fortress; the attic was demolished from its top in the 19th century. Its outline is from OpenStreetMap.
Arch of the Argentarii
AD 204
Arch of the Argentarii
set up by the money changers and the cattle merchants in honor of Septimius Severus and his family (CIL VI 1035)
Erased figures
the figures of Geta, Plautilla and Plautianus were removed after their murders
Inscription (CIL VI 1035)
The money changers (argentarii) and the cattle merchants (negotiantes boarii) set it up for Septimius Severus, Iulia Domna and their sons. Geta's name and image were chiseled out after his death.

A gate-like monument with a straight lintel, built against the wall of the church of San Giorgio in Velabro. Its reliefs show the imperial family offering sacrifice. Its outline is from OpenStreetMap.
The sacred area of Sant'Omobono (Fortuna and Mater Matuta)
6th century BC; rebuilt several times in the Republican period
Fortuna and Mater Matuta
Foundation
by tradition King Servius Tullius (Livy 5.19)
Livy 5.19
In 396 BC Camillus rededicated the temple of Mater Matuta, which had been dedicated by King Servius Tullius.
Livy 33.27
In 196 BC L. Stertinius had two arches with gilded statues erected in the Forum Boarium, in front of the temples of Fortuna and Mater Matuta.
One of its manuscripts also lists a “Fortunium”; whether this means this temple of Fortuna is uncertain.

It was discovered in 1937, during the construction of the Via del Mare. Two twin temples stand on a shared platform; beneath them are the remains of the archaic temple of the 6th century BC with terracotta decoration, including the statue group of Hercules and Minerva. Its outline is from OpenStreetMap; on the SITAR layer the excavated phases can also be seen.
Ara Maxima Herculis (location ?)
by tradition earlier than the foundation of Rome
Ara Maxima?
the altar of Hercules, set up after the defeat of Cacus (Livy 1.7; Virgil, Aeneid 8)
Livy 1.7

According to the legend of the struggle between Hercules and Cacus, the “greatest altar” was set up to Hercules in the time of Evander; this was the one foreign cult that Romulus adopted, with Greek rite.
The furrow of Romulus's pomerium started from the bronze bull of the Forum Boarium, so as to include the great altar of Hercules.
The tufa platform visible in the crypt of the church of Santa Maria in Cosmedin is identified by many with the Ara Maxima; the identification is disputed. The point marks the location of the church.
Pons Aemilius (“Ponte Rotto”)
179 BC (piers), 142 BC (arches)
Pons Aemilius
Builders
the piers by the censors M. Aemilius Lepidus and M. Fulvius Nobilior, the arches by the censors P. Scipio Africanus and L. Mummius (Livy 40.51)

In 179 BC the censors M. Aemilius Lepidus and M. Fulvius Nobilior let a contract for building the piers of a bridge over the Tiber; the arches were built on them some years later by the censors P. Scipio Africanus and L. Mummius.

The first stone bridge of Rome over the Tiber. In the Middle Ages it collapsed several times, and in 1598 the flood carried it away for good; since then only a single arch of it has stood in the middle of the river (Ponte Rotto, “broken bridge”). Its outline is from OpenStreetMap.
Porta Trigemina (location ?)
Porta Trigemina?
“triple gate”, probably from its three openings
“portam trigeminam”.
In 193 BC the aediles had a portico built outside the Porta Trigemina, and a harbor (emporium) beside the Tiber.

The three-opening gate of the Servian Wall between the Tiber and the Aventine. Its exact location is not known; the map shows the SITAR placement, which was made following F. Coarelli (2008) and the Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae.
Porta Carmentalis (location ?)
Porta Carmentalis?
Belief
one of its openings was held to be the “accursed gate” (Porta Scelerata), because by tradition it was through this that the 306 Fabii marched out, who fell at the Cremera in 477 BC (Livy 2.49)
Livy 2.49

The 306 members of the Fabian clan marched out through the right-hand opening of the Porta Carmentalis to the war against the Veientes, from which they did not return; for this reason this opening was called the “wicked gate” (porta scelerata).

A gate of the Servian Wall at the southern foot of the Capitol, beside the shrine of Carmenta. Its exact location is not known; the map shows the SITAR placement (following Coarelli 2008 and the Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae).
Theater and Portico of Pompey
inaugurated 55 BC; the portico was completed by 52 BC
Theatrum Pompei
Cn. Pompeius Magnus
Significance
the first permanent theater in Rome, built of stone
theater “Pompei”: 17,580 places (the figures in the manuscripts differ)
the curve of the auditorium lives on in the houses of the Via di Grottapinta and the Piazza del Biscione
Plutarch, Pompey 42
Pompey wanted to build a theater in Rome too, on the model of the one he had seen in Mytilene, but larger and more splendid.
Tertullian, De spectaculis 10
To avoid the disapproval of the censors, Pompey built a temple of Venus at the top of the auditorium and dedicated the whole as a temple, beneath which the seats were placed as steps.
Ammianus Marcellinus 16.10.14
On his visit to Rome in 357, Constantius II admired, among the wonders of the city, the Theater of Pompey, the Odeum and the Stadium as well.

The theater and the large portico opening behind it, which enclosed a garden, together formed a building complex c. 300 m long in the southern part of the Campus Martius. Its remains can be seen in the cellars of the houses around the Campo de’ Fiori; the curve of the auditorium still stands out in the street network today.
The map shows the FORTVNA outline (Häuber–Schütz 2022, Fig. 58), which represents the theater and the portico as a single shape.
Stadium of Domitian
Domitian (AD 81–96), probably c. 86
Stadium Domitiani
athletic contests of the Greek type (the Capitoline agon)
“stadium”: 30,088 places
the Piazza Navona preserves its shape; its remains can be visited beneath the Piazza di Tor Sanguigna
It lists the stadium, the odeum and the naumachia among the new structures of Domitian.
In 357 the emperor Constantius counted the stadium, too, among the wonders of Rome.
An elongated racetrack, rounded at the north, whose seating was built into the foundations of the houses of today's Piazza Navona. The map outline is from the FORTVNA reconstruction.
Baths of Nero (later of Alexander Severus)
Nero, early 60s AD; rebuilding c. AD 227
Thermae Neronianae
“thermas Alexandrianas”
its granite columns reused (e.g. in the 17th-century repair of the porch of the Pantheon); wall remains around the Palazzo Madama
Martial 7.34
“What is worse than Nero? And what is better than Nero's baths?” – the poet calls them the tyrant emperor's only work worthy of praise.
Historia Augusta, Alexander Severus 25.3
Alexander Severus built new baths beside the baths formerly called Nero's, and also brought water to them.

They lay west of the Pantheon, beneath the block of today's Senato (Palazzo Madama) and San Luigi dei Francesi. Their ground plan is preserved in the drawings of Palladio and other Renaissance architects; the map shows the FORTVNA outline.
Lake of Agrippa (location ?)
Agrippa, c. 25–19 BC
Stagnum Agrippae?
Nero
according to Tacitus (Annales 15.37), Tigellinus held a banquet here on a raft in AD 64
Tacitus, Annales 15.37
In AD 64 Tigellinus held a banquet in honor of Nero on a raft on the Lake of Agrippa, with brothels along the shore.

An artificial lake beside the Baths of Agrippa, fed by the water of the Aqua Virgo and drained into the Tiber by the channel called the Euripus. Its location and extent are known only indirectly; the map shows the FORTVNA proposal.
Odeum of Domitian (location ?)
Domitian (AD 81–96)
Odeum
roofed hall for musical and oratorical performances
“odium”: 11,600 places (the figures in the manuscripts differ)
It mentions the odeum among the structures of Domitian.
In 357 the emperor Constantius counted the Odeum, too, among the wonders of Rome.
Its location is sought south of the stadium, on the basis of the curved facade of the Palazzo Massimo alle Colonne and the walls found beneath it. The map shows the FORTVNA outline.
Baths of Agrippa
from 25 BC; water from 19 BC (Aqua Virgo)
Thermae Agrippae
one arc of the wall of the great round hall stands among the houses of the Via dell’Arco della Ciambella
Cassius Dio 53.27
In 25 BC Agrippa built the “Laconicum”, the Basilica of Neptune and the Pantheon.
Cassius Dio 54.29
In his will Agrippa left his baths to the Roman people, so that they could bathe free of charge.
Cassius Dio 66.24
The fire of AD 80 also destroyed the Baths of Agrippa.

Rome's first large public baths, south of the Pantheon. A section of wall of the round central hall (“la Ciambella,” the doughnut) is still visible today; this is shown by the OSM layer. The full outline is the FORTVNA reconstruction.
Saepta Iulia
Planned by Caesar (54 BC); dedicated by Agrippa in 26 BC
Saepta Iulia
voting place of the popular assembly, later an exhibition and market hall
Side porticoes
on the west the Porticus Argonautarum, on the east the Porticus Meleagri
Cicero, Ad Atticum 4.16
Caesar planned a covered voting place of marble on the Campus Martius, surrounded by a portico a mile long.
Cassius Dio 53.23
In 26 BC Agrippa dedicated the Saepta, which he surrounded with stone porticoes and decorated with paintings.
Notitia, Region IX
“porticum argonautarum et Meleagri”.

A square about 300 m long, bordered by porticoes on both sides, east of the Pantheon. It is known from the fragments of the Marble Plan (Forma Urbis) and from walls in the area of Via del Seminario and Santa Maria sopra Minerva. Its outline is the FORTVNA reconstruction.
Diribitorium (location ?)
Begun by Agrippa, completed by Augustus in 7 BC
Diribitorium?
the hall where the votes were counted
The Diribitorium was the largest building covered by a single roof; its roof could not be restored later, so it remained unroofed.
It burned down in the fire of AD 80.
It is sought south of the Saepta; its exact location and ground plan are not known. The outline is the FORTVNA proposal.
Porticus Minucia Frumentaria (?)
time of Domitian (AD 81–96) according to the SITAR excavation dating
Porticus Minucia?
the place of the free grain distribution (frumentatio)
“Minucias veterem et frumentariam” – the old Minucia and the grain Minucia
Two Minucia porticoes appear among the entries of the region: the old one (vetus) and the grain-distribution one (frumentaria).
Velleius Paterculus 2.8.3
After his triumph over the Scordisci, c. 106 BC, M. Minucius Rufus had a portico built that bore his name.

According to F. Coarelli's identification, the large rectangular portico excavated along Via delle Botteghe Oscure is the Minucia Frumentaria, while the portico surrounding the temples of Largo Argentina is the Minucia Vetus. The identification is disputed. Its outline is the FORTVNA reconstruction.

SITAR dates the eastern boundary wall and the first paving of the hall to the time of Domitian (AD 81–96) and the second floor level to the second half of the 1st century AD; the Claudian date given here before is not supported by the excavation data.
Divorum – portico of the deified Flavians (location ?)
Divorum
Contents
temples of Vespasian and Titus in a large porticoed courtyard
Chronographus anni 354
The “Divorum” appears among Domitian's building works.
“Divorum”.
On the basis of the fragments of the Marble Plan it is sought east of the Saepta, between today's Il Gesù and the Collegio Romano. The outline is the FORTVNA proposal.
Sanctuary of Isis and Serapis on the Campus Martius
Voted in 43 BC; rebuilt by Domitian
Iseum
Finds
the small obelisks in front of Santa Maria sopra Minerva and in front of the Pantheon come from here
Cassius Dio 47.15
In 43 BC the triumvirs voted a temple to Serapis and Isis.
Josephus, Antiquitates 18.65–80
Because of a scandal Tiberius demolished the temple of Isis, had its priests crucified and had the statue thrown into the Tiber.
The temple of Serapis and Isis also burned down in the fire of AD 80.
Juvenal 6.528–529
The superstitious woman sprinkles water brought from Meroe on the temple of Isis, which stands next to the old voting pen (ovile, that is, the Saepta).

East of the Saepta, in the area of today's Via del Piè di Marmo. Its ground plan is preserved by the fragments of the Marble Plan; numerous Egyptian statues and obelisks have come to light here. The outline is the FORTVNA reconstruction.
Minerva Chalcidica (location ?)
Minerva Chalcidica?
Legacy
its name is preserved by the nearby church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva
It appears among Domitian's building works.
“Minervam Chalcidicam”.
A small, probably round shrine of Minerva near the Iseum. Its location is not known; the map shows the FORTVNA proposal.
Temple of the Deified Matidia and the Basilicas of Matidia and Marciana (location ?)
Hadrian, after AD 119
Matidia
Matidia
Hadrian's mother-in-law, Trajan's niece; deified after her death (AD 119)
“basilicam Matidies et Marcianes” – the basilica of Matidia and Marciana.

The temple was dedicated to Hadrian's mother-in-law, Matidia; on its two sides stood halls bearing the names of Matidia and her mother, Marciana (Trajan's sister). Its location is probably northeast of the Pantheon, in the area of Piazza Capranica; the map shows the FORTVNA reconstruction.
Theater of Balbus and the Crypta Balbi
dedicated 13 BC
Theatrum Balbi
L. Cornelius Balbus (the Younger), the general from Gades
“Balbi” theater: 11,510 places; as a separate entry, the “cryptam Balbi”
the Crypta Balbi is one of the museums of the Museo Nazionale Romano
At Augustus's urging the leading men also built: among others, Cornelius Balbus erected a theater.
Cassius Dio 54.25
Balbus dedicated his theater in 13 BC during a flood so great that it could be reached only by boat.
The fire of AD 80 also destroyed the Theater of Balbus.

G. Gatti placed the site of the theater on the south side of Via delle Botteghe Oscure on the basis of the fragments of the Marble Plan (1960). The porticoed courtyard behind it, the Crypta Balbi, was excavated from 1981 under the direction of D. Manacorda; the area is now a museum. The map shows the FORTVNA outline, which depicts the theater and the crypta together; the outline of today's archaeological area can be seen on the OSM layer.
Porticus Philippi and Temple of Hercules Musarum
temple after 187 BC; the portico c. 29 BC
Porticus Philippi
Temple
Temple of Hercules and the Muses (Hercules Musarum)
At Augustus's urging Marcius Philippus restored the Temple of Hercules and the Muses.

A round temple built for the statues of the Muses that M. Fulvius Nobilior brought from Ambracia, which L. Marcius Philippus surrounded with a portico in the time of Augustus. Its ground plan can be seen on one of the best-known fragments of the Marble Plan. Its outline is the FORTVNA reconstruction.
Portico of Octavia
Augustus, after 27 BC; its predecessor was the Portico of Metellus (after 146 BC)
Porticus Octaviae
Temples
Temples of Juno Regina and Jupiter Stator in the courtyard
the entrance gate building (propylon) stands in front of the church of Sant’Angelo in Pescheria; its inscription records the restoration by Septimius Severus in 203
Augustus erected some of his buildings in the names of others, among them the Portico of Octavia and the Theater of Marcellus.
Velleius Paterculus 1.11.3
Q. Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus was the first to have a portico built around the two temples, and he had Lysippus's Granicus group set up here.

A rectangular portico bearing the name of Augustus's sister, Octavia, on the north side of the Circus Flaminius. Its entrance gate building still stands today at the edge of the Roman ghetto. The full outline is the FORTVNA reconstruction; the standing propylon can be seen on the OSM layer.
Theater of Marcellus
dedicated 13 or 11 BC
Theatrum Marcelli
Named after
M. Claudius Marcellus, Augustus's nephew and son-in-law (died 23 BC)
“Marcelli” theater: 20,500 places (the numbers in the manuscripts differ)
Middle Ages and modern era
fortified residence, from the 16th century the palace of the Savelli and then the Orsini family
Res Gestae divi Augusti 21
Next to the Temple of Apollo, on land bought largely from private individuals, Augustus built a theater that bears the name of his son-in-law, M. Marcellus.
He lists the Theater of Marcellus among the buildings Augustus erected in the names of others.

Begun by Caesar, completed by Augustus. The two lower, arcaded levels of the outer facade still stand today; above them rises the 16th-century Savelli palace. Between 1926 and 1932 it was freed from the structures built around it. Its outline is from OpenStreetMap.
Temple of Apollo Medicus (Sosianus)
dedicated 431 BC; rebuilding after 34 BC (C. Sosius)
Apollo
three of its columns were re-erected in 1940 along Via del Teatro di Marcello
Livy 4.25
In 433 BC, during a plague, a temple was vowed to Apollo for the health of the people.
Livy 4.29
The temple was dedicated in 431 BC by the consul Cn. Iulius.

One of Rome's oldest temples of Apollo, next to the Circus Flaminius. It was given its present form after 34 BC by C. Sosius, Antony's general, which is why it is called Apollo Sosianus. Its outline is from OpenStreetMap.
Temple of Bellona
vowed 296 BC
Bellona
Role
here the Senate received returning generals and enemy envoys, who were not allowed to enter the city
Livy 10.19
In 296 BC, in the battle against the Etruscans and Samnites, Ap. Claudius Caecus vowed a temple to Bellona.
Ovid, Fasti 6.201–208
In front of the temple stood the small “war column” (columna bellica), from which a spear was hurled as the sign of a declaration of war.
The podium excavated east of the Temple of Apollo was identified with the Temple of Bellona by 20th-century research. Its outline is from OpenStreetMap.
Temple of Juno Sospita (Forum Holitorium)
dedicated 194 BC
Iuno Sospita
the Forum Holitorium (vegetable market) belonged to Region XI
built into the walls of the church of San Nicola in Carcere
Livy 34.53
In 194 BC C. Cornelius Cethegus dedicated the Temple of Juno Sospita in the Forum Holitorium, which he had vowed as consul.

Of the three Republican temples of the vegetable market, the middle one is usually attributed to Iuno Sospita (Ianus, Iuno Sospita, Spes); the identification is debated. The outline is the SITAR reconstruction of the second building phase: in 90 BC Caecilia Metella rebuilt it as an Ionic hexastyle peripteral temple, later restored by Hadrian. The OpenStreetMap outline used here before lay about 20 m further west, between the temples and the Theatre of Marcellus.
Temple of Spes (?) (Forum Holitorium)
during the First Punic War (mid-3rd century BC)
Spes?
the Forum Holitorium belonged to Region XI
Tacitus, Annales 2.49
In AD 17 Tiberius dedicated in the Forum Holitorium the Temple of Hope (Spes), which Atilius had vowed in the First Punic War, and the Temple of Janus, which C. Duilius had built.

The southern one of the three Republican temples. The outline is the SITAR reconstruction of the second building phase after the fire of 31 BC, probably Augustan: a Doric hexastyle peripteral temple with 11 columns on each side. Which temple belonged to which deity is not certain; SITAR follows the usual (Coarelli’s) identification. The map previously followed the OpenStreetMap labelling, which put the name Spes on the column row of the northern temple.
Temple of Ianus (Forum Holitorium)
C. Duilius, after the naval victory of Mylae (260 BC); the surviving remains date from the early 1st century BC
Ianus
its remains are built into the church of San Nicola in Carcere
In AD 17 Tiberius dedicated the temple of Ianus by the Forum Holitorium; it had been built by C. Duilius, who won the first naval victory over the Carthaginians.

The northern one of the three Republican temples. The outline is the SITAR reconstruction of the second building phase (concrete-cored podium faced with travertine, peperino columns), dated on stylistic grounds to the early 1st century BC; the podium of the first phase lies in the same place. The column row in the side wall of San Nicola in Carcere, which the map previously labelled Spes, stands on the podium of this temple.
Porta Capena (location ?)
Porta Capena
Road
the Via Appia started here
Region I (Porta Capena) was named after it
Juvenal, Satires 3.11
Umbricius stopped at the old arches and the dripping Porta Capena.
Martial 3.47.1
At the great Porta Capena, where the water drips from the conduit.

A gate of the Servian Wall; the hypothetical SITAR location follows Coarelli (2008) and the LTUR. SITAR dates the construction of the wall to the 6th century BC and its restoration to 378 BC. Nearby, the plan of an 1868 excavation (Parker and Gori) shows structures which according to SITAR in all likelihood belonged to the gate.
Porta Naevia (location ?)
Porta Naevia
Varro, De lingua Latina 5.163
The Porta Naevia was named after the Naevian groves.
A gate of the Servian Wall; the hypothetical SITAR location follows Coarelli (2008) and the LTUR. SITAR dates the construction of the wall to the 6th century BC and its restoration to 378 BC.
Porta Raudusculana (location ?)
Porta Raudusculana
The Porta Rauduscula was so named because it was covered with bronze: the ancients called bronze raudus.
Porta Salutaris (location ?)
Porta Salutaris
from the nearby temple of Salus
Temple of the Flavian family (Templum Gentis Flaviae)
Domitian (according to SITAR AD 89–95)
Templum Gentis Flaviae
Region VI (Alta Semita)
beneath the octagonal hall of the Baths of Diocletian and Via Parigi
Suetonius, Domitian 1.1
Domitian was born in the sixth region, at the place called Malum Punicum, in the house which he later turned into the temple of the Flavian family.
Suetonius, Domitian 17.3
Domitian’s nurse secretly took his ashes to the temple of the Flavian family and mixed them with those of Julia.

The solid outline shows the foundations recorded in SITAR (the portico with exedra around the temple and the temple platform; concrete, brick and travertine masonry), the dashed one the SITAR reconstruction (Serlorenzi–Laurenti 2002) of the whole complex. SITAR follows its use down to AD 298, when the Baths of Diocletian were built next to it.
Nova Via
at least since the end of the 6th century BC; its present paving dates from Nero (AD 64–68)
Nova Via
Route
along the northern slope of the Palatine, parallel to the Forum
Livy 5.32.6
In 391 BC the plebeian M. Caedicius heard at night on the Nova Via, where a shrine now stands above the temple of Vesta, a superhuman voice announcing the approach of the Gauls.

According to SITAR, a street on the north-eastern Palatine existing at least since the end of the 6th century BC and later paved with basalt is tentatively identified with the Republican course of the Nova Via; in the late Republic it ran on a terrace of concrete. The basalt paving still visible on the Forum side belongs according to SITAR to the Neronian layout after the fire of 64.
Stable of the “Reds” (Stabulum Factionis Russatae)
Augustan; rebuilt in the time of Hadrian
Stabulum
Region IX (Circus Flaminius)
under Largo Perosi, next to Via Giulia
Among the items of the region are the stables of the four circus factions (stabula IIII factionum).

The stable of the Red faction of the chariot races. According to SITAR the Augustan building consisted of seven aisles about 4 m wide, with brick walls and travertine piers; “AUG” marks on the voussoirs point to an imperial building site. Parts of the foundations were adapted to the loose riverside ground. Under Hadrian three aisles were turned into a horseshoe-shaped track with basins, perhaps for the care of the horses; the walls also show repairs after an exceptional flood. The outline is the SITAR reconstruction of the Augustan building.
Hecatostylum – the “hundred-column” portico (location ?)
date uncertain; shown on the Severan Marble Plan
Hecatostylum
Martial 2.14
Selius, hunting for a dinner invitation, also goes into the portico resting on a hundred columns.

A portico in the Campus Martius, in the area of the Theatre of Pompey. The approximate SITAR marking, based on the Marble Plan (FUR 21), shows structures at the end of the portico, partly preserved under the present street. The date (55 BC) follows the Theatre of Pompey and is not excavation data.
House of Aemilia Paulina Asiatica (?)
2nd century AD (SITAR)
Domus Aemiliae
under the Palazzo delle Esposizioni (Via Nazionale)

The brick walls found south of a retaining wall in the 2003 excavation were assigned by the excavator to one building phase and one house, which according to SITAR can in all likelihood be identified with the house of Aemilia Paulina Asiatica.
House of L. Octavius Felix
early 3rd century AD; with alterations until the end of the 4th century
Domus Octavii Felicis
1872; further trenches 1998–1999
around Via Giolitti and Via Manin

According to SITAR the house of L. Octavius Felix, a man of senatorial rank (vir clarissimus), who built it in the early 3rd century AD. The walls in banded masonry went with a floor of polychrome marble pieces (pavonazzetto, giallo antico, africano, alabaster); Lanciani also described rooms with black-and-white mosaics, a small internal fountain and a small colonnaded court.
House of the Percennii
broadly dated (SITAR: 50 BC – AD 320)
Domus Percenniorum
1879, during the construction of Via Napoleone III
A house in mixed masonry, of which the bath rooms (balneum) and a stretch of water conduit survive; SITAR takes it from an 1879 survey, so its location and date are only approximate.
House of Marius Maximus
undated (SITAR); its owner lived in the early 3rd century AD
Domus Marii Maximi
the Caelian hill
Based on a literature synthesis, SITAR marks wall structures assigned to the house of L. Marius Maximus, the Severan senator and imperial biographer; it gives no date of its own.
Vicus Capitis Africae – “Head of Africa” street
the bounding walls date between Augustus and Nero (SITAR)
Caput Africae
Region II (Caelimontium)
Via Capo d’Africa preserves the name
Notitia, Region II
“Caput Africae”.

According to SITAR, two walls in mixed masonry excavated in Piazza Celimontana in 1985 probably formed the limits of the street. The imperial page school (paedagogium ad Caput Africae) stood on this street.

Constantius saw the Pantheon as a “round city district,” with high-vaulted beauty.

The building standing today was rebuilt under Hadrian (the brick stamps point to the first years of Hadrian's reign), but it repeated Agrippa's original inscription. Erected by Antoninus Pius for his deified predecessor. The reliefs depicting the provinces (now in the Capitoline Museums and in Naples) may have belonged to the decoration of the porticoed courtyard surrounding the temple. Its outline is from OpenStreetMap.

It connects the Tiber Island with the far bank (Trastevere). In the 4th century it was renovated by Valentinian, Valens and Gratian; at the end of the 19th century, when the embankments were built, it was largely rebuilt, reusing the ancient stones. Its outline is from OpenStreetMap.

Terminus
on the Campus Martius, in front of the facade of the Saepta

After his third consulship, in the year of the consulship of C. Sentius and Q. Lucretius (19 BC), Agrippa brought the water in on June 9. It got its name because a young girl showed the veins of the spring to soldiers searching for water.

The arches of the Aqua Virgo end on the Campus Martius, at the facade of the Saepta.

Claudius rebuilt from their foundations the arches damaged by C. Caesar (Caligula).

The line runs southwest beneath the city, crossed the road under Via Lata through the Arch of Claudius, and ended at the Baths of Agrippa. On Via del Nazareno three of its arches stand with the inscription of Claudius; at the corner of Via del Corso and Via Minghetti its piers and arches were found (SITAR).

In the north the aqueduct arrived on the slope of the Pincian, beneath the Villa Medici; this section too is given by the FORTVNA line, and on the SITAR layer the boundary stones (cippi) of the Aqua Virgo can be seen next to the Villa Medici.

Set up for Claudius by the Senate and the Roman people because he received the submission of eleven kings of Britain without loss, and was the first to bring the barbarian peoples beyond the Ocean under the rule of the Roman people.

The arch of the Aqua Virgo, which carried the water across the Via Lata and was at the same time a monument to Claudius's victory in Britain. Its fragments came to light in the 16th–17th centuries around Piazza Sciarra. When he returned home from Hispania and Gaul, the Senate vowed the altar of the Augustan Peace on the Campus Martius and ordered that the magistrates, priests and Vestal Virgins should sacrifice on it every year.

On January 30 the poet sings of the festival of the Altar of Peace.

In AD 65, after the Pisonian conspiracy, the consul designate Plautius Lateranus was executed.

age of Trajan (?)
Castra Priora?
Unit
the emperor's horse guard (equites singulares Augusti)

The older barracks of the horse guard in the area of the Via Tasso. SITAR marks a curved wall thought to belong to it, which resembles the structures drawn here by Lanciani; FORTVNA also places the barracks here.

Constantine had a basilica built in the Lateran Palace and endowed it with rich gifts.

A gateway arch built of travertine, probably a rebuilding of the Porta Caelimontana of the Servian Wall. Later a branch of Nero's aqueduct passed over it. It still stands today at the end of the Via di San Paolo della Croce. Outline from OpenStreetMap.

The Neronian arches branching off from the Claudia aqueduct start from beside the Spes Vetus and end at the Temple of Divus Claudius.

Nero led a branch of the Aqua Claudia to the Caelian Hill to feed the fountains of his Golden House. AD 271–275; heightened by Honorius (401–403)
Aurelian Wall
the whole wall c. 19 km
Gate on the map
Porta Metronia
Historia Augusta, Aurelianus 21 and 39
Because of the barbarian incursions Aurelian extended and strengthened the walls of Rome.
The brick wall still stands today on the south and east sides of the Caelian. On the map the line of the wall is from OpenStreetMap.

In the northern part of the Pincian (Muro Torto) the wall incorporated the terrace walls of the Horti Aciliorum; Procopius calls one stretch of this, which was already leaning in antiquity, the “broken wall” (see: Horti Aciliorum). The stretch between the Porta Flaminia and the Porta Pinciana is from OpenStreetMap.

In Transtiberim (Region XIV) the wall was largely pulled down in the 17th century, and Pope Urban VIII built a new bastioned wall. Here the dashed line follows the course drawn on Lanciani's plates 27, 33 and 39 from the Porta Septimiana through the Porta Aurelia to the Porta Portuensis (±10 m).
Sanctuary of Isis and Serapis (?) – portico with pool
the known remains are from the 2nd century AD (brick stamps of AD 123); the cult is older than this
Isis et Serapis?
Find spot
at the eastern foot of the Oppian, between today's Via Poliziano (formerly Via Buonarroti) and Via Labicana
Size (de Vos)
terrace of 58 × 76 m with a portico of granite columns, and on its axis a pool at least 37 m long and 7 m wide
Other building
in the Vigna Reinach (between the Via R. Bonghi and the Via Labicana) a brick building of at least 130 × 40 m, with brick stamps of AD 123
Historia Augusta, Tyranni triginta 25.4
The house of Tetricus stood on the Caelian, “opposite the Iseum Metellinum” – this is the only ancient mention of the Metellan sanctuary of Isis.
Notitia and inscriptions
The name of Region III is “Isis et Serapis”; a street leading here may have been called “Ab Isis et Serapis” (CIL VI 2234, 32462).

The location of the sanctuary that gave the region its name is disputed; scholarship has proposed at least four placements. The most frequently cited of these is M. de Vos's proposal: the terrace with a portico and a long pool, found during road construction in 1885, was already drawn by Lanciani under the name “Tempio Egizio (Regio III) Isis et Serapis” on plate 30 of the Forma Urbis, and Ch. Häuber and F. X. Schütz also place the sanctuary here (FORTVNA Map 3, 2014). The map shows their outline, together with the building in the Vigna Reinach; FORTVNA also connects these with the forum of Petronius Maximus (5th century).

Other ideas: the old tradition placed it in the area of the church of Santi Pietro e Marcellino (an “Egyptian temple” was seen there in the 17th century), while Lafaye and Coarelli placed it on the summit of the Caelian, in the area of the Villa Mattei. Nor is it settled whether the sanctuary that gave the region its name is identical with the Iseum Metellinum.

The ruins of the central bath building still stand today: the domed caldarium, c. 35 m in diameter, the tepidarium, the frigidarium (basilica), the natatio (swimming pool) and the two palaestrae. On the sides of the enclosure there are exedrae; on the southwestern side, above the cisterns, a stepped, stadium-like area with a library hall at each end. In the system of underground corridors, in the northwestern part of the enclosure, was the largest known mithraeum in Rome.

The outline of the enclosure and of the central building comes from FORTVNA Map 7 (Häuber 2014). The wall remains are shown by the SITAR and OSM layers. Lanciani's plates 41 and 42 show the complete ground plan (the fit of plate 41 here is ±10–15 m).

No ancient author mentions the building by name. Its name and function are known from the building inscription still to be seen in the Capitoline Museums (CIL VI 1314) and from another inscription, now lost (CIL VI 1313). According to these, the consul Q. Lutatius Catulus had the “substructio”, that is, the substructure, and the “tabularium” built.

At the same time Catulus also directed the rebuilding of the Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus, which had burned down in 83 BC. Tacitus (Historiae 3.72) notes that his name could be read on the temple as well.

A huge substructure built of peperino and tufa, which closed off the saddle between the two summits of the Capitol toward the Forum. On the side facing the Forum ran an arcade articulated by Doric half-columns; a few of its arches can be seen today from the gallery of the Capitoline Museums.

In the 12th century the seat of the Roman commune was built on top of it; this became the Palazzo Senatorio, remodeled in the 16th century to Michelangelo's designs. Whether the building really was the state archive is disputed by some scholars; the name is known only from the inscription.

The temple was begun by Titus after the death of his father, Vespasian (AD 79), and completed by Domitian, who also included his elder brother, Titus, in the dedication. The 4th-century regionary catalog already mentions it as “templum Vespasiani et Titi”.
On the fragment of the architrave inscription the word [R]ESTITVER(unt) can still be read today: the temple was restored by Septimius Severus and Caracalla in the early 3rd century.

The narrow plot lay between the Tabularium and the Temple of Concord, so the stairway led up between the columns of the facade, cut into the podium. On the frieze of the three standing corner columns sacrificial implements (bull's skull, libation bowl, holy-water sprinkler, axe) can be seen.

In the early 19th century the columns stood half buried in the ground and were leaning; around 1811 Giuseppe Valadier and Giuseppe Camporese dismantled them and set them up again. A piece of the original cornice is on display in the gallery of the Tabularium.

According to Plutarch (Camillus 42), Camillus vowed the temple in 367 BC in memory of the reconciliation of the patricians and the plebeians. In 121 BC the consul L. Opimius had it rebuilt after the massacre of Gaius Gracchus and his followers; according to Plutarch (C. Gracchus 17), someone wrote beneath it at night: “a work of discord builds the Temple of Concord”.

On December 5, 63 BC the Senate met here when it decided the fate of Catiline's arrested associates; Cicero's fourth speech against Catiline was delivered here. The temple as rebuilt by Tiberius was dedicated on January 16, AD 10 (Ovid, Fasti 1.637–650; Cassius Dio 56.25).

The temple of Tiberius also served as a museum. Pliny (Nat. hist. 34–36) mentions numerous famous Greek statues and paintings in it; Augustus dedicated four obsidian elephants here (Nat. hist. 36.196).

Today only the concrete core of the podium stands; on the marble threshold of the cella a relief of a staff of Mercury (caduceus) can be seen. A piece of the cornice is in the gallery of the Tabularium.

According to Livy (1.33.8), King Ancus Marcius had the first prison built “in the middle of the city, towering above the Forum”. Varro (De lingua Latina 5.151) links the name Tullianum to King Servius Tullius.

Sallust (Catilina 55) describes it in detail: in the prison there is a place called the Tullianum, sunk about twelve feet below the ground, enclosed by walls, with a stone vault above it; its neglect, darkness and stench make it dreadful. Catiline's associates were executed here in 63 BC. Jugurtha, king of Numidia, died here (Plutarch, Marius 12), and Vercingetorix was executed here after Caesar's triumph (Cassius Dio 43.19).

Two rooms, one above the other. The lower, round chamber was built of tufa blocks; originally it may have been a cistern or a spring house. On the facade of the upper room, trapezoidal in ground plan, stands the inscription of the consuls C. Vibius Rufinus and M. Cocceius Nerva (early 1st century AD).

According to Christian tradition St Peter and St Paul were imprisoned here; this is why the place is also called the Mamertine Prison, and why the church of San Giuseppe dei Falegnami was built above it.

According to Varro (De re rustica 1.1.4), the gilded statues of the twelve “counseling gods”, six male and six female, stood in the Forum. The names of the twelve chief gods are listed in a line of verse by Ennius: Juno, Vesta, Minerva, Ceres, Diana, Venus, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Neptune, Vulcan, Apollo.

According to the inscription of AD 367 (CIL VI 102), the city prefect Vettius Agorius Praetextatus had the “sacred statues” restored together with the entire decoration of the place. Praetextatus was one of the leading figures of the late antique pagan aristocracy.
A portico with two wings meeting at an obtuse angle along the Clivus Capitolinus, with small rooms behind it, set against the substructure of the Tabularium.
It was re-erected by Luigi Canina in 1858; the missing columns were replaced in travertine, so the original and the new parts are clearly distinguishable.

According to Macrobius (Saturnalia 1.8), tritons stood on the pediment of the temple, and the feet of the statue of Saturn in the cella were bound with a woolen band, which was untied only at the festival of the Saturnalia. According to Pliny (Nat. hist. 15.32), the inside of the statue was filled with oil.

Plutarch (Roman Questions 42) discusses why it was precisely the Temple of Saturn that became the state treasury: in the golden age of Saturn there was no greed and no fraud. Besides the aerarium, the bronze tablets of the laws and the military standards were also kept here.

The podium of Plancus (42 BC) is a concrete core faced with travertine, with the chamber of the aerarium inside it. The eight columns standing today belong to a late antique (probably 4th-century) restoration: their shafts, of gray and pink granite, come from different buildings, and one of them was set up upside down.

The inscription that can be read on the frieze (SENATVS POPVLVSQVE ROMANVS INCENDIO CONSVMPTVM RESTITVIT) speaks of the restoration after the fire. The Vicus Iugarius ran in front of the temple, and the Clivus Capitolinus turned uphill beside the facade.
Tip: turn on the “Excavation data (SITAR)” layer and drag the year slider between 498 BC and AD 476: the early temple, the temple of Plancus, and then the temple after 283.

According to the inscription (CIL VI 1033), the Senate and the people set it up in AD 203 for Septimius Severus and his sons, Caracalla and Geta, for the restoration of the state and for the victories over the Parthians.

In 211 Caracalla had his younger brother, Geta, killed and ordered his memory to be erased. Geta's name and titles were chiseled out of the fourth line of the inscription, and in their place were put the words “optimis fortissimisque principibus” (to the most excellent and bravest rulers). The old text can still be read today from the fixing holes of the original bronze letters.

An arch with three openings, faced with marble. The four large relief panels show scenes from the two Parthian campaigns, probably including the siege of Ctesiphon. According to depictions on coins, the four-horse chariot of the emperor and his sons stood on top of it.
In the Middle Ages a church (Santi Sergio e Bacco) and houses were built against it, which is why it survived so intact. Near it was the old Volcanal, the shrine of Vulcan.

According to Cassius Dio (51.22), in 29 BC Augustus set up in the Curia the statue of Victoria brought from Tarentum and had an altar erected in front of it; the senators sacrificed on it before each session. The Altar of Victoria became the symbol of the religious disputes of late antiquity: Constantius II had it removed in 357, Julian restored it, and Gratian had it removed again in 382. In 384 the urban prefect Symmachus asked for its restoration in a famous speech (Relatio 3); Ambrose, bishop of Milan, opposed it.

Cicero (De finibus 5.2) still calls the old Hostilian building “our Curia.” The new building was begun by Caesar and completed by Augustus; Domitian had it rebuilt in AD 94, and Diocletian after the fire of 283.

The present building dates from the time of Diocletian and is built of brick; originally it was faced with marble below and stucco above. The interior hall measures 25.20 × 17.61 m; its floor is opus sectile laid in porphyry and green serpentine. The senators' seats stood on the low, broad steps running along both sides, and at the end was the platform of the presiding magistrate.

In 630 Pope Honorius I converted it into the church of Sant'Adriano, and this saved it. The original bronze doors were taken to the Lateran basilica around 1660; the present door is a copy. Between 1930 and 1937 the church was stripped back to its ancient state. Inside are displayed the “Trajanic reliefs” (Plutei Traiani), which also depict the buildings of the Forum.

Varro (De lingua Latina 5.155) derives the name from the verb “coire” (to come together): this is where the curiae assembled. According to Pliny (Nat. hist. 34.26), during the Samnite wars statues of Pythagoras and Alcibiades were set up at the corners of the Comitium, because the oracle of Delphi had asked for statues of the “wisest” and the “bravest” Greek; they were removed when Sulla built his Curia.

According to Livy (1.36), the razor and the whetstone with which the augur Attus Navius cut the stone in two before Tarquinius Priscus were buried here, and the statue of Navius also stood here. One of the traditions about the Ficus Ruminalis, the fig tree of Romulus and Remus, is also tied to this place (Tacitus, Annales 13.58).

Boni's excavations in the area in front of the Curia uncovered a long sequence of superimposed pavement levels, starting from the 7th century BC. These show that the assembly place was rebuilt several times before Caesar did away with it by relocating the Curia and the Rostra.

Its shape is disputed: earlier scholarship reconstructed a circular space on the model of the round, stepped comitia excavated at Paestum and Cosa, while the atlas of Carafa and Carandini draws an irregular quadrangle.

Under the entry “niger lapis,” that is, black stone, Festus writes that it marks an ill-omened spot in the Comitium: according to some the place of Romulus's death, according to others that of the shepherd Faustulus, who raised the boys, or of Hostus Hostilius, the grandfather of Tullus Hostilius.
According to Dionysius of Halicarnassus (1.87), Faustulus was buried at the most conspicuous point of the Forum, near the Rostra, and his tomb was marked by a stone lion.
In 1899, beneath the late Republican black marble paving, Boni found a U-shaped altar, a column stump and a four-sided stone pillar (cippus), with votive offerings around them (6th century BC).

The inscription on the cippus is an archaic Latin text written boustrophedon (in alternating directions); the words “sakros esed” (let him be sacred/accursed), “recei” (to the king), “kalatorem” (herald) and “iouxmenta” (draft animals) can be read in it. It appears to be a sacred regulation that also mentions the king; it is one of the earliest Latin inscriptions of Rome.
Several ancient traditions place the tomb or memorial of Romulus in the area of the Comitium, behind the Rostra (Festus; Dionysius 1.87). This is why the find of 2020 attracted so much attention.

The underground chamber, beneath the staircase of the Curia built in the 1930s, was presented by the Parco archeologico del Colosseo in February 2020. In it stand a tufa sarcophagus about 1.4 m long and, beside it, a cylindrical stone (perhaps an altar), from the 6th century BC.

Boni had already seen it in 1899–1900 and described it in his notes, but attached no importance to it. According to the archaeologists the sarcophagus is not a real tomb: it may have been a symbolic memorial that was deliberately preserved during later building works.

According to Livy (8.14), in 338 BC, after the defeat of the fleet of Antium, the bronze prows of the ships were nailed to the speakers' platform of the Comitium; hence the name Rostra (ships' prows). In 44 BC Caesar moved it to the western end of the Forum (Cassius Dio 43.49).

In 43 BC, at the time of the proscriptions, Cicero's severed head and hand were put on public display on the Rostra (Plutarch, Cicero 49; Appian 4.20). It was also from here that Mark Antony delivered his speech at Caesar's funeral.

The present remains are the platform of the time of Caesar and Augustus: about 24 m long and 3 m high, with the fixing holes of the bronze ships' prows visible on its front. The Rostra also appears on the Trajanic reliefs (Plutei Traiani), with the emperor delivering a speech on it.
Its northern end was lengthened with a brick extension in the 5th century AD; this is known as the Rostra Vandalica.
The 4th-century regionary catalogue mentions it as “umbilicum Romae,” that is, the navel of Rome: the symbolic center of the city, the counterpart of the gilded milestone.

The round, brick-faced core standing beside the Arch of Severus dates from the Severan period. Besides the traditional identification, some scholars also connect it with the old underworld shrine, the mundus.

According to Cassius Dio (54.8), in 20 BC, when he took on the supervision of the roads, Augustus had a gilded column set up bearing the distances to the major cities of Italy. According to Pliny (Nat. hist. 3.66), the extent of the city was measured from this milestone “standing at the head of the Forum.”
According to Plutarch (Galba 24) and Tacitus (Historiae 1.27), in AD 69 Otho met the praetorians at the gilded milestone, near the Temple of Saturn, and they proclaimed him emperor.

Its exact location is not known for certain. It is placed between the southern end of the Rostra and the Temple of Saturn; fragments of an ornate marble base were found nearby and are identified with it.
According to Tacitus (Annales 2.41), in AD 16 an arch was erected beside the Temple of Saturn to commemorate Germanicus's recovery of the military standards lost in the Varus battle (AD 9).

Only its foundations have been found, at the northwest corner of the Basilica Iulia, above the Vicus Iugarius. On the relief of the Arch of Constantine depicting the Forum (the emperor's speech from the Rostra), the Arch of Severus and the Arch of Tiberius can be seen on either side of the Rostra.

According to Livy (44.16), in 169 BC Ti. Sempronius Gracchus had the Basilica Sempronia built on its site, in place of the house of Scipio Africanus and the shops behind it. Caesar began it in 54 BC and Augustus completed it; after it burned down, he had it rebuilt on a larger scale in the name of his adopted sons, Gaius and Lucius (Res Gestae 20); it was dedicated in AD 12 (Cassius Dio 56.27).

The four panels of the court of the hundred (centumviri) sat here. According to Quintilian (12.5.6), the voice of the orator Trachalus was so powerful that he was heard in all four panels. Pliny the Younger (Letters 6.33) describes how the hearing of an inheritance case was followed by a jostling crowd even from the upper galleries.

After the fire of 283 Diocletian had it rebuilt; in 377 the urban prefect Gabinius Vettius Probianus adorned it with statues, as recorded by inscriptions on their bases. Fragments of the Marble Plan also depict it.

The game boards scratched into the steps and the floor are traces of those who waited during breaks in the hearings. Today only the floor, the bases of the piers and a few re-erected piers can be seen; in the Middle Ages it was a stone quarry and a lime-burning site.

According to Livy (40.51), it was built in 179 BC by the censors M. Aemilius Lepidus and M. Fulvius Nobilior. According to Plutarch (Caesar 29), Caesar gave fifteen hundred talents to L. Aemilius Paullus, who used them to rebuild the famous basilica; it was dedicated in 34 BC (Cassius Dio 49.42).

It burned down in 14 BC and Augustus had it rebuilt (Cassius Dio 54.24); according to Tacitus (Annales 3.72), in AD 22 M. Lepidus restored the building of his ancestors at his own expense. Pliny (Nat. hist. 36.102) counts it among the most beautiful buildings in the world because of its columns of Phrygian marble.

In front of the basilica, toward the Forum, ran a row of shops (tabernae novae) and a portico erected in honor of Gaius and Lucius Caesar; a fragment of the dedicatory inscription has been found. From the interior frieze, fragments survive of reliefs depicting the early legends of Rome (the rape of the Sabine women, the punishment of Tarpeia).
It burned down in AD 410, during the sack by Alaric's Goths: the bronze coins melted into the floor can still be seen today.

According to Pliny (Nat. hist. 15.119), the Romans and the Sabines purified themselves with myrtle branches at this spot after the war, which is why it is the shrine of Venus Cloacina (Cluacina, the purifier). According to Livy (3.48), it was here, near the tabernae, that Verginius killed his daughter so that the decemvir Appius Claudius could not make her his slave.

A round marble base in front of the steps of the Basilica Aemilia; a denarius of L. Mussidius Longus of 42 BC depicts it with two statues of goddesses and a balustrade. The Cloaca Maxima entered the area of the Forum nearby.

According to the inscription (CIL VI 1200), in AD 608 Smaragdus, exarch of Ravenna, had a gilded statue of the Byzantine emperor Phocas set up on top of the column. It was Phocas who gave the Pantheon to Pope Boniface IV, who consecrated it as a church.

The last ancient monument of the Forum. The 13.6 m Corinthian column was taken from a 2nd-century building; the stepped base was built around it later. It was excavated in the 1810s, when the inscription was identified.

Varro (De lingua Latina 5.148–150) gives three explanations: the horse of the Sabine warrior Mettius Curtius sank into the marsh here; the young Marcus Curtius leaped into the chasm that had opened here; or the consul C. Curtius fenced off the spot struck by lightning. Livy (1.13) tells the Sabine version, and elsewhere (7.6) the self-sacrifice of Marcus Curtius: according to the soothsayers the chasm would close only if Rome's greatest treasure were sacrificed, and according to Curtius this was valor in arms.

According to Suetonius (Augustus 57), every year the people threw coins into the Lacus Curtius for the health of Augustus. According to Pliny (Nat. hist. 15.78), a fig tree, an olive tree and a vine grew beside it.

An irregular depression in the paving of the square, bordered by stone slabs, with several building phases. The original of the marble relief depicting the mounted Mettius Curtius is in the Capitoline Museums; a copy can be seen on the site.

Statius (Silvae 1.1) glorifies in a long poem the colossal bronze equestrian statue standing in the middle of the Forum: the horse's hoof rested on a defeated personification of the Rhine, and the emperor held Minerva. The statue was removed after Domitian's murder in AD 96 and the erasure of his memory.

Around 1903 Boni uncovered the large concrete foundation in the middle of the square, which he identified with the equestrian statue. The Carandini–Carafa atlas identifies the same spot with the Doliola, an archaic sacred place; according to Varro (De lingua Latina 5.157), the Doliola was a place beside the Cloaca Maxima where spitting was forbidden. The identification is therefore an open question.

According to Suetonius (Iulius 84–85), the people spontaneously cremated Caesar's body in the Forum and set up a column on the spot with the inscription “Parenti patriae” (to the father of the fatherland). According to Appian (2.148) and Cassius Dio (47.18), the triumvirs decided on the temple in 42 BC. According to Dio (51.19), the platform at its front was decorated with the prows of the ships captured in the battle of Actium.

According to Pliny (Nat. hist. 2.94), the comet that appeared during Caesar's festival games (sidus Iulium) was venerated as the sign of Caesar's deification; for this reason Augustus had a star placed on the head of Caesar's statue. According to Pliny (35.91), Augustus placed in the temple the famous painting by Apelles, Venus rising from the sea.

The first temple in Rome dedicated to a deified human being. Today the concrete core of the podium and the semicircular niche in front of the facade can be seen, with the base of a round altar in it; according to tradition this was the place of the cremation.
On March 15, the anniversary of Caesar's death, flowers are still laid on the altar today.

According to Cassius Dio, the Senate voted Augustus an arch in 29 BC for the victory at Actium (51.19), and in 19 BC for the military standards recovered from the Parthians (54.8). A denarius of the Augustan period depicts an arch with three openings.

Between the Temple of Divus Iulius and the Temple of Castor the foundations of an arch with three openings were found. According to Coarelli's hypothesis, the Fasti consulares and triumphales, the lists of the consuls and of the triumphs (now in the Capitoline Museums), were carved on this arch; according to others they stood on the wall of the Regia.

According to Livy (2.20, 2.42), the dictator A. Postumius vowed it at the battle of Lake Regillus, and his son dedicated it in 484 BC. According to Dionysius (6.13), after the battle two young horsemen appeared in the Forum, watered their horses at the spring of Juturna, announced the victory and vanished.

In 117 BC L. Caecilius Metellus Dalmaticus had it rebuilt; in 73 BC Verres supervised its repair, and Cicero (In Verrem 2.1.129–154) exposes in detail his frauds involving the columns. According to Suetonius (Caligula 22), Caligula extended his palace as far as the temple and called the twins his own doorkeepers.

The three standing columns (12.50 m high, 1.45 m in diameter) belong to the temple of Tiberius, dedicated in AD 6. The podium was articulated by walls projecting at the sides, with chambers fitted with metal doors between them: these were used as strongrooms, and the office for verifying weights and measures also operated here; the inscription “ad Castoris” can be read on weights that have been found.

The building was excavated between 1983 and 1989 by a joint mission of the Scandinavian academies and published in several volumes. A speakers' platform (tribunal) stood in front of the facade; the excavations revealed two side staircases.

Tip: turn on the “Excavation data (SITAR)” layer and drag the year slider between 500 BC and AD 400: the four building phases of the temple (from the temple of 484 BC to the temple of Tiberius) can be seen one after another.

Ovid (Fasti 1.705–708) places the shrine of the nymph Juturna beside the temple of the Dioscuri. Varro (De lingua Latina 5.71) derives the nymph's name from the verb “iuvare” (to help), because her water healed. According to Dionysius (6.13), this is where the Dioscuri watered their horses.

In 1900 Boni excavated the rectangular, marble-lined basin with a base in its center; fragments of the marble statues of the Dioscuri were found in the basin. Beside it stand the small shrine (aedicula) of Juturna and an altar with reliefs.
In the 4th century the city's water office (statio aquarum) operated nearby, as recorded by inscriptions.

According to Livy (5.39–40), at the time of the Gallic invasion (390 BC) the Vestal Virgins carried the sacred objects to safety out of the city. According to Livy (26.27), in 210 BC thirteen slaves rescued the sacred objects from the fire that devastated the Forum. According to Dionysius (2.66), the round shape of the temple is ancient, and the sacred objects may be seen by no one but the virgins.

According to Ovid (Fasti 6.257–282), there is no statue of the deity in the temple, only the eternal fire, because Vesta is the blazing Earth itself. The fire was renewed every year on March 1. The cult was abolished by the decrees of Theodosius I at the end of the 4th century.

The round foundation is 15.05 m in diameter. In the middle of the podium there is a trapezoidal shaft about 5 m deep; this may have been the penus, the hidden repository of the sacred objects. The marble temple was surrounded by twenty Corinthian columns with a metal grille between them; the roof was conical, with a smoke vent in the center.
The temple was demolished in 1549, and its stones were used for lime and as building material. In 1930 one section of it was partially re-erected from the pieces that had been found.
Tip: turn on the “Excavation data (SITAR)” layer and drag the year slider from 600 BC to AD 394: the archaic, Republican and Severan phases of the temple.

According to Plutarch (Numa 13), the shield of Mars that fell from the sky (ancile) and the eleven copies made to deceive were kept here. According to Aulus Gellius (4.6), if the spears of Mars kept in the Regia moved of their own accord, it was an ill omen, and the Senate ordered an expiatory sacrifice. According to Varro (De lingua Latina 6.21), the shrine of Ops Consiva was in the Regia, and only the Vestal Virgins and one priest were allowed to enter it.
The office of the pontifex maximus operated here, and the annals (annales maximi) were kept here. According to Cassius Dio (48.42), Cn. Domitius Calvinus had it rebuilt in marble in 36 BC.

It was excavated by Boni in 1899 and then by Frank E. Brown (American Academy) in the 1960s; they identified phases built one on top of another from the late 7th century BC onward, and the irregular, trapezoidal ground plan was retained throughout.
Whether the lists of the consuls and triumphs (Fasti) stood on the marble walls is disputed; according to Coarelli they were on the Arch of Augustus.

Tip: turn on the “Excavation data (SITAR)” layer and drag the year slider between 625 and 510 BC: the six archaic building phases of the Regia appear one after another in the excavators' reconstruction, followed by the Republican building and the one after 36 BC.

According to Gellius (1.12) and Plutarch (Numa 10), the Vestal Virgins were chosen between the ages of six and ten and served for thirty years: for ten years they learned, for ten years they served, and for ten years they taught. If one of them broke her vow of chastity, she was buried alive in the Campus Sceleratus beside the Porta Collina.

Among their privileges were that they could dispose freely of their property, were accompanied by a lictor, and had a seat of honor in the theater. They also kept wills in their custody: according to Suetonius (Augustus 101), the will of Augustus too was deposited with them.

The house was built after the fire of AD 64 and was later enlarged several times; two-story wings surrounded the colonnaded courtyard adorned with pools. In the courtyard stand statues of the chief priestesses (virgo Vestalis maxima) on inscribed bases, from the 3rd–4th centuries.

From one base, dated 364, the name was chiseled out; according to tradition it belonged to a chief priestess who became a Christian. The house was excavated by Lanciani in 1883–1884. Beneath its eastern part lie the remains of the Republican-era Domus Publica.

Tip: turn on the “Excavation data (SITAR)” layer and drag the year slider from 600 BC: the archaic and Republican predecessors of the House of the Vestal Virgins, then the phases of the imperial-era house.
According to Suetonius (Iulius 46), Caesar first lived in a modest house in the Subura, and after his election as pontifex maximus (63 BC) on the Sacra Via, in the state house (domus publica).

According to Cassius Dio (54.27), when Augustus became pontifex maximus in 12 BC, he gave the Domus Publica to the Vestal Virgins and himself remained on the Palatine, where he made part of his house state property.

The excavations of Carandini and his colleagues beneath the eastern part of the House of the Vestal Virgins, along the Summa Sacra via, uncovered a large Republican-era house with a peristyle, which is identified with the Domus Publica. Formerly the remains beneath the western part of the house were taken to be it; the identification is still not final.

According to the Historia Augusta (Antoninus Pius 6.7), after Faustina's death (AD 141) the Senate deified her and voted her a temple, with priestesses and statues. After the death of Antoninus Pius (161) the temple was rededicated with him included as well; the second line of the inscription was carved above the first at that time.

It survived because between the 7th and 11th centuries it was converted into the church of San Lorenzo in Miranda; the present Baroque facade was made in 1602. In 1536, for the entry of Emperor Charles V into Rome, the medieval buildings in front of the temple were demolished.

The church door now hovers above the staircase, because the level of the ancient Sacra Via lies 12 m lower than the medieval ground level; the staircase was excavated only in the 19th century. The deep grooves visible on the cipollino columns are probably the traces of a failed medieval attempt at demolition.

The ancient writers knew nothing of the cemetery in the Forum valley. Roman law (the Twelve Tables) forbade burial within the city, so the find shows that in the 10th–8th centuries BC this area still lay outside the settlement.

Boni excavated it between 1902 and 1905 in the deep excavation beside the Temple of Antoninus and Faustina. Cremation and inhumation graves came to light, among them house-shaped urns that imitate the huts of the time; the finds can be seen in the Antiquarium Forense. The valley was paved as a public square only after it was drained, in the late 7th century BC.

On the commemorative coins of Romulus (DIVO ROMVLO), the son of Maxentius who died in 309, a domed building can be seen. This is why the traditional identification takes this building to be the Temple of Romulus; the building on the coins, however, may rather be the tomb beside the Via Appia.

A round, domed brick building, flanked on both sides by apsed halls. Its entrance is framed by two porphyry columns, and the 4th-century bronze door, with its original lock, is still in place today. Its identification is disputed: some scholars take it to be the shrine of Jupiter Stator or of the Penates, others the vestibule of the city prefecture.

In 527 Pope Felix IV converted the hall behind it, which belonged to the Temple of Peace, into the church of Santi Cosma e Damiano, whose apse mosaic is one of the masterpieces of early Christian art; the round building became its vestibule.

According to Aurelius Victor (40.26), everything that Maxentius had built, the basilica among them, was dedicated by the Senate to the merits of Constantine after the Battle of the Milvian Bridge in 312. The 4th-century regionary catalogue mentions it as “basilicam Constantinianam”.

The largest vaulted hall of ancient Rome: the cross vault of the nave spanned at a height of c. 35 m, on eight giant marble columns. Constantine changed its orientation: it was given a new entrance from the Sacra Via and a new apse on the north side.

In the western apse stood the colossal acrolithic statue of Constantine; its head, hand and foot were found in 1486–87 and are now in the courtyard of the Capitoline Museums. The last standing column was moved by Pope Paul V in 1614 to the front of Santa Maria Maggiore. Today only the three barrel vaults of the north aisle stand.

The inscription (CIL VI 945): “Senatus populusque Romanus divo Tito divi Vespasiani f(ilio) Vespasiano Augusto”: the arch was erected after the death of Titus (81). Josephus (Jewish War 7.148–150) describes the triumph of 71, in which the treasures of the Temple of Jerusalem, the golden table, the seven-branched lampstand and the scroll of the Torah, were also carried in procession.

The two reliefs of the passageway show the triumph: on one the Temple treasures are being carried, among them the menorah, on the other Titus stands in a four-horse chariot. In the center of the vault Titus rises among the gods on the back of an eagle.

In the Middle Ages it was built into the fortress of the Frangipani family. Giuseppe Valadier freed it in 1821 and completed it in travertine; the additions are deliberately plainer, so the original marble parts can be clearly distinguished.
The 4th-century regionary catalogue mentions it in Region VIII as “horrea Germaniciana et Agrippiana”; it was named after Agrippa, the son-in-law and general of Augustus.

A three-story warehouse building around a courtyard along the Vicus Tuscus, with travertine and tufa walls and rooms opening onto the courtyard. In the courtyard an inscription addressed to the genius of the warehouses came to light. The detailed ground plan of the Carandini–Carafa atlas also shows it this way.
It is mentioned in the papal biographies of the 6th–8th centuries (Liber Pontificalis); Pope John VII (705–707) decorated it, and some of its frescoes were made at that time.

It was set up in the 6th century in a hall of a Domitianic building complex leading toward the Palatine. In 847 an earthquake buried it; Santa Maria Nova was built in its place. Above it Santa Maria Liberatrice was built in 1617, which was demolished in 1900 so that it could be excavated.

Its frescoes from the 6th–8th centuries have survived in exceptional condition; on the so-called palimpsest wall several layers painted one over another can be seen. It has been open to visitors since 2016.

According to Suetonius (Caligula 21–22), Tiberius began it and Caligula completed it, and Caligula had a bridge thrown over the temple so that he could get from the Palatine to the Capitol. Martial and Suetonius also mention it as “templum novum”, the new temple.
It appears on the coins of Caligula (37) and Antoninus Pius (c. 158); Antoninus restored it. From these we know that it was of the Ionic order; its size and exact location are not known.

There are two main hypotheses about its location: the unexcavated area behind the Basilica Iulia (this is followed by the map and the Carandini–Carafa atlas), and the large Domitianic hall behind the Temple of Castor (Lanciani's identification). The hall is now generally thought to have had a different function.

According to Livy (39.44), Cato as censor in 184 BC bought up two private houses and four shops beside the Lautumiae and had a basilica built there. According to Plutarch (Cato minor 5), the tribunes of the plebs held their sessions here, and they also argued about removing a column that was in the way.
According to Asconius (commentary on the Pro Milone), in 52 BC it burned down together with the Curia from the pyre of Clodius's corpse.
The first basilica in Rome, but its remains have not been identified. The map follows the reconstruction of the Carandini–Carafa atlas (Tab. 21).

According to Livy (1.30) and Varro (De lingua Latina 5.155), it was built by King Tullus Hostilius and was named after him. Sulla enlarged it c. 80 BC. Cicero (De finibus 5.2) still calls this one “our Curia”, distinguishing it from the new one.

In 52 BC it burned down from the funeral pyre of Clodius; Faustus Sulla rebuilt it (Curia Cornelia), but Caesar had this demolished in order to build a temple on its site and a new Senate house on the site of the Curia Iulia (Cassius Dio 44.5).
Its remains have not been identified with certainty. The map follows the reconstruction of the Carandini–Carafa atlas (Tab. 21): north of the Comitium, west of the present Curia Iulia.

According to Livy (1.19), Numa built it at the foot of the Argiletum: its gate stood open in war and closed in peace. According to Augustus (Res Gestae 13), since the founding of Rome it had been closed only twice, and under his principate three times.
According to Procopius (Gothic War 1.25), the bronze shrine was still standing in the 6th century, and in 537, during the Gothic siege, someone secretly opened its gate.
A small bronze gate shrine, depicted on the coins of Nero. Its location is to be sought at the beginning of the street between the Curia and the Basilica Aemilia, but no trace of it has been found.

According to Livy (8.14), the prows of the ships of Antium captured in 338 BC were nailed to this platform standing at the edge of the Comitium. From here speakers addressed the popular assembly, at first facing the Comitium, later the Forum.
Its remains can be identified among the paving layers of the Comitium, near the Lapis Niger. Its outline is the reconstruction of the Carandini–Carafa atlas.

According to Livy (44.16), Ti. Sempronius Gracchus had the Basilica Sempronia built in 169 BC on the site of the houses behind the old shops (veteres). Plautus (Curculio 480) places the moneylenders below the old shops.

The row of shops and columns running along the south side of the Forum was the place of the money changers (argentarii); it disappeared when the Basilica Iulia was built. Its outline is the reconstruction of the Carandini–Carafa atlas (Tab. 21).
The columns are not mentioned by the ancient authors; their 4th-century inscriptions have largely been lost.

The brick-cored bases were faced with marble, and statues stood on top of the columns; along the Sacra Via, in front of the Basilica Iulia, they formed a spectacular row. Two were re-erected in the 19th century. The Carandini–Carafa atlas marks them as numbers VIII 17–23.
Ammianus Marcellinus (16.10) describes the visit of Constantius II to Rome in 357; at that time and afterward several statues were set up in his honor in the Forum.
The location of the base is OpenStreetMap data. In this area the Carandini–Carafa atlas marks the equestrian statue of Constantine (Equus Constantini); whether the two are the same cannot be decided.

Cicero (Ad Atticum 4.16.8) writes in 54 BC that he and his friends are buying up the plots for Caesar's monument for sixty million sesterces. According to Suetonius (Iulius 26), the price of the land in the end came to more than one hundred million sesterces.
According to Suetonius (Iulius 61) and Pliny (Nat. hist. 8.155), in front of the temple stood a statue of Caesar's favorite horse, whose hooves resembled human toes.

The forum was rebuilt by Trajan in 113 and restored by Diocletian after the fire of 283. The temple and most of the square were excavated in 1930–1932, during the construction of the Via dell'Impero; after 1998 further parts of the square were excavated as well, right down to the Iron Age layers.
On the west side of the square a row of shops (tabernae) survives, with the slope of the Capitol behind them.
Tip: turn on the “Excavation data (SITAR)” layer and drag the year slider between 54 BC and AD 283: the first phase of the Forum of Caesar, of 54–43 BC, and its second, post-Augustan phase.

According to Appian (2.68, 2.102), Caesar vowed the temple before the battle of Pharsalus, and beside Venus Genetrix, the ancestress of the Julian clan, he had a gilded statue of Cleopatra set up. According to Pliny, Caesar dedicated here six collections of engraved gems (37.11) and two paintings by Timomachus, Ajax and Medea (35.136).
The high podium and three columns from the Trajanic rebuilding, which were re-erected in the 1930s. The richly carved fragments of the cornice can be seen on site.
The 4th-century regionary catalogue mentions it in Region VIII as “basilicam argentariam”.
The colonnaded hall between the Forum of Caesar and the slope of the Capitol, of Trajanic date. It was named after the money changers (argentarii).

In the Res Gestae (35) Augustus also mentions that, by decree of the Senate, the title “Pater patriae” (father of the fatherland) was inscribed in the forum beneath his statue in a four-horse chariot. According to Suetonius (Augustus 29), criminal trials were held in the forum, and here boys put on the toga of manhood.
According to Ovid (Fasti 5.563–566), in the porticoes stood the statues of Aeneas, the ancestor of the Julii, and of Romulus, the founder of Rome, surrounded by the statues of the great Romans.

Toward the Subura it was closed off by a high firewall built of peperino and Gabine stone, which still stands today; one of its gates is the Arco dei Pantani. In the Middle Ages the house of the Knights of Rhodes (Casa dei Cavalieri di Rodi) was built into it, and this can still be seen today.

The statues stood in the wall niches of the exedras, with the elogia inscriptions beneath them, fragments of which have come to light. The square was excavated in the 1920s–30s, and further parts of it after 1998.

According to Suetonius (Augustus 29), Augustus vowed it at the battle of Philippi (42 BC), for the vengeance to be taken on Caesar's murderers (ultor = avenger). According to Cassius Dio (55.10), it was dedicated in 2 BC, and from then on it was here that the Senate decided on war and triumph.

A Corinthian temple with an eight-column facade and a colonnade along the sides; its rear wall abutted the firewall. Today the podium, the remains of the staircase and three columns of the right side stand. In the cella stood statues of Mars, Venus and perhaps the deified Caesar.

At the rear wall of the hall in the north corner of the forum, the base of a colossal statue, estimated at c. 11–12 m in height, survives. Whom it depicted (perhaps the genius of Augustus) is disputed.

According to Suetonius (Domitianus 5), Domitian began it, and it is already called the “Forum of Nerva”. According to the Historia Augusta (Alexander Severus 28), Alexander Severus had colossal statues set up here to the deified emperors.

The walls of the narrow square were decorated with closely spaced columns placed near the wall; the only standing section of this is the Colonnacce. Part of the square lies beneath the Via dei Fori Imperiali.
According to Suetonius (Domitianus 15), Domitian especially venerated Minerva, which is why she was given a temple in the forum.

The temple stood in good condition until the early 17th century and is clearly visible in old drawings too. Pope Paul V had it demolished in 1606, and its stones were used for the monumental fountain of the Acqua Paola. Today only the core of the podium is visible.
Ovid (Metamorphoses 6.1–145) tells the story of Arachne, who dared to compete with Minerva in weaving and whom the goddess turned into a spider; the frieze depicts this myth.

The only standing section of the decorative wall of the Forum of Nerva, with two Corinthian columns. On the frieze weaving and the punishment of Arachne can be seen, on the attic the figure of Minerva.

According to Pliny (Nat. hist. 34.84), Vespasian placed here the famous Greek works of art that Nero had collected in the Golden House. Galen (On the Avoidance of Grief) complains that in the fire of 192 his books and medicines kept near the Temple of Peace were burned; according to Herodian (1.14), the fire destroyed the temple as well.

Ammianus Marcellinus (16.10), in connection with the visit to Rome in 357, counts it among the wonders of the city; according to Procopius (Gothic War 4.21), works by Phidias and Lysippus were still standing in front of the temple in the 6th century.

The fragments of the Marble Plan of the city came to light from 1562 onward behind Santi Cosma e Damiano; today they are kept by the city of Rome. The Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae project has also published the fragments online.
The excavations of 1998–2000 uncovered the rows of the garden's planting beds and part of the porticoes; most of the square now lies beneath the Via dei Fori Imperiali and the Via Cavour.

According to Cassius Dio (69.4), the forum was designed by Apollodorus of Damascus; Hadrian later hated him because Apollodorus had mocked his designs. According to Gellius (11.17), old praetorian edicts were kept in the “library of the Temple of Trajan”.
