The forum remained one of the wonders of the city in late antiquity as well: according to a 6th-century poem by Venantius Fortunatus, readings and recitals of Virgil were still being held here even then.

In the center of the square stood the equestrian statue of Trajan, with exedras on the two sides of the forum. The entrance side was adorned with a triumphal arch, which is also depicted on coins. Corrado Ricci carried out large excavations here between 1928 and 1934, Roberto Meneghini between 1998 and 2007.
On the basis of Meneghini's excavations it is disputed whether the Temple of Trajan really stood at the north end of the square, or whether there was a monumental entrance there.

The building complex was freed from later construction and restored by Corrado Ricci in the 1920s–30s. The medieval name of the street running inside it is Via Biberatica. Above it stands the 13th-century Torre delle Milizie. Since 2007 it has housed the Museum of the Imperial Forums.
It is depicted on the coins of Trajan with the legend “BASILICA VLPIA”; it was named after Trajan's clan name, the Ulpii.

An apse at each end, a double colonnade running around the interior, and the facade facing the forum. According to some scholars, the Atrium Libertatis, the place where slaves were freed, operated in one of the apses. Some of the gray granite columns of the nave were re-erected in the 1930s.

According to the inscription on the base (CIL VI 960), the column shows how high the hill and the area were that were carried away for the building of the forum. According to Cassius Dio (68.16), it was made as both a grave marker and a monument; according to Eutropius (8.5), Trajan's ashes were placed beneath the column in a golden urn.

The spiraling band of relief shows the two Dacian wars: army movements, construction, battles, the death of Decebalus. Inside, a spiral staircase leads up; the small windows light it. In the Middle Ages, in 1162, the Roman Senate forbade damaging it on pain of death.
In 1587 Pope Sixtus V had a statue of St Peter placed on top of it. A plaster cast of it can be seen in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London.

According to Ammianus Marcellinus (16.10.15–16), Constantius II in 357 admired the equestrian statue standing in the middle of the forum and wanted to have a similar one made; the Persian prince Hormisdas replied that he would first have to build a stable like this for the horse.
A large foundation excavated in the middle of the square, which the more recent excavations identify with the equestrian statue. Its location is taken from OpenStreetMap data.
According to Aurelius Victor (14.3), Hadrian founded a school for the liberal arts, which was called the Athenaeum.

They came to light under Piazza Venezia in 2008–2009, during the construction of Metro Line C: three large halls with stepped, marble-clad seating, for lectures and recitations. The identification with the Athenaeum is a hypothesis.

According to the inscription on the facade of the tomb (CIL VI 1319), by decree of the Senate and order of the people, C. Poplicius Bibulus, plebeian aedile, was granted the burial place at public expense for his merits, for himself and his descendants.

The tomb stood at the beginning of the Via Flaminia, outside the boundary of the Republican-era city; the travertine-faced part of its facade can still be seen today at the northern foot of the Capitol.
The circus procession

The festive procession before the chariot races (pompa circensis) went from the Capitol through the Forum to the Circus Maximus. The most detailed description is given by Dionysius of Halicarnassus (Roman Antiquities 7.72), who lived in Rome in the time of Augustus and cites Fabius Pictor of the 3rd century BC.

Dionysius says only this much about the route: that it led “from the Capitol through the Forum to the Circus Maximus”; the section in between is supplied by a remark of Cicero. Where there is evidence, the line follows the known ancient streets; exactly which way the procession went we know only where the text tells us.
Setting out from the Capitol

The procession set out from in front of the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus. The emblems of the gods were carried on sacred wagons (tensae), which were kept on the Capitol. According to Cicero, the boy leading the wagon, whose father and mother were both alive, had to hold the reins the whole way: if he let go, the games were considered invalid and had to be repeated (De haruspicum responso 23).

At the head of the procession went the magistrate presiding over the games. In Juvenal's mocking picture, the praetor stands on the high chariot in the tunic of Jupiter and an embroidered toga, while a slave holds the heavy wreath above his head (10.36–42). The dress was that of a general celebrating a triumph, and the routes of the two processions were also partly the same, only in opposite directions: the triumph arrived at the Capitol, the circus procession set out from it.
Down the slope of the Capitol

The procession descended to the Forum on the Clivus Capitolinus, beside the Temple of Saturn. According to Dionysius, the adolescent boys went in front: those whose fathers had the property of a knight on horseback, the others on foot, arranged in troops, “as if they were going to school.” In this way, he writes, strangers could see how numerous and how fine the city's rising youth was (7.72.1).

They were followed by the competitors: the drivers of the four-horse and two-horse chariots and the riders of the unsaddled horses, and after them the athletes, who marched naked except for a loincloth. Dionysius singles out this detail because he means it as proof: with the whole description he wants to show that the customs of the Romans are of Greek origin (7.72.2–4).
In the Forum and on the Vicus Tuscus

From the Forum the procession turned beside the Temple of Castor and Pollux into the Vicus Tuscus, the street of the Etruscans. We know this from Cicero: in his speech against Verres he asks whether there is anyone who walks all the way from the statue of Vertumnus to the Circus Maximus without seeing a trace of Verres's greed at every step, since he was also the one who contracted out the maintenance of the route of the sacred wagons and the procession (In Verrem 2.1.154). The statue of Vertumnus stood on the Vicus Tuscus (Propertius 4.2).

Here marched the dancers in three groups: men, youths and boys, accompanied by flute players and lyre players. They wore scarlet tunics with bronze belts, a sword at their side and a short spear in their hand; on the men's heads were plumed, crested bronze helmets. They performed a war dance to a fast, martial rhythm (7.72.5–9).
In the Velabrum

The Vicus Tuscus led through the Velabrum valley toward the Tiber. The four-way arch is much later (4th century) and did not yet stand at the time of the processions, but it roughly marks the place where the valley opened onto the cattle market.

After the armed dancers came the jesters: dancers dressed as silenoi and satyrs, in shaggy tunics, with garlands of flowers, goatskins and manes standing on end on their heads. They imitated and mocked the solemn movements of those going before them. Dionysius adds that he saw the same kind of mocking dancers in the funeral processions of distinguished Romans as well, in front of the bier (7.72.10–12).
In the cattle market

The procession reached the starting gates of the circus through the Forum Boarium. The round temple is the Temple of Hercules; nearby stood the ancient altar of Hercules, the Ara Maxima, as well. According to Pliny, an old statue of Hercules stood in the square, which was dressed in triumphal costume at the time of triumphs (Naturalis historia 34.33).

At the end of the procession the gods were brought. First went lyre players and flute players, then the bearers of censers, who burned frankincense and perfumes, and after them the bearers of the sacred vessels of gold and silver. Last of all came the images of the gods on men's shoulders: Jupiter, Juno, Minerva, Neptune and the rest, in the form and with the emblems, Dionysius writes, in which the Greeks depict them (7.72.13).
Arrival at the Circus Maximus

The procession entered the track from the side of the starting gates and passed along its whole length in front of the spectators. Ovid describes it from the stands: Victoria in front with outspread wings, then Neptune, Mars, Apollo, Minerva, Ceres, Bacchus, the Dioscuri and Venus, each applauded by its own devotees (Amores 3.2.43–58). In 45 BC an ivory statue of Caesar was also carried among the gods; Cicero remarks that “because of the bad neighbor” the people did not applaud even Victoria (Ad Atticum 13.44).

The gods were placed on the pulvinar, the box of honor; Augustus lists this among his own building works (Res Gestae 19). The consuls and the priests sacrificed oxen, and only then did the races begin (Dionysius 7.72.15).

According to Dionysius, the circus held 150,000 spectators (3.68). The last known races were held here by Totila, king of the Goths, in 550.
The conspiracy of Catiline (63 BC)

Lucius Sergius Catilina, an impoverished patrician, organized an armed seizure of power after his defeat in the consular election. The consul, Marcus Tullius Cicero, exposed him and had five of his associates executed. The story is told by Cicero's four speeches against Catiline, Sallust's book (The Conspiracy of Catiline) and Plutarch's Life of Cicero.

Of the sites of the events, the Tullianum can still be visited today. Where there is evidence, the line follows the known ancient streets; the sources rarely give the exact routes of the people involved.
Consular election on the Campus Martius

The elections were held on the Campus Martius, in the voting enclosure (Ovile); the Saepta Iulia was later built on its site. Catiline was standing for the consulship for the year 62 BC, and promised the cancellation of debts.

Cicero, who presided over the election, reportedly feared an assassination attempt. By his own account he went down to the Campus with a strong escort, and under his toga he wore a broad, conspicuous breastplate: not because it would have protected him, since he knew that Catiline usually aimed at the head and the neck, but so that the good citizens would see that the consul was in danger (Pro Murena 52; Plutarch, Cicero 14).

Catiline lost. After this he decided on an uprising; in Etruria Gaius Manlius was raising an army for him. On October 21 the Senate gave the consuls emergency powers (Sallust 29).
The first speech: the Temple of Jupiter Stator

On November 8 (by another reckoning the 7th) Cicero convened the Senate not in the Curia but in the Temple of Jupiter Stator; at the beginning of the speech he himself mentions that the place is heavily guarded. At dawn the day before, two conspirators had tried to get into his house on the pretext of the morning greeting in order to kill him, but they were not let in (In Catilinam 1.9–10; Sallust 28).

Catiline appeared at the session nevertheless. According to Cicero, when he sat down, those sitting next to him stood up and left the bench around him empty (1.16). It was then that the most famous opening sentence of Latin oratory was spoken: “How long, Catiline, will you go on abusing our patience?”

According to Sallust, Catiline answered that Cicero was a mere newcomer in the city, and when he was shouted down, he cried out: “If they set me ablaze, I will put out the fire with ruins” (31). That same night he left Rome.

The location of the temple on the map is uncertain.
The second speech: the Rostra

The next day Cicero spoke to the people from the speakers' platform, which at that time still stood on the edge of the Comitium. The speech begins with four verbs that have been quoted ever since: “He has gone, he has departed, he has slipped away, he has burst out” (In Catilinam 2.1).

Cicero said that Catiline had left the city by the Via Aurelia (2.6) and was heading for Manlius's camp. But the danger had not passed: his associates remained in Rome. Their leader was Publius Cornelius Lentulus Sura, a praetor in office and a former consul, who appealed to a prophecy: according to the Sibylline Books three Cornelii are to rule over Rome, and after Cinna and Sulla he is the third (3.9; Sallust 47).
Ambush at the Milvian Bridge

The bridge stands beyond the northern edge of the map, on the Via Flaminia, some three kilometers from the city.

At this time envoys of a Gallic tribe, the Allobroges, were staying in Rome. Lentulus tried to win them over to the uprising, but through their patron they informed Cicero, who asked them to obtain written proof. The conspirators gave them sealed letters.

On the night of December 2 to 3 the envoys set out for home, and with them the conspirators' man, Titus Volturcius. At the bridge two praetors, Lucius Flaccus and Gaius Pomptinus, lay in wait for them, with armed men hidden at the two ends of the bridge. They struck toward the end of the third watch of the night; swords were drawn, but the envoys surrendered. The letters were taken to the consul unopened (In Catilinam 3.5–6; Sallust 45).
The new statue of Jupiter on the Capitol

On the morning of December 3, while the prisoners were being led through the Forum before the Senate, the new statue of Jupiter was just being set up on the Capitol.

Two years earlier lightning had struck the Capitol. The soothsayers said then that a larger statue must be set up in place of the old one, and that it must be turned toward the east, so that it would look upon the Forum and the Curia; then the secret plans would come to light. The work dragged on, and it was completed on this very morning.

In his speech that evening Cicero presented this to the people as a sign from the gods: in the very hour when the statue was put in its place, the conspirators and their accusers were crossing the Forum on his orders (In Catilinam 3.19–21).
The Senate in the Temple of Concord

On December 3 the Senate met in the Temple of Concord. Cicero had the conspirators brought in one by one and laid the letters before them. Each recognized his own seal. On Lentulus's seal was the likeness of his grandfather; Cicero remarked that even the mute image of this excellent man could have held him back from the crime (In Catilinam 3.10). Lentulus resigned the praetorship, and the five prisoners were each entrusted to the house custody of a senator (Sallust 47).

On December 5 their fate was decided here. The consul designate proposed the death penalty. Then Julius Caesar, the praetor designate, rose to speak: to execute a Roman citizen without trial is a dangerous precedent; he proposed that their property be confiscated and that they be held in custody for life in towns of Italy (Sallust 51). The Senate wavered, until Cato's speech turned the mood back (52).

According to Plutarch, a letter was brought to Caesar during the debate. Cato thought it had come from the conspirators and demanded that he read it aloud. Caesar handed it over: it was a love letter from Servilia, Cato's half-sister. Cato threw it back: “Keep it, you drunkard” (Cato minor 24).
The Tullianum

Cicero had the sentence carried out that same evening. He himself led Lentulus from the Palatine along the Sacra Via and through the middle of the Forum to the prison, escorted by the most eminent citizens; the people watched in silence (Plutarch, Cicero 22).

Sallust describes the place: in the prison, when you go up a little to the left, there is a chamber called the Tullianum, about twelve feet below ground. Walls protect it all around, and above it is a vault built of stone; its neglect, darkness and stench make it loathsome and terrifying (55). Lentulus was lowered into it, and the executioners strangled him with a rope; Cethegus, Statilius, Gabinius and Caeparius were executed in the same way.

Cicero then turned to the crowd waiting in the Forum and said a single word: “They have lived” (vixerunt). On his way home lamps and torches were set out in the doorways, and the women lit his way from the rooftops (Plutarch, Cicero 22).

Catiline fell with his army near Pistoria at the beginning of the following year (Sallust 60–61). Five years later Cicero was exiled for this very execution, for the killing of citizens without trial. The Tullianum can still be visited today.
Caesar's last day and funeral (44 BC)

On March 15, 44 BC, the Ides of March, Gaius Julius Caesar, dictator in perpetuity, was killed at a session of the Senate. The following days can be traced from site to site on the basis of Suetonius (Divus Iulius 80–85), Plutarch (Caesar 63–68, Brutus 14–20), Appian (Civil Wars 2.115–148) and Cassius Dio (Book 44).

The accounts differ in certain details; where they do, I indicate it. Where there is evidence, the line follows the known ancient streets; the sources rarely give the exact routes of the people involved.
The background: the Temple of Venus Genetrix

Caesar dedicated the temple standing in his own forum to Venus, the ancestress of the Julian clan, in 46 BC. According to Suetonius, one of the main causes of the hatred was an incident that took place here: when the entire Senate came before him with the decrees passed in his honor, he received them sitting in front of the temple and did not stand up (Divus Iulius 78).

On February 15, at the festival of the Lupercalia, Caesar sat on the Rostra in a purple toga, on a gilded chair. Mark Antony, his fellow consul, held out a royal diadem to him. Caesar declined it, and the people applauded; Antony tried again, Caesar refused again, and sent the diadem to the Capitol for Jupiter (Cicero, Philippica 2.85–87; Plutarch, Caesar 61).

Many thought he was only testing the mood of the people. According to Suetonius, more than sixty people took part in the conspiracy (80).
The Domus Publica: the last night

As chief priest (pontifex maximus), Caesar lived in the official residence beside the Sacra Via (Suetonius 46). On the evening of March 14 he dined at the house of Lepidus. The talk turned to which is the best death; Caesar answered: the unexpected one (Plutarch 63; Suetonius 87).

During the night the doors and windows of the bedroom flew open of their own accord. His wife, Calpurnia, dreamed that the gable of the house was collapsing and that her husband was being stabbed in her arms (Suetonius 81; Plutarch 63). In the morning she asked him not to go, and the sacrificial omens were bad as well. Caesar hesitated for a long time and was already about to cancel the session. Then Decimus Brutus arrived, one of the conspirators, whom he trusted so much that he had made him his heir in the second degree; it was he who persuaded him not to keep waiting a Senate that had assembled in full numbers.

He set out around the fifth hour (Suetonius 81). On the way someone pressed into his hand a document that exposed the conspiracy. He put it among the other petitions to read later, and carried it with him, holding it in his left hand.

The Senate was not meeting in the Forum that day: the old Curia had been demolished, and the new one was still under construction. The session was convened on the Campus Martius, in one of the halls of the portico attached to the Theater of Pompey.

Gladiatorial games were being held in the theater that day. The gladiators of Decimus Brutus could thus be nearby without attracting attention, to protect the conspirators if necessary (Appian 2.118; Cassius Dio 44.16). The conspirators arrived early and waited in the portico; meanwhile Brutus and Cassius, as praetors, were hearing lawsuits (Plutarch, Brutus 14).

In front of the entrance Caesar caught sight of Spurinna, the soothsayer, who had earlier warned him that danger threatened him until the Ides of March. Laughing, he called out to him that the Ides of March had come and no harm had been done. “They have come, but they have not yet passed,” the soothsayer replied (Suetonius 81; Plutarch 63).
The Curia of Pompey: the murder

Antony, whose physical strength they feared, was detained in conversation by Trebonius outside the door. When Caesar sat down, the conspirators gathered around him as if to pay their respects. Tillius Cimber, who was pleading for his exiled brother, seized his toga at both shoulders. “But this is violence!” Caesar cried. Then one of the Cascas wounded him from behind, a little below the throat. Caesar seized his arm and ran it through with his stylus (Suetonius 82).

When he saw daggers pointed at him from every side, he drew his toga over his head and with his left hand let its folds down to his feet, so that he would fall with decency. He was stabbed twenty-three times. According to Suetonius he died without a word, with a single groan at the first thrust; he adds that, according to some, he said in Greek to Marcus Brutus as he rushed at him: “You too, my son?” The physician Antistius later established that of the wounds only the second, the one in the chest, was fatal.

According to Plutarch he collapsed at the base of Pompey's statue, and his blood spattered it (Caesar 66). The senators scattered. The body lay abandoned for a long time, until three slaves put it on a litter and carried it home; one arm hung down (Suetonius 82).

The foundation walls of the hall can be seen at the edge of the sacred area of Largo Argentina, behind Temples B and C. The hall was later walled up (Suetonius 88).
The Capitol: the conspirators' refuge

The assassins marched to the Forum with bloody daggers in their hands, cheering for liberty, but the city did not side with them: people shut themselves in and the shops were closed. Under the protection of Decimus Brutus's gladiators they went up to the Capitol and entrenched themselves there (Appian 2.120; Cassius Dio 44.21).

The next day Marcus Brutus went down to the Forum and spoke to the people. They heard him out in silence, but when another speaker began to revile Caesar, the crowd erupted, and the conspirators withdrew to the hill (Plutarch, Brutus 18).

They came down for good only after Antony and Lepidus had each sent his own son up to them as a hostage. That evening Cassius dined with Antony and Brutus with Lepidus (Plutarch, Brutus 19; Cassius Dio 44.34).
The Senate in the Temple of Tellus

On March 17 Antony, as consul, convened the Senate in the Temple of Tellus. The temple stood in the Carinae quarter, near Antony's house, which had formerly been Pompey's (Appian 2.126); its location on the map is uncertain.

What was at stake in the debate was whether Caesar had been a tyrant. If so, the assassins deserved a reward, but then all of Caesar's measures were invalid, and most of those present would lose the offices and provinces they had received from him. Antony pointed out this contradiction.

A compromise was reached, proposed by Cicero with reference to the Athenian example: the assassins would receive impunity, while Caesar's measures would remain in force (Cicero, Philippica 1.1; Cassius Dio 44.22–34). Caesar's father-in-law, Piso, won the concession that the will be read out in public and the dead man be honored with a state funeral. This decided the events of the following days.
The Rostra: the will and the funeral oration

The will was opened in Antony's house. Caesar made his sister's grandson, the eighteen-year-old Gaius Octavius, his principal heir, and at the end adopted him as his son. To the people he left his gardens across the Tiber and three hundred sesterces per person. Among the heirs in the second degree was Decimus Brutus, one of the assassins (Suetonius 83).

A small gilded shrine was set up in front of the Rostra, a replica of the Temple of Venus Genetrix. In it the dead man lay on an ivory couch, covered with purple and gold; at the head of the couch, on a stand, was the garment in which he had been killed (Suetonius 84).

Two traditions survive about the funeral oration. According to Suetonius, instead of a speech Antony had a herald read out the decree of the Senate that granted Caesar every human and divine honor, and the oath by which they had all sworn to protect his life; to this he added only a few words. Appian describes a long, theatrical speech: Antony lifted the pierced, bloody toga high on the point of a spear, and then a mechanism turned a wax effigy of Caesar around, with all twenty-three wounds on it (2.144–147).
The site of the pyre: the Temple of Divus Iulius

The pyre was built on the Campus Martius, beside the tomb of Caesar's daughter Iulia. The crowd, however, would not let the dead man be carried that far. Some wanted to cremate him on the Capitol, in the Temple of Jupiter, others in Pompey's Curia. Then, Suetonius writes, two armed figures suddenly set fire to the couch with burning wax tapers, and the bystanders threw on dry branches, the benches of the judges' tribunals and everything else that came to hand. The flute players and the actors tore off their triumphal garments and threw them into the fire, the veterans their weapons, the women their jewelry (84).

The crowd then rushed with burning torches to the houses of Brutus and Cassius. On the way they killed Helvius Cinna, because they mistook him for Cornelius Cinna, who had reviled Caesar the day before, and carried his head around on a spear (Suetonius 85).

On the site of the pyre the people set up a column of Numidian marble almost twenty feet high, with the inscription “To the Father of his Country”; for a long time they sacrificed here, made vows and swore oaths by Caesar's name (85). During the funeral games a comet shone in the sky for seven days, which was held to be the soul of Caesar received into heaven (88).

The building of the temple was decided on in 42 BC, and Octavian dedicated it on August 18, 29 BC. In the niche in the middle of the platform the core of the altar can still be seen today; visitors still lay flowers on it.
Augustus's Rome

Based on Augustus's own account, the Res Gestae divi Augusti (chapters 19–21), in which he lists what he built and what he restored. “I received a city of brick, I leave behind a city of marble,” he said, according to Suetonius (Augustus 28).

The stops lead from the Palatine through the Forum to the northern end of the Campus Martius. The line is not a historical route: between the stops it follows the known ancient streets, where there is evidence for them.
The House of Augustus on the Palatine

According to Suetonius, Augustus first lived near the Forum, then moved to the Palatine, into the former house of the orator Hortensius. The house was neither large nor ornate: its short porticoes were built of Alban stone, and in the rooms there was neither marble nor artistic flooring. For more than forty years he slept in the same bedroom, winter and summer (Augustus 72).

In January 27 BC, when he received the name Augustus, the Senate ordered that his doorposts be decorated with laurel and that a civic crown be placed above the door, the oak leaves awarded for saving the lives of citizens (Res Gestae 34).

The house with painted rooms on the hillside, excavated from the 1960s onward, is traditionally identified as his house; some of its rooms can be visited.
The Temple of Apollo

“I built a temple to Apollo on the Palatine, with porticoes” (Res Gestae 19). When lightning struck part of his house, the soothsayers interpreted it to mean that the god wanted the place for himself. Augustus built the temple here and attached a Latin and a Greek library to it; in his old age he often held the meetings of the Senate here as well (Suetonius, Augustus 29).

The temple was dedicated on October 9, 28 BC (Cassius Dio 53.1). Propertius, who was present at the opening, describes the golden portico, the statues of the daughters of Danaus between the columns, the gleaming marble temple and its doors of carved ivory (2.31).

Augustus had the Sibylline Books brought here from the Capitol and placed them in two gilded cases beneath the base of the cult statue (Suetonius 31). The temple, built together with the emperor's house, thus became one of the centers of the state religion.

At the eastern end of the Forum, on the site of Caesar's pyre, stands the temple of the deified Caesar (Res Gestae 19). Octavian dedicated it on August 18, 29 BC, a few days after his triple triumph.

The platform in front of the temple was decorated with the prows of the Egyptian ships captured at Actium (Cassius Dio 51.19). From then on the Forum had two speakers' platforms, facing each other at its two ends: the old Rostra and this new one, that of the Julii.

In this way Augustus tied both ends of the square to his family. On the front of the platform, in the semicircular niche, the core of the altar marking the site of the pyre can still be seen today.
The Curia Iulia

“I built the Curia and the Chalcidicum adjoining it” (Res Gestae 19). The Senate's new meeting hall was begun by Caesar, and completed and dedicated by Octavian on August 28, 29 BC. In the hall he set up the statue of Victoria brought from Tarentum, and decorated it with Egyptian spoils (Cassius Dio 51.22).

Here too hung the golden shield that the Senate and the people gave him, according to the inscription for his courage, clemency, justice and piety (Res Gestae 34).

For more than three hundred years sacrifice was offered before the statue and altar of Victoria at the beginning of the sessions; its removal at the end of the 4th century became the great dispute between the pagan and the Christian senators. The building standing today is a rebuilding of the time of Diocletian after the fire of 283, but on the site and with the dimensions of Augustus's hall.
The Basilica Iulia

Augustus writes of it as follows: the hall standing between the Temple of Castor and the Temple of Saturn, which his father had begun and almost finished, he completed; when a fire destroyed it, he began to rebuild it on an enlarged site, in the name of his sons (Res Gestae 20). The sons were his adopted sons and grandsons, Gaius and Lucius Caesar, both of whom died young.

In the hall sat the court of the Hundred Men, which heard inheritance cases. Pliny the Younger describes a speech for the defense that he delivered here: the four panels sat together, one hundred and eighty judges, and from the galleries men and women leaned down to hear something (Epistulae 6.33).

The game boards scratched into the marble of the steps can still be seen today; those who were waiting passed the time here.
The Temple of Mars Ultor and the Forum of Augustus

“On private ground, from the spoils of war, I built the Temple of Mars Ultor and the Forum of Augustus” (Res Gestae 21). He vowed the temple to Mars the Avenger before the battle of Philippi, in 42 BC, when he was fighting against his father's assassins (Suetonius, Augustus 29). It was dedicated only forty years later, in 2 BC.

The square turned out narrower than planned, because Augustus did not want to expropriate the owners of the neighboring houses (Suetonius 56). The high rear wall, still standing today, protected it from the fires of the Subura quarter.

In the two porticoes stood statues of Rome's great generals in triumphal dress, with inscriptions. Augustus proclaimed that he had set them up so that the citizens would measure him, as long as he lived, and the rulers who came after him against their example (Suetonius 31). The military standards recovered from the Parthians were placed here (Res Gestae 29), and from here the governors set out for their provinces.

“I built a theater next to the Temple of Apollo, on ground largely purchased from private owners, and had it inscribed with the name of my son-in-law, Marcus Marcellus” (Res Gestae 21). Marcellus, the son of Augustus's sister and the husband of his daughter, whom he intended as his successor, died in 23 BC at the age of nineteen.

The theater was begun by Caesar. At the dedication, according to Suetonius, the joints of Augustus's chair of office came apart and he fell on his back (Augustus 43). Cassius Dio dates the opening to 13 BC (54.26).

Two stories of the curved facade of the auditorium still stand today, because it was converted into a fortress in the Middle Ages and then into a palace in the 16th century; the upper floors are still lived in today.

Augustus erected several buildings not in his own name but in the names of members of his family; among these Suetonius lists the porticoes of his wife, Livia, and of his sister, Octavia (Augustus 29). The latter was built on the site of the old Porticus Metelli and enclosed the temples of Jupiter Stator and Juno Regina. Octavia founded a library in it in memory of her son, Marcellus (Plutarch, Marcellus 30).

The portico was a veritable museum: Pliny lists at length the Greek statues and paintings exhibited here (Naturalis historia 36). Here too stood Lysippus's sculptural group of the mounted companions of Alexander the Great.

A clarification: the “Porticus Octavia” mentioned in chapter 19 of the Res Gestae is not this one but another portico standing nearby, which Gnaeus Octavius built in 168 BC and which Augustus restored under the name of its original builder. The gateway structure visible today dates from the time of Septimius Severus (203).
The Pantheon

The first Pantheon was built by Marcus Agrippa, Augustus's general and son-in-law, who completed it in 25 BC. According to Cassius Dio, Agrippa also wanted to set up the emperor's statue in it and to name the building after him. Augustus accepted neither; so a statue of Caesar was placed in the temple, and those of Augustus and Agrippa in the porch (53.27).

Dio gives two explanations for the name: perhaps it got it from the statues of the many gods, but he himself thinks it was rather because its dome resembles the vault of heaven.

The building standing today dates from the time of Hadrian. Yet the name of Agrippa can be read on its facade: “Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, consul for the third time, built this.” For Hadrian had the name of the original builder inscribed on the buildings he rebuilt.
The Saepta Iulia

The voting place of the popular assemblies, a huge square surrounded by porticoes. Caesar planned it in marble, with a portico a mile long; Agrippa completed and dedicated it in 26 BC, and named it Iulia in honor of Augustus (Cassius Dio 53.23).

By the time it was finished, voting had already lost its importance. Augustus held gladiatorial games in it (Suetonius, Augustus 43), and later it served as a market hall where expensive antiques and luxury goods were sold.

Its western wall ran alongside the Pantheon; a stretch of it can still be seen today on the east side of that building.
The sundial of Augustus

In 10 BC Augustus had an obelisk brought from Egypt and dedicated it to the Sun; according to the inscription on the base, after “Egypt had been brought under the power of the Roman people.”

Pliny describes what it was for: the shadow of the obelisk showed the length of the days and the nights. Bronze strips were laid into the pavement, on which the length of the midday shadow could be read as it grew shorter day by day and then lengthened again. A gilded ball was placed on its tip so that the end of the shadow would be sharper. Pliny adds that in his time the instrument had not shown correctly for about thirty years (Naturalis historia 36.72–73).

A stretch of the meridian line with Greek inscriptions was found in 1979–80 beneath a cellar on Via di Campo Marzio. Since 1792 the obelisk has stood in Piazza di Montecitorio.
The original site of the Ara Pacis

“When I returned to Rome from Hispania and Gaul, after the successful settlement of affairs there, the Senate resolved to consecrate an altar to the Augustan Peace on the Campus Martius for my return, and ordered that the magistrates, the priests and the Vestal Virgins offer sacrifice on it every year” (Res Gestae 12). The decree was passed in 13 BC, and the altar was dedicated on January 30, 9 BC.

The altar stood beside the Via Flaminia. On its reliefs a sacrificial procession moves along: Augustus, the priests and the members of the imperial family with their children.

Fragments of it came to light from beneath a palace from the 16th century onward. The great excavation took place in 1937–38, when the waterlogged ground was frozen so that the pieces could be lifted out from under the foundations. The altar was then set up again on the bank of the Tiber, beside the Mausoleum of Augustus; it can be seen there today.

Augustus had his tomb built as early as 28 BC between the Via Flaminia and the bank of the Tiber, and opened the groves and walks around it to the people (Suetonius, Augustus 100).

Strabo, who saw it, describes it as follows: a great mound beside the river, standing on a high base of white marble, planted with evergreen trees up to its top; on its summit stands a bronze statue of Augustus (5.3.8).

Marcellus was the first to be buried here, then Agrippa, Octavia and the grandsons who died young. Augustus outlived almost all of those he had intended as his successor. In his will he directed that the record of his deeds be cast on bronze tablets and set up in front of the mausoleum (Suetonius 101). The tablets are lost; the text was preserved by a copy carved on the wall of a temple in Ankara.

The mausoleum was reopened in 2021 after a long restoration.
The funeral of Augustus (AD 14)

Augustus died at Nola on August 19, AD 14, a few weeks before his seventy-sixth birthday. His funeral is described by Suetonius (Augustus 99–101), Cassius Dio (56.31–46) and Tacitus (Annales 1.8–10).

The exact route of the procession between the Forum and the Campus Martius is not known; the line follows the known ancient streets, where there is evidence for them.
Homecoming along the Via Appia

Augustus died at Nola, in the same room where his father once had. According to Suetonius, on the last day he asked for a mirror, had his hair combed, then asked his friends whether he had played the comedy of life well to the end; and he quoted a closing line from the theater: if the play had pleased them, they should applaud (Augustus 99).

The body was carried from Nola to Bovillae on the shoulders of the councilors of the towns. Because of the summer heat they traveled by night; by day the dead man was placed in the basilica or the largest temple of the towns along the way. At Bovillae, twelve miles from Rome, the equestrian order took it over and brought it into the city along the Via Appia (Suetonius 100).
In the vestibule of the house

The equestrians laid the body in state in the entrance hall of the house on the Palatine (Suetonius 100). In the same house in which he had lived for more than forty years, and whose door the Senate had decorated with laurel and an oak wreath.

Meanwhile Tiberius, his adopted son and heir, warned the people in an edict not to try to burn the dead man in the Forum, as they once had Caesar, but to let him be carried to the Campus Martius, to his appointed resting place. On the day of the funeral soldiers stood guard. Tacitus remarks that many laughed at this: those who had themselves seen the day of Caesar's murder, or had heard of it from their parents, found it strange that a military guard was now needed for the peaceful funeral of an aged ruler (Annales 1.8).
The Senate meets: the will

The sources do not name the place where the Senate met; its regular meeting hall was the Curia Iulia.

The will was brought by the Vestal Virgins, with whom Augustus had deposited it a year earlier. His principal heir was Tiberius, with two thirds, and Livia, with one third; at the same time he adopted Livia into the Julian family and gave her the name Augusta. He left forty million sesterces to the people, a thousand each to the soldiers of the Praetorian Guard, and three hundred to the legionaries. He excluded his daughter and his granddaughter, the two exiled Julias, from his tomb (Suetonius 101).

Together with the will, three sealed scrolls were also read out: one contained the instructions for his funeral, the second the record of his deeds, the third a statement of the condition of the empire, with the number of soldiers and the money in the treasury.

The senators outdid one another in proposals: the procession should be led through the triumphal gate, and the titles of his laws and the names of the conquered peoples should be carried before it. In the end they agreed that the senators would carry the dead man to the pyre on their own shoulders (Tacitus, Annales 1.8).
Tiberius's funeral oration

The funeral couch was made of ivory and gold, with coverings of purple and gold. The body lay below, in a coffin; above it a wax likeness of him could be seen in triumphal dress. Another likeness of him, in gold, was brought from the Curia, and a third was carried on a triumphal chariot (Cassius Dio 56.34).

Behind them came the images of the ancestors. Caesar's was missing, because he was already a god; but the great figures of Roman history from Romulus onward were there, Pompey among them, and the procession carried the images of all the peoples that Augustus had added to the empire.

Two funeral orations were delivered at the two ends of the Forum. The first was given by Tiberius in front of the Temple of Divus Iulius (Suetonius 100): the adopted son spoke from the platform of the temple that Augustus had built for his own adoptive father.
Drusus's funeral oration

The second speech was given by Drusus, the son of Tiberius, at the other end of the square, from the old Rostra (Suetonius 100; Cassius Dio 56.34).

From here the senators took the funeral couch on their shoulders and set off toward the Campus Martius. According to Cassius Dio the procession passed through the triumphal gate, as the Senate had decided (56.42). The location of the gate is disputed; most scholars look for it at the foot of the Capitol, near the Porta Carmentalis.

Thus Augustus's last journey followed the route of the triumphs in reverse: from the Forum out of the city, to the field where the armies of victorious generals used to assemble.
The pyre on the Campus Martius

The procession arrived in the northern part of the Campus Martius, among Augustus's own monuments: here stood the Altar of Peace, the obelisk of the sundial and the mausoleum. The exact place of the cremation is not known. Strabo describes how in the middle of the field stood the enclosure of the pyre site, built of white stone, with an iron railing around it and planted with poplars inside (5.3.8).

The priests, the equestrians and the soldiers walked around the pyre; the soldiers threw onto it the decorations they had received from him. Centurions lit it with torches. From among the flames, writes Cassius Dio, an eagle was released, as if it were carrying his soul to heaven (56.42).

Livia remained at the site for five days with the most distinguished equestrians. It was they who gathered up the bones, barefoot and in unbelted tunics (Suetonius 100).

A former praetor swore that he had seen the dead man's figure rising to heaven (Suetonius 100). Cassius Dio also knows his name, Numerius Atticus, and that Livia gave him one million sesterces (56.46).
The mausoleum

The ashes were placed in the tomb that Augustus had built for himself forty-two years earlier between the Via Flaminia and the Tiber (Suetonius 100). Already resting there before him were his nephew Marcellus, his friend Agrippa, his sister Octavia, his stepson Drusus and his two grandsons, Gaius and Lucius.

In front of the entrance the record of his deeds, the Res Gestae, was engraved on two bronze pillars, as he had asked in his will. According to the first sentence of the text, at the age of nineteen he raised an army on his own initiative and at his own expense, with which he restored freedom to the state.

Tacitus records what people said about him on the day of the funeral. According to some, he had been driven to the civil wars by devotion to his parents and by the emergency of the state, and he left the empire behind at peace, enclosed by seas and rivers. According to others, the devotion was only a pretext, and he had won the peace at the price of blood (Annales 1.9–10).
The Temple of the Deified Augustus

On September 17 the Senate voted him a temple and divine honors (Tacitus, Annales 1.10). Livia became his priestess.

Tiberius and Livia began building the temple; until it was finished, a golden likeness of Augustus was placed on a couch in the Temple of Mars Ultor, and there it received all the honors that were later due to his own statue (Cassius Dio 56.46). The house at Nola where he died was turned into a shrine.

In the end the temple was dedicated only by Caligula, in AD 37. It stood in the valley between the Palatine and the Capitol; its exact location on the map is a conjecture.
The Great Fire (AD 64)

In the night before July 19, AD 64, a fire broke out at the Circus Maximus and burned for six days. Tacitus, who was a child at the time, describes it in detail (Annales 15.38–44); alongside him Suetonius (Nero 31, 38) and Cassius Dio (62.16–18) are the main sources.

According to Tacitus it is not known whether it was an accident or the emperor's intention; the authors know both versions. The order of the stops follows the spread of the fire and the years that came after it; the line is not the path of the fire, it only connects the stops along the known ancient streets.
The Circus Maximus: the fire breaks out

The fire started in the part of the circus that adjoins the Palatine and Caelian hills. The shops there held flammable goods; the flames gathered strength at once, the wind caught them, and they ran the whole length of the circus. There were no houses protected by stone walls in their path, no temples enclosed by walls, nothing that could have held them back (Tacitus, Annales 15.38).

Tacitus notes the date: July 19, the same day on which the Gauls had once set fire to Rome (15.41).

The fire first raced across the level parts, then climbed the hills, then swept down again into the valleys. Because of the narrow, winding streets and irregular blocks of old Rome it could not be stopped. People were rescuing the old and the children and getting in one another's way; many who had lost everything, or whose loved ones had perished, chose to stay in the fire themselves. No one dared to fight the flames: many people made threats and openly threw torches, shouting that they were acting on orders (15.38).
The Forum Boarium: the altar of Hercules

Tacitus lists separately the most ancient sanctuaries that were lost. Among them was “the great altar and the shrine that the Arcadian Evander dedicated to the present Hercules” (15.41): the Ara Maxima in the cattle market, beside the starting gates of the circus. According to tradition it dated from the time before the founding of the city.

The Temple of Luna on the Aventine, founded by King Servius Tullius, also burned down. Tacitus considers what was inside the buildings an even greater loss than the buildings themselves: the spoils won in victories, the masterpieces of Greek art and the original manuscripts of the old writers. The old people, he writes, for all the beauty of the rebuilt city, still remembered many things that could not be replaced.

The location of the altar on the map is uncertain.
The Palatine: Nero's first palace

When the fire broke out Nero was at Antium, on the coast. He returned only when the flames were approaching his own house, with which he had linked the Palatine to the Gardens of Maecenas on the Esquiline. It could no longer be saved: the fire swallowed the Palatine, the palace and everything around it (15.39).

From this first palace, the Domus Transitoria, this hall with an ornamental fountain survives beneath the later imperial palace. Its floor and walls were made with colored marble inlay; after the fire it was filled in and built over.

On the side facing the Forum the house of King Numa, the Regia, burned down, and so did the shrine of Vesta with the household gods of the Roman people (15.41).
The Forum: the shrine of Vesta

In the round Temple of Vesta burned the sacred fire of the state, which was tended by the Vestal Virgins; if it went out, this was considered the gravest of omens. Inside the temple, locked away, were kept the Penates, the household gods of the Roman people, and the sacred objects that according to tradition Aeneas had brought from Troy.

In Tacitus's list it reads: “Numa's royal house and the shrine of Vesta burned down together with the Penates of the Roman people” (15.41). The temple was rebuilt; on Nero's coins it appears as a round, domed building. Later it burned down at least once more, and the ruins visible today come from the last rebuilding, in the time of Septimius Severus.
The Temple of Jupiter Stator

The next item in the list: “the Temple of Jupiter Stator, which Romulus had vowed” (15.41). According to tradition, in the battle against the Sabines, when the Romans were already in flight, Romulus here asked Jupiter the Stayer to stop the fugitives, and promised him a temple (Livy 1.12).

The temple stood at the upper end of the Sacra Via, at the foot of the Palatine; its location on the map is uncertain.

Tacitus's summary: of Rome's fourteen regions four remained intact, three were burned to the ground, and in the other seven only a few mutilated, half-burned remains of the houses were standing (15.40).
The Esquiline: the Gardens of Maecenas

The fire stopped on the sixth day at the foot of the Esquiline, after buildings had been demolished over a large area so that the flames would meet empty space. Then it flared up again on the estate of Tigellinus, the Praetorian prefect, which fed the suspicion further (15.40).

The most famous story of the fire is connected with the Gardens of Maecenas. Tacitus words it cautiously: the rumor spread that while the city was burning, Nero sang of the destruction of Troy on his private stage, comparing the present disaster to the ancient catastrophe (15.39). Suetonius already writes it as fact and also gives the place: he watched the fire from the Tower of Maecenas, delighted in the beauty of the flames, and sang the whole Fall of Ilium in stage costume (Nero 38). According to Cassius Dio, from the roof of the palace (62.18).

The three versions thus name three different locations, and the earliest author mentions it only as a rumor.
The Campus Martius: the homeless

Nero opened the Campus Martius, the buildings of Agrippa and even his own gardens to the refugees, and had emergency shelters put up in haste for the crowd. He had food brought from Ostia and the neighboring towns, and lowered the price of grain to three sesterces per modius (15.39).

The buildings of Agrippa stood in the middle of the Campus: the baths, the Pantheon, the Saepta and the Hall of Neptune.

Tacitus adds: all this, however much it favored the people, was in vain because of the rumor (15.39). For the rebuilding Nero introduced strict rules: measured, wide streets, limited building height, and colonnaded porches in front of the facades, from the roofs of which fires could be fought; the lower stories had to be built without beams, of fireproof Alban and Gabine stone, and the houses could not have shared walls. The rubble was carried by the grain ships on their return voyage to fill in the marshes of Ostia (15.43).
The Golden House

“Nero profited from the ruin of his country and built a palace in which the marvel was not so much the precious stones and the gold as the fields and the lakes, and the woods, clearings and views that imitated solitude.” Tacitus also names the two architects: Severus and Celer (15.42).

According to Suetonius's description the entrance hall was so large that the emperor's statue, one hundred and twenty feet high, fit inside it; the triple colonnade ran for a mile; the lake resembled a sea, with buildings around it shaped like cities. The ivory ceilings of the dining rooms could be turned so that flowers could be scattered, and perfume could be sprayed on the guests from pipes. The main dining room was round and revolved day and night, like the universe. When Nero dedicated it, he said only this: at last he could begin to live in a way worthy of a human being (Nero 31).

The wing on the Oppian Hill survived because Trajan filled it in and built his baths on top of it. At the end of the 15th century painters who let themselves down through the vaults discovered its wall paintings; grotesque decoration got its name from the “caves” (grotte).
The Colossus

In the entrance hall of the Golden House stood Nero's bronze statue, made by the Greek Zenodorus; Pliny also saw the clay model in the workshop (Naturalis historia 34.45). Suetonius says it was one hundred and twenty feet high (Nero 31).

After Nero's death Vespasian had it converted into a statue of the Sun god. Hadrian, when he built the Temple of Venus and Roma on the site of the entrance hall, had the statue hauled here, to the side of the amphitheater, standing upright, by twenty-four elephants (Historia Augusta, Hadrian 19).

By the Middle Ages the statue had disappeared, but its name survived: from it the amphitheater got the name Colosseum. The site of its base is marked today by paving.
On the site of the lake: the amphitheater

The lake of the Golden House was in this valley. Vespasian had it drained and built the amphitheater on its site, which his son Titus dedicated in AD 80.

Martial builds on exactly this in the poem he wrote for the opening: where the mass of the venerable amphitheater now rises, there were Nero's lakes; where we admire the quickly finished baths, an arrogant estate had taken the houses of the poor. “Rome has been given back to herself,” and what was the delight of one master now belongs to the people (Liber spectaculorum 2).

In this way the Flavian emperors reversed the expropriation that followed the fire, and with it justified their own rule.
The Vatican: the Gardens of Nero

The rumor that the fire had been set on orders did not die down. To put an end to it, writes Tacitus, Nero put forward scapegoats and inflicted the most exquisite punishments on those whom the people called Christians. Tacitus explains the name: Christus was executed under the reign of Tiberius by the governor Pontius Pilate (15.44). This sentence is one of the earliest mentions of the execution of Jesus in pagan Roman literature.

For the executions Nero offered his own gardens, and he staged circus games at which he mingled with the people in a charioteer's dress. The condemned were sewn into the skins of wild animals and torn apart by dogs, crucified, or burned after dusk as lighting for the night. Tacitus, who despised the Christians, nevertheless writes: pity arose for them, because they perished not for the public good but because of the cruelty of a single man.

The gardens and the circus were on the Vatican. On the center line of the circus stood the obelisk that was moved in 1586 to the middle of St Peter's Square. Christian tradition places the martyrdom of the apostle Peter here.
The Year of the Four Emperors (AD 69)

After Nero's death four emperors followed one another within a single year: Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian. Two of them were killed in the center of Rome, and the Capitol burned down in the fighting. The main source is Tacitus's work titled Historiae (1.27–49 and 3.69–86), alongside the imperial biographies of Suetonius and Plutarch.

The first half of the walk follows the events of January 15, the second half those of December 18–20. Where there is evidence, the line follows the known ancient streets; the sources rarely give the exact route of the participants.
January 15: sacrifice in front of the Temple of Apollo

Galba, the emperor, who was in his seventies, sacrificed in the morning in front of the Temple of Apollo on the Palatine. From the entrails of the sacrificial animal the soothsayer read an imminent plot and an enemy within the household. Beside him stood Otho, who took all this as a good sign for his own plan (Tacitus, Historiae 1.27).

Otho had expected Galba to adopt him as his son and successor. Five days earlier, however, Galba had chosen a young aristocrat, Piso. Otho was up to his ears in debt; according to Suetonius he used to say that it made no difference to him whether the enemy finished him off in battle or his creditors in the Forum (Otho 5).

During the sacrifice one of his freedmen stepped up to him and reported that the architect and the contractors were waiting for him. This was the agreed signal. Otho excused himself by saying that he had to look at a house that was for sale, and left.
The Golden Milestone

Leaning on his freedman, Otho went down through the Palace of Tiberius to the Velabrum, and from there to the Golden Milestone, below the Temple of Saturn (1.27). From this column the distances of the empire's roads were reckoned; Augustus had set it up.

Here twenty-three soldiers of the Praetorian Guard were waiting for him, and they hailed him as emperor. Otho was alarmed that there were so few of them. The soldiers hurriedly put him in a litter, drew their swords and carried him at a run toward the camp. On the way roughly the same number joined them: some as accomplices, the majority in astonishment, some shouting, others silent, intending to decide according to events (1.27).

Tacitus adds the sentence that has been quoted about this day ever since: few ventured on the most monstrous deed, more wanted it, and everyone tolerated it (1.28).
The camp of the Praetorian Guard

In the camp the officer on duty did not dare to resist. The soldiers placed Otho among the standards, on the platform where a golden statue of Galba had stood before. They did not let the officers near him (1.36).

Otho, Tacitus writes, stretched out his hands toward the crowd, paid homage to the mob, threw kisses, and did everything slavishly for the sake of power. He had the armory opened; the soldiers snatched up the weapons without regard for unit or rank (1.36–38).

The camp of the Praetorian Guard had stood on the northeastern edge of the city since Tiberius. In the 3rd century it was built into the Aurelian Wall, which is why three of its sides are still visible today.
The Lacus Curtius: the death of Galba

Contradictory reports reached the Palatine. A guardsman with a bloody sword reported that he had killed Otho; Galba asked: “Comrade, who gave you the order?” (1.35). In the end the emperor had himself carried down to the Forum in a litter. The crowd filled the halls and the temples; no one shouted, Tacitus writes, but the silence of great fear and great anger prevailed (1.40).

Then Otho's cavalry burst in. They scattered the people, trampled the senators, and were deterred neither by the sight of the Capitol nor by the sanctity of the temples standing all around (1.40). The standard-bearer of the unit escorting Galba tore the emperor's image from the standard and dashed it to the ground.

The litter-bearers panicked, and Galba was thrown out of it at the Lacus Curtius. His last words were recorded in two ways: according to some he pleaded and asked for a few days' grace so that he could pay the money promised to the soldiers; according to others he offered his neck for them to strike, if that was for the good of the state (1.41). Nothing certain is known about his killer either; Tacitus mentions three names.

The paved site of the Lacus Curtius, marked by a railing, can still be seen in the middle of the Forum.
The death of Vinius in front of the Temple of Divus Iulius

Titus Vinius, Galba's fellow consul and chief adviser, got as far as the other end of the square. They caught up with him in front of the Temple of Divus Iulius: the first blow struck the back of his knee, then a legionary soldier ran him through from side to side (1.42).

According to Tacitus he shouted that Otho had not given orders for him to be killed. Either fear made him say it, or he betrayed by it his part in the conspiracy; his life and reputation make the latter more likely, he adds.

The heads were carried before Otho fixed on lances, among the eagles of the legions. According to Suetonius, a common soldier carried Galba's bald head in the fold of his garment, because he could not grasp it by the hair (Galba 20).
The death of Piso on the threshold of the Temple of Vesta

Piso, the son the emperor had adopted a few days earlier, fled wounded. A centurion, Sempronius Densus, stood alone before the armed men, dagger in hand, and while they were killing him Piso reached the Temple of Vesta. The public slave who guarded the temple took pity on him and hid him in his room (1.43).

Tacitus remarks: it was not the sanctity of the place nor respect for the rites but the hiding place that postponed his end. Otho sent two men expressly for him. They dragged him out and slaughtered him in the doorway of the temple.

Otho, they say, looked at no other head with such insatiable joy as at Piso's (1.44). By evening the Senate and the people were already flattering him. Tacitus sums up Galba like this: everyone would have thought him fit to rule, if he had not ruled (1.49).

Otho was emperor for three months. In April, after the defeat he suffered from the army of Vitellius, he killed himself.
December 19: siege on the Capitol

In July the eastern legions proclaimed Vespasian emperor. By December his armies had reached Rome. On December 18 Vitellius wanted to abdicate, but his soldiers and the people would not let him. The escort of Vespasian's elder brother, the city prefect Flavius Sabinus, was attacked; he withdrew to the Capitol, and during the night had his children and his nephew, the eighteen-year-old Domitian, brought up there as well (3.69).

The next day Vitellius' soldiers stormed the hill without a leader, on their own initiative. They pushed up from the Forum as far as the gate. The defenders pelted them with stones and tiles from the roofs of the porticoes lining the slope. The attackers hurled burning torches onto the portico and followed the fire. Sabinus barricaded the gate with the statues that had been pulled down, the monuments of the ancestors.

Then the attackers set out from two other sides as well: from the grove of the Asylum and by the hundred steps beside the Tarpeian Rock. On the Asylum side the neighboring houses reached the height of the hill, and it was possible to cross over from their roofs (3.71).
The destruction of the Temple of Jupiter

“Here it is uncertain whether the besiegers threw fire onto the roofs, or the besieged, which is the more common version, in order to drive back those climbing up.” The flames spread from the porticoes to the temple; the old wooden eagles supporting the pediment caught fire and fed it. “Thus the Capitol burned down, with its gates closed, undefended and unplundered” (3.71).

Here Tacitus breaks off the narrative: this was the saddest and most shameful crime to befall the Roman people since the foundation of the city. With no foreign enemy, with the gods favorable, had our morals allowed it, the seat of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, which our ancestors founded as the pledge of empire, and which neither Porsenna nor the Gauls had been able to desecrate, was destroyed by the frenzy of the emperors (3.72).

Sabinus was captured unarmed, taken before Vitellius, and killed despite the emperor's protest. His mutilated body was dragged to the Gemonian Stairs (3.74).

The temple was rebuilt by Vespasian; according to Suetonius he himself began the clearing of the ruins and carried away the first basket of rubble on his own shoulder (Vespasianus 8).
Domitian's escape: Iuppiter Custos

During the siege Domitian hid in the dwelling of the temple attendant. Through the ingenuity of a freedman he put on a linen garment, mingled with a group of priests of Isis, and got down from the hill unrecognized. He lay low at the house of one of his father's clients near the Velabrum (3.74). According to Suetonius he spent the night with the temple attendant, and in the morning, dressed as a devotee of Isis, crossed the Tiber with a single companion to the mother of a schoolmate (Domitianus 1).

When his father came to power, he had the temple attendant's house demolished and on its site built a small shrine to Jupiter the Preserver, with an altar whose marble relief depicted his own adventure. Later, as emperor, he dedicated a huge temple to Jupiter the Guardian, Iuppiter Custos, and had himself depicted on the statue in the god's lap (3.74).

The identification of the temple on the map is a conjecture.
December 20: fighting at the Gardens of Sallust

The next day Vespasian's army pushed into the city in three columns: one along the Via Flaminia, the second along the bank of the Tiber, the third along the Via Salaria toward the Porta Collina (3.82).

The hardest task fell to those who turned left, toward the Gardens of Sallust, through narrow and slippery streets. From the top of the stone walls of the gardens Vitellius' soldiers drove them back with stones and javelins right up to evening, until the cavalry that had broken in through the Porta Collina attacked the defenders from the rear.

The people, Tacitus writes, stood by the combatants as spectators, as at the circus games: they cheered on now one side, now the other, with shouts and applause. If someone fled into a shop or a house, they demanded that he be dragged out and killed. The baths and the taverns were open; side by side were blood and heaps of corpses and the prostitutes. It happened to be the festival of the Saturnalia (3.83).
The Porta Collina and the siege of the camp

The cavalry broke in through the northern gate of the old city wall, the Porta Collina; the location of the gate on the map is a conjecture. Vitellius' most loyal soldiers then withdrew to the camp of the Praetorian Guard, which we saw at the start of the walk at the proclamation of Otho.

The siege of the camp was the bloodiest fighting of the day. Among the attackers were the former guardsmen whom Vitellius had dismissed; they wanted to win back the camp at any cost. They brought to bear everything that had been devised for besieging the strongest cities: the shield roof, artillery, a siege mound, fire arrows.

The defenders, though they knew they had lost, did not surrender. All of them fell from wounds received in front, facing the enemy; even as they were dying, Tacitus writes, they took care to die an honorable death (3.84).
The Palatine: the empty palace

When the city fell, Vitellius had himself carried in a litter through the rear part of the palace to the Aventine, to his wife's house. Then, in his indecision, he returned. The palace was deserted: even the lowest slave had run away or avoided his path. “The solitude and the silent halls terrify him; he tries the closed doors, he shudders at the empty rooms” (3.84).

According to Suetonius he tied on a belt full of gold coins and hid in the doorkeeper's lodge; he tied a dog in front of the door and barricaded it with a bed and a mattress (Vitellius 16).

An officer dragged him out. His hands were tied behind his back, his clothes were torn, a rope was thrown around his neck. In 69 the imperial palace meant the Domus Tiberiana, standing on the side of the hill facing the Forum; the great palace visible today was built only under Domitian.
The Gemonian Stairs: the death of Vitellius

He was dragged along the Sacra Via and across the Forum. They held the point of a sword under his chin, so that he had to raise his head and could not hide his face. He had to see his statues falling, the Rostra, and the place where Galba had been killed (3.85). The people, who had still been cheering him a few days earlier, pelted him with mud and jeered at him as an arsonist and a glutton (Suetonius, Vitellius 17).

A single sentence of his was recorded, one that according to Tacitus was not unworthy: to the officer mocking him he replied that he had nevertheless been his emperor.

He was killed on the Gemonian Stairs, beside the prison, on the slope of the Capitol: at the spot where the body of Flavius Sabinus had lain the day before (3.85). His body was dragged with a hook into the Tiber (Suetonius, Vitellius 17).

Eleven months had passed since Galba fell out of his litter in this same square. The location of the stairs is not known exactly; they were in the immediate vicinity of the Carcer.
The route of the triumph (AD 71)

In the summer of AD 71 Vespasian and his son Titus held a joint triumph to mark the end of the Judean war. Josephus, the Jewish historian of the war, who by then was living in Rome, describes it in detail (Jewish War 7.123–162). Of the earlier triumphs, that of Aemilius Paullus (167 BC) is recounted in detail by Plutarch (Aemilius Paullus 32–34).

The route is known for certain only at a few points; on the intervening stretches the line follows the known ancient streets, where there is evidence for them.
The night before the start

The army marched out while it was still night and drew up by centuries under the command of its officers. Josephus gives the place: not at the gates of the upper palace, but near the Temple of Isis, because the two generals had spent the night there (7.123).

By ancient rule, a general celebrating a triumph could not cross the sacred boundary of the city before the ceremony; that is why they assembled on the Campus Martius. Vespasian also had a personal attachment to Isis and Serapis: it was in Alexandria, in the Temple of Serapis, that he received the signs confirming his rule (Tacitus, Historiae 4.81–82).
Assembly at the Portico of Octavia

At dawn Vespasian and Titus, wearing laurel wreaths and the traditional purple robes, went over to the Portico of Octavia. There the Senate, the chief magistrates and the equestrian order were waiting for them. A platform had been set up in front of the portico, with two ivory chairs on it (7.124–125).

When they sat down, the army broke into cheers all at once. The soldiers stood unarmed, in silk garments, wearing laurel wreaths. Vespasian signaled for silence. He stood up, covered most of his head with his cloak, and recited the prescribed prayers; Titus did the same (7.126–128).

After this Vespasian spoke briefly to everyone, then dismissed the soldiers to the breakfast that the emperors by tradition gave them on such occasions.
The triumphal gate and the theaters

Vespasian then withdrew to the gate that got its name from the fact that triumphs always pass through it. There they ate something, put on the triumphal dress, sacrificed to the gods standing at the gate, and set the procession in motion “through the theaters, so that the crowd could see more easily” (7.129–131).

The location of the triumphal gate (Porta Triumphalis) is disputed; most scholars look for it at the foot of the Capitol, near the Porta Carmentalis. Of the theaters, that of Marcellus stands right next to the Portico of Octavia; the theaters of Balbus and Pompey were also nearby.

According to Josephus, no one in the city stayed at home that day: everyone went out, and they left only as much room as was needed for the procession to pass (7.122).
Through the vegetable market: the spoils

The procession passed the temples of the Forum Holitorium toward the Velabrum and the Circus Maximus. Here Josephus gives up trying to describe everything: the silver, the gold and the ivory, he writes, did not move as in a procession but flowed like a river. Purple tapestries embroidered in the Babylonian manner, precious stones set in gold, huge statues of the gods and animals covered with ornate trappings followed one another (7.132–138).

The greatest wonder was aroused by the moving stages: scaffolds three or four stories high, covered with gold and ivory, on which scenes of the war came to life. A devastated countryside, slaughtered troops, walls collapsing under siege engines, burning temples, houses falling on their owners. On each scaffold stood the commander of the captured city, just as he had been taken prisoner (7.139–147).

Josephus himself had been there in this war, first as a Jewish commander, then in the retinue of Titus; the scenes showed the destruction of his own people.
In the Circus Maximus: the treasures of the Temple

Hundreds of thousands could watch the procession from the stands of the circus. According to Plutarch, the people, dressed in white, also watched the triumph of Aemilius Paullus from stands set up in the circuses and in the Forum (Aemilius 32).

What had been found in the Temple in Jerusalem was carried separately from the rest of the spoils. A golden table weighing many talents and a golden lampstand that was different from what we use in everyday life: from its base rose a central shaft, from which slender branches extended, in an arrangement resembling a trident, with a lamp at the end of each; there were seven of them. Last of all was carried the Law of the Jews (7.148–150).

Ten years later a triumphal arch was erected for Titus at the eastern, curved end of the circus. According to its inscription, following his father's counsels he defeated the Jewish people and destroyed the city of Jerusalem, which all generals, kings and peoples before him had either besieged in vain or not even attempted to attack. The remains of the arch were excavated in 2015.
Behind the Palatine: the triumphant general

From the circus, according to scholars, the procession continued through the valley between the Palatine and the Caelian toward the Sacra Via; Josephus does not describe this stretch. Two and a half centuries later the Arch of Constantine was built on precisely this route.

After the spoils came the ivory and gold statues of Victoria. Behind them came Vespasian in his chariot, with Titus behind him; Domitian rode beside them in splendid dress, on an admirable horse (7.151–152).

On this day the triumphant general was the image of Jupiter. According to Pliny, in early times his face too was painted red, like that of the god's statue on feast days (Naturalis historia 33.111). Behind him in the chariot stood a public slave who, according to Tertullian, kept saying to him: “Look behind you! Remember that you are a man!” (Apologeticum 33). Meanwhile the soldiers sang mocking songs about him (Plutarch, Aemilius 34).
The Arch of Titus

The arch standing at the highest point of the Sacra Via was erected by Domitian after his elder brother's death; the inscription is already addressed “to the divine Titus.”

This triumph can be seen on the two sides of the passageway. On one relief soldiers carry the treasures of the Temple on litters: the seven-branched lampstand, the golden table and the silver trumpets, exactly as Josephus describes. The procession is passing through an arch. On the other side Titus stands in the four-horse chariot, behind him Victoria crowns him with a wreath, and the horses are led by a helmeted goddess, Roma or Virtus. In the center of the vault an eagle carries the deified emperor to heaven.

The reliefs were originally painted; traces of yellow paint have been detected on the lampstand. This is the most famous ancient depiction of the Temple's menorah.
Across the Forum

Along the Sacra Via the procession descended to the Forum. The Arch of Septimius Severus did not yet stand in 71; at this end of the square began the slope leading up to the Capitol.

Plutarch writes about the three-day triumph of Aemilius Paullus as follows: on the first day the captured statues and paintings were carried on two hundred and fifty wagons. On the second, the Macedonian weapons, piled up in such a way that they clashed against one another and inspired fear even in defeat; after them three thousand men carried the silver coin in seven hundred and fifty vessels. On the third day came the trumpeters, the one hundred and twenty sacrificial oxen with gilded horns, the gold coin, then the chariot of the defeated King Perseus with his weapons and his diadem (32–33).

Behind the chariot walked the king's children with their tutors, who, weeping, taught them to stretch out their hands in supplication. The children were so small that they did not understand what was happening to them; for this reason the Romans pitied them more than their father (33).
The Carcer: the death of the enemy leader

The procession halted in front of the Temple of Jupiter. It was an ancient custom to wait until the death of the enemy commander was reported (7.153).

This was Simon son of Giora, one of the leaders of the Jerusalem revolt, who had been led among the prisoners in the procession. A rope was thrown around him, and he was dragged under the lash to the place above the Forum where, by Roman law, criminals condemned to death are executed (7.154). This place is the Carcer, in whose lower chamber, the Tullianum, Jugurtha and the leaders of the Catilinarian conspiracy were also executed.

When it was reported that it was over, the crowd broke into cheers, and the sacrifice began (7.155). Not every defeated leader ended this way: King Perseus was not executed; he died in captivity in Italy.
Temple of Jupiter on the Capitol

The destination of the procession was the Capitol. Here the commander offered the sacrifice to Jupiter Optimus Maximus, and here he laid the laurel wreath in the lap of the god's statue.

According to Josephus, after the prayers and the favorable omens the emperors went to the palace. Some they invited to their own table; for the rest, banquets were held at home. On this day the city of Rome celebrated at once its victory over its enemies, the end of the civil wars and its hope for the future (7.155–157).

The temple they stood before had burned down barely a year and a half earlier, in the last days of the civil war; at this time its rebuilding was still only under way. For the new Flavian dynasty the triumph also showed that order had been restored.
The Temple of Peace: where the treasures went

After the triumph Vespasian decided to build a temple to Peace. According to Josephus it was completed extremely quickly and surpassed all human imagination; Vespasian gathered here everything for which people had previously traveled the whole world (7.158–160). The temple was dedicated in AD 75.

Here he placed the gold objects of the Temple in Jerusalem, of which he was proud. The scroll of the Law and the purple hangings of the sanctuary, however, he had kept in the palace (7.161–162).

According to Procopius, the treasures of the Jews, which Titus had brought to Rome, were carried off to Carthage by the Vandals when they sacked the city in 455. From there Belisarius brought them to Constantinople in 534, and Justinian had them sent to the Christian churches of Jerusalem (Wars 4.9). After that all trace of them is lost.
The visit of Constantius II (AD 357)

Constantius II, son of Constantine the Great, saw Rome for the first time at the age of thirty-nine, in the twentieth year of his reign. By then the emperors had long since ceased to live here. Ammianus Marcellinus, the historian of the age, devotes an entire chapter to the visit (Res gestae 16.10).

Ammianus lists what the emperor admired. The list is not a route; the stops follow his order, and the line connects them along the known ancient streets.
The entry

The emperor arrived from the north, by way of Ocriculum (16.10.4); from there the Via Flaminia led into the city. Ammianus does not name the gate.

The procession was arranged as if it were setting out on campaign. In front came standards interwoven with gold, then the emperor alone, on a golden chariot glittering with precious stones.
