Around him were dragons woven of purple thread and fixed to spearheads, which caught the wind through their gaping mouths and hissed as if roused to anger. On either side was the armored cavalry: according to Ammianus, one might have thought they were statues polished by Praxiteles, not men (16.10.6–8).

Constantius sat motionless. He was a short man, yet he bowed his head whenever he passed under a high gate. He kept his gaze fixed rigidly ahead, as if his neck had been locked in a vise; he turned his face neither right nor left, did not nod when the wheel jolted, and no one saw him spit, wipe his nose or his face, or move his hand (16.10.9–10).

Ammianus does not hide his disapproval: the emperor entered as if he were celebrating a triumph, although he had been victorious only in civil war, at the cost of Roman blood (16.10.1–2).
At the Rostra

“When he came to the Rostra, the most famous forum of the old power, he stopped in amazement; wherever he turned his eyes, he was dazzled by the density of marvels” (16.10.13).

The Forum was still standing intact at this time. In the middle of the square stood Constantius's own equestrian statue as well, which the urban prefect had set up for him a few years earlier; its base, together with its inscription, survives beside the Arch of Septimius Severus.

Ammianus's word for the amazement (obstipuit) stands in sharp contrast to the motionless, statue-like emperor of the entry.
Before the Senate

The emperor addressed the nobility in the Curia, then the people from the platform (16.10.13).

The prelude to a great later dispute is connected with this visit. In the Curia the statue and altar of Victoria had stood since Augustus, and on the altar the senators sacrificed at the beginning of their sessions. The Christian Constantius had the altar removed (Ambrose, Epistulae 18.32).

A generation later the pagan senator Symmachus nevertheless cited him as an example when he asked for the altar to be restored: Constantius took nothing away from the privileges of the Vestal Virgins, filled the priestly offices with nobles, and did not refuse the costs of the Roman ceremonies. Accompanied by the Senate he went through the streets of the eternal city, looked at the shrines with a calm face, read the names of the gods carved on the pediments, asked about the origins of the temples, and admired their builders (Relatio 3.7).
Chariot races and an obelisk

He stayed on the Palatine, in the old imperial palace, and held chariot races on several occasions. According to Ammianus he enjoyed the biting jokes of the people, who were neither insolent nor forgetful of their old freedom; and he did not determine the outcome of the races to suit his own pleasure, as he used to do in other cities, but left it to chance, as is the custom here (16.10.13–14).

Before his departure he thought for a long time about what he could add to the city's ornaments. In the end he decided to set up an obelisk in the Circus Maximus (16.10.17).

The obelisk had already been brought by his father from Thebes in Egypt as far as Alexandria. Ammianus describes its journey: it was brought up the Tiber on a ship of three hundred oarsmen, put ashore three miles from the city, and hauled on rollers through the Porta Ostiensis to the circus. There a forest of beams was erected, and many thousands of men pulled it aloft with ropes, where it hung in the air for a long time before it settled into place (17.4.13–15).

This is the tallest obelisk in Rome. In 1587 it was dug out of the circus broken into three pieces; since then it has stood in front of the Lateran basilica.
Temple of Jupiter on the Tarpeian Rock

When the emperor surveyed the city spread out among the summits of the seven hills, on the slopes and on the plain, Ammianus writes, he felt that whatever he caught sight of first surpassed everything else. In first place in the list stands the Capitoline temple: “the sanctuary of Tarpeian Jupiter, which surpasses the rest as much as divine things surpass earthly ones” (16.10.14).

In 357 the temple still stood in its full splendor, with Domitian's gilded bronze roof tiles. Ammianus was a pagan, and this sentence is his own judgment: he has a Christian emperor declare that the greatest sight in Rome is the house of Jupiter.

Half of the roof tiles were carried off by the Vandals a century later (Procopius, Wars 3.5).
The baths

“The baths built on the scale of provinces” (16.10.14). Ammianus does not name them. In 357 several large imperial baths were operating in Rome; the largest was Diocletian's, which had been opened barely half a century earlier, c. 306, the second Caracalla's.

The comparison is no great exaggeration. The main building of the Baths of Diocletian, together with the gardens and the enclosure wall, occupied thirteen hectares. The cold-water hall is now a church, Santa Maria degli Angeli, which Michelangelo created beneath the Roman vaults; the National Roman Museum operates in the other halls.

The baths operated as long as the aqueducts did: the Goths cut them in 537.
The amphitheater

“The solid mass of the amphitheater, joined together from Tivoli stone, to whose top the human eye can barely reach” (16.10.14).

The building was almost three hundred years old at this time and was still in use. Tivoli stone is travertine: the outer ring was built of it, held together with iron clamps. In the Middle Ages the clamps were pried out for the metal; their places are the many holes visible on the facade today.

Gladiatorial games were held in it until the first half of the 5th century, animal fights until the beginning of the 6th century.

“The Pantheon, like a round city district, with its high vault, in its beauty” (16.10.14).

Ammianus's comparison refers to the size: the inner diameter and the height of the dome are both about forty-three meters. It is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

In 357 it was still a temple, with statues in its niches. Two hundred and fifty years later, in 609, the emperor Phocas gave it to the pope, and it became a Christian church; to this it owes the fact that it has remained intact.
The columns

“And the columns raised on high, whose summit can be climbed, and which bear the likenesses of the earlier emperors” (16.10.14).

There were two such columns: Trajan's in his forum and Marcus Aurelius's on the Campus Martius. Inside both a spiral staircase leads to the top, and around the shaft of both a relief of the emperor's wars runs in a spiral.

The statues of the emperors were lost in the Middle Ages. Since the end of the 16th century a statue of St Peter has stood on Trajan's Column and one of St Paul on that of Marcus Aurelius.
The Temple of the City

Ammianus calls it simply this: “the Temple of the City” (16.10.14). This was the double temple of Venus and Roma at the end of the Sacra Via, the largest temple in Rome, which Hadrian had built to his own designs.

The two sanctuaries stood back to back: that of Venus faced the amphitheater, that of Roma the Forum. According to Cassius Dio the architect Apollodorus criticized the designs: the seated goddesses are so large that if they wanted to stand up, they would hit their heads on the ceiling (69.4).

The temple was rebuilt by Maxentius after the fire of 307; the apses visible today date from this time. In 357, then, this was one of the city's newest great buildings.
The Forum of Peace

By the 4th century Vespasian's Temple of Peace was already being called a forum. It was a large garden surrounded by porticoes, with fountains and statues; in the halls were a library and an art collection.

Here were kept the treasures of the Temple in Jerusalem, which Titus had brought away in 70. On the wall of one of its rooms hung the huge marble map of the city, the Forma Urbis, whose fragments can be seen on one of the layers of the map.

Two hundred years later Procopius still saw Myron's famous bronze cow here beside a fountain (Wars 8.21).
The Theater of Pompey

Rome's first stone theater was four hundred years old at this time. Pompey had it built in 55 BC; on top of the auditorium he raised a temple of Venus, so that the building would count as a temple and the tiers of seats as the temple's steps.

The emperors restored it again and again. Elsewhere Ammianus remarks that the Romans loved the theater passionately, and he records with resentment that in a time of famine the foreigners, among them the scholars, were expelled from the city, but three thousand dancing girls were kept there together with their attendants (14.6.19).

The curve of the auditorium is preserved today by the ground plan of the houses built on top of it beside the Campo de' Fiori.
The Odeum

Domitian's roofed hall for musical performances, beside the stadium. Its location on the map is a conjecture; according to the traditional identification, the curved facade of the Palazzo Massimo follows the line of its auditorium.

Today this is the least known building in the list, because hardly anything of it survives. According to Cassius Dio, Apollodorus of Damascus, the architect of the Forum of Trajan, worked on it (69.4).
The Stadium

The Stadium of Domitian was built for athletic contests held in the Greek manner, for about thirty thousand spectators. Its shape is preserved exactly by the Piazza Navona: the houses stand on the foundation walls of the seating, and the square is the running track.

Ammianus closes the list here: “and among these the other ornaments of the eternal city” (16.10.14). The expression “eternal city” recurs several times in his work; a native speaker of Greek and a soldier from Antioch, he wrote his historical work in Rome, in Latin.
Forum of Trajan

“But when he came to the Forum of Trajan, this structure unparalleled under heaven, which in our opinion is marvelous even in the judgment of the gods, he stopped transfixed and let his gaze wander around the gigantic complex of buildings, which can neither be described in words nor ever again be created by mortals” (16.10.15).

He gave up hope of building anything similar. He said only this much: Trajan's horse, which stands in the middle of the court and carries the emperor, that he wished to have copied and was able to.

Beside him stood Hormisdas, the exiled Persian prince, who answered thus: “First, my emperor, command such a stable to be built, if you can; so that the horse you wish to have made may range over a space as wide as this one that we see.” When he was asked what he thought of Rome, he said: the only thing that pleased him was that he had learned that here too people die (16.10.15–16).

Archaeologists have found the foundation of the equestrian statue in the middle of the square; a separate element marks it on the map. Constantius left Rome on the thirtieth day, May 29, and never returned again (16.10.20).
Christian Rome in the 4th–5th centuries

From the great basilicas of the age of Constantine to the smaller community churches (tituli). The dates come mainly from the Liber Pontificalis, the collection of the lives of the popes, whose early parts were written in the 6th century.

In most places the early church survives beneath the present building or in its walls. The line is not a historical route: between the stops it runs along the known ancient streets, where there is evidence for them.
The Lateran basilica

Constantine's first great church, the cathedral of the bishop of Rome. In the fall of 312, after the victory at the Milvian Bridge, the emperor disbanded the imperial horse guard, which had fought on the side of his opponent, Maxentius, and gave the site of their demolished barracks to the Church. The walls of the barracks are still there beneath the floor of the church.

The five-aisled basilica was about a hundred meters long. It was built not in the center of the city, among the forums and the old temples, but on its edge, beside the city wall, on imperial property: in this way it did not offend the pagan senatorial aristocracy.

The Liber Pontificalis lists Constantine's gifts at length: a silver pediment with statues, seven silver altars, gold and silver lamps, and the estates whose income provided the oil for the lighting (Life of Silvester).

The present building is largely a rebuilding of the 17th–18th centuries, but the ground plan is Constantine's. According to its inscription it is “the mother and head of all the churches of the city and the world.”
Santa Croce in Gerusalemme

The Sessorium was an imperial palace in the southeastern corner of the city; Constantine's mother, Helena, lived in it. One of the palace's large halls was converted into a church: the walls of the present church are the walls of the 3rd-century hall.

According to the Liber Pontificalis, Constantine founded a basilica in the Sessorian palace, where he placed a piece of the wood of the holy Cross set in gold and precious stones; the church was called Jerusalem (Life of Silvester).

Helena visited the Holy Land c. 326. That she found the cross is something the contemporary Eusebius does not yet mention; the story appears at the end of the 4th century, and among the surviving Latin texts first in Ambrose (395).

The neighboring amphitheater and the circus also belonged to the palace; both can be seen on the map.

Pope Sixtus III (432–440) had it built, immediately after the Council of Ephesus (431), which declared that Mary is the Mother of God. The dedication can still be read on the mosaic of the triumphal arch: “Bishop Sixtus to the people of God.”

This is the only one of the great Roman basilicas that has preserved its 5th-century interior: the forty Ionic columns, with the mosaic panels of the nave above them. The panels show scenes from the Old Testament from Abraham to Joshua; of the original forty-two, twenty-seven survive. Their style is still that of late antique painting: landscapes, shadows, figures in motion.

The triumphal arch depicts scenes from the childhood of Jesus; on it Mary wears the dress of an empress.

The story of the miracle of the snowfall, according to which August snow marked out the site of the church, is a medieval legend.
Santa Pudenziana

The church was created at the end of the 4th century in the hall of a 2nd-century bath building; the Roman brick walls can still be seen from the outside.

Its apse mosaic was made c. 400 and is one of the oldest surviving church apse mosaics in Rome. Christ, in a golden robe, sits enthroned among the apostles, who wear togas in the manner of Roman senators. Behind them a city with porticoes is visible; in the buildings of the background scholars recognize the churches of Constantinian Jerusalem. Above it a jeweled cross stands on a hill, with the winged symbols of the four evangelists in the sky.

The image still speaks the language of imperial art: Christ sits like an emperor in the circle of his council. The lower band and the two edges of the mosaic were cut off during the 16th-century rebuilding.
San Clemente

Three buildings one above the other. At the top is the 12th-century church. Beneath it, four meters below the present street level, is the 4th-century basilica, which Jerome mentions in 392: the memory of Clement “is preserved in Rome to this day by the church built in his name” (De viris illustribus 15).

Still lower are 1st-century buildings: a large public building with tufa walls and a dwelling house, in whose courtyard a sanctuary of Mithras was installed at the end of the 2nd century. The altar still stands in its place, with the bull-slaying god on it. On the lowest level one can still hear the water flowing behind the walls.

The 4th-century church was filled in after the Norman sack of 1084, and the present one was built on top of it. It fell into oblivion for seven hundred years, until in 1857 the church's Irish Dominican prior, Joseph Mullooly, began to dig.
Santi Giovanni e Paolo

Beneath the basilica an entire Roman city block survives: several houses and shops of the 2nd–3rd centuries, which were joined into a single elegant house in the 3rd century. Twenty of their rooms can be visited, with wall paintings.

Some of the paintings have pagan subjects, and there is a small 4th-century niche in whose pictures scholars see Christian martyrdom scenes; it is one of the earliest such depictions. According to tradition, John and Paul, two court officials, were killed and buried in the house under the emperor Julian (361–363).

The basilica was built over the house c. 400 by the senator Pammachius, a friend of Jerome. The houses were discovered in 1887 by one of the church's monks.
Santa Sabina

The best-preserved church of 5th-century Rome. The mosaic inscription above the entrance names the builder and the period: it was erected by the presbyter Peter, of Illyrian origin, in the time of Pope Celestine (422–432).

The nave is lined by twenty-four Corinthian marble columns, with colored marble inlay above them. The light pouring in through the large windows and the spacious, undivided interior show exactly what a late antique basilica was like.

Its cypress-wood door dates from the time of construction. Eighteen of its carved panels survive, with biblical scenes. In the upper left corner Christ stands with outstretched arms between two other figures: this is one of the earliest public depictions of the crucifixion. For a long time the early Christians avoided this image, because death on the cross was the punishment of slaves and rebels.
Santa Maria in Trastevere

According to the Liber Pontificalis, Pope Julius I (337–352) built a basilica “across the Tiber, in the fourteenth region, next to Callistus.” Tradition links Pope Callistus (217–222) with this quarter.

In antiquity Trastevere was the quarter of harbor workers, craftsmen and immigrants, with a large Jewish and Syrian community; Christianity took root here early.

The present church is a 12th-century rebuilding on the 4th-century foundations. The columns of the nave and their Ionic capitals come from ancient buildings.

An old story is attached to the place: according to Jerome's chronicle, around 38 BC oil burst out of the ground from an inn across the Tiber and flowed all day. Christians later regarded this as a portent of the birth of Christ.
San Marco

Pope Mark was in office for only eight months, in 336. According to the Liber Pontificalis, he founded this church “next to the Pallacinae,” at the foot of the Capitol; it is one of the earliest community churches in the city founded by a pope.

The early tituli usually bore the name of the founder or the donor, not that of a saint. Later the name-giver was identified with a saint of the same name: this is how the church of Pope Mark became the church of Mark the Evangelist.

The remains of the 4th-century building lie beneath the present church. The apse mosaic is of the 9th century; in the 15th century the church was rebuilt as part of the Palazzo Venezia.
San Lorenzo in Damaso

It was founded by Pope Damasus (366–384), according to tradition in his father's house, next to the Theater of Pompey. According to his verse inscription, he wanted to build a new home here for the archives of the church.

Damasus was the pope who marked the tombs of the martyrs in the catacombs with verse inscriptions, and who commissioned his secretary, Jerome, to revise the Latin text of the Bible. His election was accompanied by bloody street fighting; according to Ammianus Marcellinus, after the clash between his supporters and those of the rival candidate, one hundred and thirty-seven dead were found in a single church (27.3.12–13).

The early basilica was demolished at the end of the 15th century, when the palace of the Cancelleria was built, and the church was moved into a wing of the palace. Its foundation walls were found beneath the palace courtyard by the excavations begun in 1988.

Constantine began building it in the 320s on the side of the Vatican hill, above a cemetery still in use. The site was not chosen for its suitability: the hillside had to be cut away, the side toward the valley had to be filled in, and the tomb buildings were stripped of their roofs and buried, so that the center of the basilica would lie exactly above one particular tomb.

The five-aisled church with a transept was, together with its forecourt, more than two hundred meters long. According to the Liber Pontificalis, Constantine and Helena placed a gold cross on the tomb (Life of Silvester).

The basilica stood for twelve hundred years. In 1506 Pope Julius II began its demolition to make room for the new one; the work lasted more than a hundred years. Beneath the floor of the present church, at the level of the Vatican Grottoes, runs the floor level of the old basilica.
Tomb of St Peter

At the end of the 2nd century a Roman priest named Gaius wrote this in a polemical work: “I can show you the trophies of the apostles; if you go out to the Vatican or to the road to Ostia, you will find the trophies of those who founded this church” (quoted by Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 2.25).

The excavations of 1940–49 found this memorial beneath the high altar: a small structure with a niche and two columns, erected c. 160 in front of a red-plastered wall, at the edge of a cemetery full of pagan tomb buildings. Around it the walls are densely covered with prayers scratched in by visitors.

Constantine encased this small structure in marble and built the basilica around it. The cemetery street beneath the excavations, with its tomb buildings, can be visited by prior booking.
The sieges of Rome in the Gothic War (536–552)

Belisarius, the general of the emperor Justinian, recaptured Rome from the Ostrogoths in 536. In the following sixteen years the city changed hands five times. The main source is Procopius of Caesarea, Belisarius' secretary, who lived through the first siege in the city (Wars, books 5–8).

The walk proceeds along the walls, from gate to gate. Between the gates the line follows the Aurelian Wall, elsewhere the known ancient streets; it is not a historical route.
December 536: Belisarius enters the city

Belisarius arrived from Naples, on the Via Latina, with only five thousand soldiers. The Romans, who did not want their city to share the fate of Naples, sent an envoy to meet him and invited him in.

He marched in through the Porta Asinaria on December 9, 536. At the same hour the Gothic garrison left at the other end of the city, through the Porta Flaminia. Procopius remarks: after sixty years Rome came into the hands of the Romans again (5.14.14).

The Gothic commander alone remained at his post; Belisarius sent him and the keys of the gates to the emperor.

The gate still stands today beside the Lateran basilica, with its two round towers. Ten years later this same gate became the city's undoing.
Strengthening the walls

Belisarius knew that the Goths would come back. He immediately set about repairing the Aurelian Wall, built in the 270s. He had a protective wing built on the left side of every merlon of the battlements, so that the defenders could not be hit by shots from the side, and had a deep ditch dug in front of the wall (5.14.15).

The Romans admired the work, but they were uneasy: they did not understand why he wanted to undergo a siege in a city that cannot receive supplies from the sea, and whose circuit is so great that it can hardly be defended. The wall was nineteen kilometers long; with Belisarius' five thousand men there was not even one defender for every meter.

Procopius counts fourteen gates and a few smaller posterns (5.19.1). He had the grain brought from Sicily, and he forced the inhabitants of the surrounding area to carry their stores into the city.
March 537: the Gothic camps

Vitigis, king of the Goths, arrived with his army in the early spring of 537. He was unable to encircle the wall completely. He built six fortified camps on the northern and eastern sides of the city, from the Porta Flaminia to the Porta Praenestina, facing five gates; and a seventh on the far bank of the Tiber, on the Plain of Nero (5.19.2–3, 12).

Belisarius himself took over the most dangerous section, the stretch between the Porta Pinciana and the Porta Salaria (5.19.14).

On the eighteenth day of the siege the Goths launched a general assault. Against the Porta Salaria they brought wheeled siege towers drawn by oxen, as tall as the wall. The Romans were terrified. Belisarius laughed, and forbade anyone to shoot. When the towers reached the ditch, he drew his bow himself and shot two Gothic officers; then he gave the order that everyone should aim only at the oxen. The animals fell dead, and the towers were left standing there in the field (5.22.1–9).
The walled-up gate

At the beginning of the siege Belisarius had the Porta Flaminia, opposite which one of the Gothic camps stood, walled up with large stones, so that it could not be opened even from the inside (5.19.16).

The Goths did not attack this gate during the entire siege. According to Procopius, this was because it stood on a steep slope and was hard to approach (5.23.2).

The siege ended after one year and nine days, in March 538. The Goths set fire to their camps and marched away northward, across the Milvian Bridge. Belisarius waited until half of their army had crossed the bridge, then sallied out through the Porta Pinciana and attacked those left behind (6.10.12–20).
The Porta Pinciana and the “broken wall”

Belisarius set up his headquarters on the Pincian Hill, near the gate. According to the Liber Pontificalis, it was to this palace that in March 537 he summoned Pope Silverius, who was accused of intending, by letter, to open the Porta Asinaria to the Goths. The pope was stripped of his office and sent into exile in a monk's habit (Life of Silverius; Procopius 5.25.13).

Between the Porta Flaminia and the Porta Pinciana a section of the wall had long ago split, up to half its height, and leaned so much that one part of it inclined outward and the other inward. The Romans called it the “broken wall.” When Belisarius wanted to have it pulled down and rebuilt, the Romans would not let him: they said that the apostle Peter had promised them that he himself would watch over this place.

And indeed, writes Procopius: neither on that day nor during the whole time of the siege did a single enemy come there, which he himself considers worthy of wonder. Nor did anyone dare to repair the wall later (5.23.3–8).

The leaning section of wall still stands today; its name is Muro Torto.
The cut aqueducts

In the first days of the siege the Goths cut all fourteen aqueducts, so that no water would reach the city (5.19.13).

Drinking water remained: the Tiber and the wells were sufficient. The great imperial baths, however, shut down, and never started up again. Belisarius had the channels of the aqueducts walled up for a long stretch at their city end, lest the enemy get in through them; he himself had taken Naples this way a year earlier (5.19.18).

The Goths set up one of their camps south of the city, at the place where the arcades of two aqueducts cross each other twice and enclose a closed space; they blocked the openings of the arches with stones and earth, and stationed seven thousand men in it, to cut off the supplies coming from the south (6.3.3–7).

In this way the siege changed Rome more than any earlier sack. The hills, where water came up only by aqueduct, became depopulated in the following centuries; the population withdrew into the bend of the Tiber.
The mills of the Janiculum and the ship mills

The city's grain was ground on the slope of the Janiculum, where the water of Trajan's aqueduct rushed down with a great fall and drove a row of mill wheels. When the Goths cut the aqueduct, the mills stopped. Nor could the grinding be done with animals, because during the siege there was scarcely enough fodder even for the horses (5.19.19–20).

Belisarius found a solution. Below the bridge, where the current of the river is strongest, he had ropes stretched between the two banks. To these he tied boats in pairs, two feet apart from each other, placed two millstones on each pair, and hung between them a wheel, which the river drove. The row of boats stood one behind the other, and they ground as much as the city needed (5.19.21–22).

The Goths floated tree trunks and corpses downstream to smash the wheels. In response Belisarius stretched iron chains in front of the bridge, which caught everything (5.19.23–27).

After this the ship mills of the Tiber operated for more than thirteen hundred years; the last ones were removed at the end of the 19th century, when the embankments were built. The location of the Janiculum mills on the map is conjectural.
Tomb of Hadrian: the statues

On the same day of the assault the Goths also attacked the Mausoleum of Hadrian on the far bank of the Tiber. Procopius describes what it was like at that time: it stands a stone's throw in front of the wall, built of blocks of Parian marble that fit together without any binding material. It has four equal sides, each a stone's throw wide, and it is higher than the city wall. On top stand marvelous statues of men and horses, carved from the same marble. The men of old joined it to the city wall by two walls, to make a fortress of it (5.22.12–14).

The Goths approached it unnoticed, under cover of the colonnade leading to St Peter's Basilica, beneath large shields, with ladders. They got so close that the defenders' missile engines could no longer reach them.

For a moment the defenders froze. Then by common resolve they broke up most of the statues, lifted the huge pieces of marble with both hands, and hurled them down on the heads of the enemy. The Goths fell back (5.22.19–22).

This is how the sculptural decoration of the mausoleum perished. From then on the building was a fortress; today its name is Castel Sant'Angelo.
The Porta Praenestina and the menagerie

On the eastern side of the city, in front of today's Porta Maggiore, stood an old enclosure surrounded by a low wall, the Vivarium, where the lions and the other wild animals had once been kept for the games in the arena. The city wall was especially weak here, because most of the mortar had fallen out from between the bricks.

Vitigis knew this, and directed the main assault here. The Goths broke through the low outer wall and pushed into the enclosure (5.22.10; 5.23.13–17).

Belisarius, who was called over from the Porta Salaria, did not defend from the wall. He let the Goths crowd into the narrow space, then suddenly had the gate opened and sallied out. The Goths could neither deploy nor flee; they trampled one another. The Romans pursued them beyond the gate and set fire to their siege engines (5.23.18–23).

According to Procopius, the Goths lost thirty thousand men on that one day; the number is an obvious exaggeration, but the general assault failed, and Vitigis never attempted it again.
Torches in the aqueduct

Toward the end of the siege the Goths tried to get in through a dried-up aqueduct. By night, with lamps and torches, they walked along the channel all the way into the interior of the city, until Belisarius' masonry stopped them. They took a stone out of it as proof and went back to report (6.9.1–2, 5–7).

Near the Porta Pinciana there was a gap in one of the arches of the aqueduct. One of the guards saw the light through it and told his comrades. They laughed at him: he must have seen the eyes of a wolf shining. The aqueduct ran low above the ground there (6.9.3–4).

The next day the wolf came up again among the guards. The story reached Belisarius, who did not wave it away. He sent men down into the channel; they found the lamps the Goths had dropped, the ashes of the torches and the place from which the stone had been taken. Belisarius posted a guard in the aqueduct, and the Goths gave up the plan (6.9.8–11).

Procopius does not name the aqueduct; on the basis of its location scholars identify it with the Aqua Virgo, which enters the city beneath the Pincian.
The gates of Janus in the Forum

During the siege, writes Procopius, some Romans secretly tried to force open the doors of the Temple of Janus.

He also describes the temple, which at that time still stood intact in the Forum, in front of the Senate house: it is made entirely of bronze, is rectangular, and is just large enough to hold the statue of Janus. The statue too is bronze, at least five cubits high, and has two faces: one looks east, the other west. Opposite each face stands a bronze door (5.25.18–21).

The Romans of old kept the doors closed in time of peace and opened them in war. Since they became Christians the custom had ceased, and the doors were not opened even in war. Now some people, in whom the old faith still lived, secretly tried to do so. They could not open them completely, but after this the door leaves no longer closed together properly. The perpetrators were never found, and in the confusion no one investigated them (5.25.22–25).

This is the last report of the temple. Its location on the map is conjectural.
December 546: Totila in St Peter's

Totila, the new king of the Goths, laid siege to Rome again in 545. He starved it for a year. According to Procopius, in the end the inhabitants were boiling nettles, and the commander, Bessas, was selling the army's grain to the senators at a high price (7.17).

On the night of December 17, 546, four Isaurian soldiers who were guarding the Porta Asinaria let themselves down from the wall on ropes and came to an agreement with Totila. The Goths climbed up, smashed the lock of the gate with axes, and the army marched in. The garrison fled through the other gate (7.20.4–16).

In the morning Totila went to St Peter's Basilica to pray. There the deacon Pelagius, the later pope, stepped before him with the Gospel in his hand: “Spare your own people, my lord.” Totila forbade the killing (7.20.22–25). According to Procopius, only five hundred citizens were by then left in the city; the wives of the senators, among them the widow of Boethius, went from house to house begging for bread (7.20.19, 27).

Totila had about a third of the walls torn down, and planned to turn the city into pasture. Belisarius appealed to him in a letter: whoever destroys Rome sins against all mankind, and disgraces his own name before posterity. Totila gave up his plan, but took the entire population with him (7.22.7–19). According to a contemporary chronicle, for forty days or more Rome was so deserted that no human being, only wild beasts, stayed in it (continuator of Marcellinus Comes, 547).
January 550: the Gate of St Paul

Belisarius returned to the empty city in the spring of 547. In twenty-five days he had the demolished stretches of wall piled up again from the stones lying around, without mortar. There were still no gate leaves when Totila appeared; Belisarius posted his best soldiers in the gateways and had iron spikes scattered in front of them against the horses. The Goths attacked for several days, then withdrew (7.24).

Belisarius was recalled in 549. Totila marched on Rome for a third time. The story repeated itself: the Isaurians guarding the gate named after the apostle St Paul, the Porta Ostiensis, whom the emperor had not paid for years and who had seen how much money the earlier traitors received, came to terms with the king (7.36.7–8).

On the night of January 16, 550, Totila sent trumpeters across the Tiber in two boats to sound the alarm on the far side of the wall. The defenders rushed there. Meanwhile the Isaurians opened St Paul's Gate (7.36.9–14).

Four hundred horsemen fled into Hadrian's tomb and also seized the bridge. The next day they beat back the Goths' assault. Totila then surrounded them; the horsemen were already thinking of eating their horses, then resolved to break out and die fighting. At that point Totila offered them free passage, or the chance to join his army. All but two went over to the Goths (7.36.17–28).
The last chariot race

This time Totila did not destroy. He meant Rome to be his seat: he called back the senators and the inhabitants held in Campania, had food brought in, and had rebuilt what he had earlier burned or demolished.

Procopius mentions in a single sentence that the king then watched the horse races, and afterwards prepared his army for the Sicilian campaign (7.37.1–4).

This is the last known race in the Circus Maximus. According to tradition, the track had been laid out eleven hundred years earlier by the Tarquin kings; every triumph and circus procession passed through here, here the city burned in 64, and here Augustus and Constantius II set up their obelisks.

A Gothic king sat in the emperors' box, and in the stands the inhabitants of a starved, shrunken city.
552: Narses and the keys

Totila fell in the battle of Busta Gallorum in the summer of 552. Justinian's new general, the eunuch Narses, of Armenian origin, marched on Rome.

The Gothic garrison was too small to defend the walls. For this reason Totila had earlier enclosed a short stretch of the city wall around Hadrian's tomb with a low wall and made a small fortress, and had the valuables carried there too. Narses' men attacked at several points at once; where there were no defenders, they climbed up on ladders and opened the gates. The Goths fled into the fortress and, after brief bargaining, surrendered (8.33.14–25).

Narses sent the keys of the gates to the emperor. Procopius sums up as follows: Rome was captured for the fifth time during Justinian's reign (8.33.27).

He adds: for the Romans and the Senate this victory became the cause of even greater destruction. The retreating Goths killed the Romans who came in their way and the senators' sons held as hostages; and Narses' barbarian mercenaries, when they marched in, treated everyone as an enemy (8.34.1–8).

The bridge that Hadrian had built to his tomb still stands today.
Quo Vadis (Henryk Sienkiewicz, 1896)

Sienkiewicz's novel is set in Nero's Rome. It begins around AD 63 and ends with Nero's fall. Its main thread is the love between the patrician Marcus Vinicius and the Christian Lygia; its background is the great fire of 64 and the persecution of the Christians.

This is a literary walk: it follows the plot of the novel, not a historical account. The places are named by the novel itself. Where it gives only a district, the stop is at a nearby point shown on the map, and the text says so. Chapter numbers in parentheses follow Jeremiah Curtin's English translation (1896); they may differ in other editions. The real fire has its own walk among the historical walks.
Aulus Plautius's house on the Vicus Patricius

At the start of the novel Petronius, Nero's “arbiter of elegance,” and his nephew Marcus Vinicius, just back from the eastern campaign, have themselves carried in a litter to the house of Aulus Plautius on the Vicus Patricius (chapter 2). Vinicius had earlier recovered here from a dislocated arm and fallen in love with Lygia, who was being raised in the house. Lygia is the daughter of a Lygian king who came to Rome as a hostage; Aulus and his wife, Pomponia Graecina, raise her as their own child.

Aulus Plautius and Pomponia Graecina are real people. Aulus led the conquest of Britain in AD 43. According to Tacitus, Pomponia was tried in AD 57 on a charge of “foreign superstition,” and her husband acquitted her before a family court (Annales 13.32). The novel turns this into her being a secret Christian.

The novel puts Petronius's house on the southern slope of the Palatine, “near the Carinae” (chapter 2). This is inaccurate: the Carinae lay northeast of the Palatine, between the Velia and the Oppian.
Lygia in the imperial palace

Vinicius asks Petronius to intercede so that he can have Lygia. On Nero's order a centurion takes the girl from Aulus's house to the Palatine, to Caesar's house, where Acte, Nero's former mistress, takes her into her care (chapters 5–7).

Lygia is also taken to the imperial feast (chapter 8). The drunken Vinicius presses himself on her; at the end of the feast Acte and Ursus carry her to Acte's rooms. There Lygia learns that Caesar has given her to Vinicius, and that she will be taken to his house that same evening (chapter 8).

In AD 63 Nero's palace on the Palatine was the Domus Tiberiana and the Domus Transitoria; the novel speaks only of “the Palatine” and “Caesar's house.” The stop is therefore the Domus Tiberiana, on the side of the hill facing the Forum.
Ambush in the Carinae

In the evening slaves carry Lygia in a litter to Vinicius's house, which stands in the Carinae. A feast is already being prepared there. As the procession turns toward the Carinae in the dark, armed men attack it; the slaves think it is Caesar and his companions out for fun, as Nero often was at night in the Subura (chapter 10).

The attackers are Lygia's supporters, among them Ursus, the girl's giant Lygian servant. Ursus takes Lygia in his arms and carries her off toward the Subura. When the bloodied slaves return, Vinicius in his rage kills Gulo, his old nurse, with a bronze lamp, and has the others flogged until morning (chapter 10).

That same night he sets out to search for her himself: he goes through the Esquiline, the Subura and the Vicus Sceleratus, around the Capitol, over the Fabrician bridge to the island, and from there into the district across the Tiber (chapter 11). The stop is the Clivus ad Carinas, the street leading into the district.
By night at the Viminal gate

Lygia is tracked down for Vinicius's money by Chilo Chilonides, a dubious Greek “philosopher.” He learns that the Christians gather at night in the Ostrianum, where a great apostle is to speak, and that Lygia will be there (chapters 17–19).

Vinicius sets out in disguise with Chilo and the wrestling champion Croton. The novel describes their route: through the Vicus Patricius, along the Viminal to the old Viminal gate, near the plain where Diocletian's baths were later built, then on past the remains of the Servian wall (chapter 20).

The location of the gate on the map is conjectural; this stretch of the Servian wall is shown on one of the map's layers.
The Nomentan Gate and the Ostrianum

They leave the city through the Nomentan Gate; according to the novel they have to hurry to get out before it is closed (chapter 19). In the novel the Ostrianum is an old underground cemetery between the Via Salaria and the Via Nomentana, enclosed by a wall overgrown with ivy; it lies beyond the edge of the map.

All the Christians of Rome gather in the cemetery to hear the Apostle Peter. Vinicius watches the ceremony from a dark corner and catches sight of Lygia. The novel describes Peter's sermon at length, and how his listeners almost see the Sea of Galilee before them (chapter 20).

Christian tradition does indeed associate a cemetery called the Ostrianum with the work of the Apostle Peter.
Across the Tiber

At dawn Vinicius and his companions follow Lygia and her escort into the district across the Tiber, where the girl lives in a narrow street. When Vinicius tries to force his way in, Ursus kills Croton in the gateway and badly injures Vinicius (chapter 21). Chilo flees.

The Christians nurse the wounded Vinicius in the house; Lygia is with him, and the Apostle Peter visits him too. Here Vinicius begins to change: the Christians forgive him, and this shakes him deeply (chapters 22–25).

The novel does not give the exact location of the house, only that it is across the Tiber, in a narrow street. Later Lygia lives in the house of Linus, on the Vicus Judaeorum (chapter 43). The stop is the Cestian bridge, which links the island with Trastevere and also appears in the novel.
The outbreak of the fire

Vinicius is with Nero's court at Antium when the news arrives: Rome is burning. According to the novel the fire broke out at the Circus Maximus, in the part facing the Palatine and the Caelian, and with incredible speed engulfed the center of the city (chapter 42). This agrees with Tacitus's account (Annales 15.38).

Nero returns as well. He climbs onto the arches of an aqueduct, which the novel calls the “Appian aqueduct,” and with a golden lute, surrounded by his entourage, sings of the fall of Troy above the burning city (chapter 46). Below, the people murmur; Petronius rides out on horseback in front of the crowd and promises them bread and games.

Here the novel works up one of the ancient rumors about the fire, which Tacitus mentions only as hearsay. The Aqua Appia ran mostly underground; it has no row of arches on the map.
Vinicius's ride to Rome

Vinicius leaps onto a horse at once and gallops toward Rome on the Via Appia, changing horses everywhere along the way without stopping (chapter 42). As he nears the city the crowd grows ever larger: refugees, carts, people camping among the tombs and gardens. The doors of the temple of Mars, which according to the novel stood near the “Porta Appia,” have been broken down by the crowd so that they can spend the night inside (chapter 43).

With great difficulty Vinicius reaches the gate, but he cannot get into the city toward the Porta Capena: the crowd and the heat make it impossible. So he takes some soldiers with him, turns back, skirts the city to the south across the Via Latina and the Ardea and Ostia roads, crosses the Tiber at a village called Vicus Alexandri, and sets off along the Via Portuensis toward the district across the Tiber (chapter 43).

The novel speaks of the Via Appia's city gate. In AD 64 the city gate here was the Porta Capena of the Servian wall; the Porta Appia of the Aurelian wall was built only two centuries later.
Along the Via Portuensis into the flames

The Via Portuensis leads straight into the district across the Tiber (chapter 43). At the gate he learns that most of the district has not yet been reached by the fire; only the alleys toward the island are burning. Linus's house on the Vicus Judaeorum stands right there; Vinicius finds it empty. On the way back the flames and smoke chase him toward the Via Portuensis, and he collapses.

He is picked up by Christians who are pulling down houses so that the fire will not reach the Via Portuensis. Among them he finds Chilo, who tells him that Linus went out two days earlier through the Nomentan Gate to the Ostrianum (chapter 43). Vinicius finds Lygia there and also speaks with the Apostle Peter (chapters 45–47).

Here too the novel closely follows the real fire: according to Tacitus, of the fourteen regions of the city three burned down completely, seven were badly damaged, and only four remained intact (Annales 15.40).
The Mamertine prison

The people want a scapegoat. Tigellinus, the commander of the guard, and Poppaea pin the arson on the Christians; Chilo betrays them. Lygia is arrested at her house and taken to the Mamertine prison (chapters 49–50). Vinicius and Petronius arrive at dawn, but the prison is already surrounded by guardsmen.

According to the novel's footnote, Lygia was not thrown into the Tullianum, the lowest, entirely underground part of the prison, where Jugurtha had once starved to death. A fever epidemic breaks out in the prisons; Lygia falls ill too (chapter 54).

This is the map's real Carcer: its lower chamber is the Tullianum, which Sallust also describes. According to the novel the Apostle Peter is later held here too, and his two guards, Processus and Martinianus, are baptized here (chapter 70).
The Esquiline prison and the arena

At night Lygia is moved to the Esquiline, to an improvised prison set up in the cellars of houses torn down to stop the fire; the novel describes it as better guarded than the Tullianum (chapters 56, 59). Vinicius gets in to see her disguised as a corpse-bearer, and they say farewell to each other. Tigellinus's house also stands on the Esquiline (chapter 53).

Meanwhile the Christians are being killed at the games. According to the novel, after the fire Nero had new amphitheaters built, mostly of wood, among them an enormous one (chapter 55). At the last evening games a German aurochs is driven in with Lygia tied to its horns; Ursus breaks the beast's neck with his bare hands. The people demand mercy, and Nero is forced to grant it (chapter 65).

The novel does not say where the amphitheater stood; the Colosseum was built only later, by the Flavians. Nor does it give the exact location of the Esquiline prison; the stop is the old Esquiline gate, which the novel also mentions.
Nero's gardens on the Vatican

Nero stages an evening spectacle in his Vatican gardens: Christians are tied to pitch-smeared posts and set alight as living torches (chapter 61). The crowd streams into the gardens over the Aemilian bridge and along the Triumphal Way, around Nero's circus.

Chilo rides in a chariot beside Nero. On one of the burning posts he recognizes Glaucus, the physician whom he himself betrayed. The sight breaks him: he cries out to the crowd that innocent people are dying here, and, pointing at Nero, names the emperor as the incendiary (chapter 61). His story is one of the turning points of the novel.

Here the novel follows Tacitus's account of the execution of the Christians in Nero's gardens (Annales 15.44). On the central line of the circus stood the obelisk that is now in the middle of St. Peter's Square.
Quo vadis, Domine?

The faithful persuade the Apostle Peter to leave the city. At dawn he sets out with the young Nazarius along the Via Appia toward Campania (chapter 69). On the way he stops, and in a vision Christ comes toward him. Peter asks: “Quo vadis, Domine?”, that is, “Where are you going, Lord?” The answer: if Peter abandons his people, he will go to Rome to be crucified again. Peter turns around and goes back to the city.

This scene gives the novel its title. The story comes from a late 2nd-century apocryphal text, the Acts of Peter; it is not among the historical sources.

At the traditional site there now stands the church of Domine Quo Vadis, about 800 meters south of the Porta Appia, beyond the edge of the map. The Porta Appia was built only in the 3rd century; at the time of the novel the Via Appia here still ran outside the city.
Peter's last journey

Peter is arrested and held in the Mamertine prison. Nero is not in Rome; according to the novel two of his freedmen, Helius and Polythetes, pass sentence. He is flogged, and the next day he is led out of the city toward the Vatican Hill (chapter 70). A huge crowd gathers in front of the gates; the faithful go with him. The soldiers lead him across the Pons Triumphalis, toward the Naumachia and the circus.

The novel remarks that the bridge of triumphs seemed, as if unwittingly, to proclaim the apostle's triumph.

The Pons Triumphalis is usually identified with the Neronian bridge, whose pier remains can be seen near today's Ponte Vittorio Emanuele when the water is low.
The deaths of Peter and Paul

Peter is crucified between the circus and the Vatican Hill (chapter 70). According to the novel, from the cross he looks at the city in the light of the setting sun and blesses it: “Urbi et orbi.” That same evening soldiers lead the Apostle Paul along the Ostian Way, through the Trigemina gate, to a place called Aquae Salviae, and behead him there.

The novel follows Christian tradition; contemporary sources say little about the year and circumstances of Peter's and Paul's deaths in Rome. Tradition places Peter's grave here, in the Vatican cemetery; the remains of the 2nd-century memorial have been found beneath St. Peter's Basilica.

At the end of the novel Petronius takes his own life at Cumae before Nero's death sentence can reach him (chapter 73). Vinicius and Lygia live in Sicily (chapter 72). The epilogue tells of Nero's fall and death.
Nero, the Bloody Poet (Dezső Kosztolányi, 1922)

Kosztolányi's first novel follows Nero from the death of Claudius (AD 54) to his own death (68): how the awkward, verse-writing youth becomes a murderous emperor who turns his power to the service of his art. It appeared in book form in 1922, with a letter from Thomas Mann meant as a preface.

This is a literary walk: it follows the plot of the novel, not a historical account. Most of the novel takes place in the palace; its city settings are rarer and sketchier than in Quo Vadis. The great fire of 64 and the persecution of the Christians do not appear in it at all. Where the novel mentions only a district or a type of building, the stop is at a nearby point shown on the map, and the text says so. The novel's chapters are not numbered, so the chapter title appears in parentheses (in English translation). Each stop ends with a short comparison with the main ancient sources.
The death of Claudius on the Palatine

The novel opens on a sweltering summer afternoon in the Forum Cupidinis, the delicacies market. An old fruit seller looks up at the hill where the aged emperor Claudius now lives in the former house of Tiberius (“Sweltering Heat”).

Up in the palace the empress Agrippina gives the thirsty Claudius water in a gourd, and he falls down dead. Nero, Agrippina's son and Claudius's adopted son, watches it all; his mother does not let him leave the room (“The Miracle”). The next day soldiers carry the youth off from the palace steps and acclaim him emperor (“Young Emperor”).

According to Tacitus and Suetonius, Claudius was poisoned with mushrooms (Annales 12.66–67; Claudius 44); the gourd of water is the novel's version. The Forum Cupedinis was one of the markets around the Forum; its exact location is unknown, and it is not on the map. The stop is the Domus Tiberiana.
Funeral oration in the Forum

At Claudius's funeral Nero delivers the eulogy from the speakers' platform in the Forum; Seneca wrote it for him. The dead man is declared a god (“The Miracle”). Tacitus also records that the speech was Seneca's work, and that the older people noted that Nero was the first emperor who needed someone else's eloquence (Annales 13.3).

Years later, one autumn morning, Seneca comes down to the Forum through the Argiletum, past the row of bookshops, and goes on from there to the steam bath. The novel lists what he sees: the statues of Alcibiades and Marsyas, the back-street lawyers near the sundial, the money changers, and a street boy selling matches in front of the statue of the she-wolf (“Three Poets in the Steam Bath”).

Martial also mentions the booksellers of the Argiletum; the statue of Marsyas really did stand in the Forum. The stop is the Rostra.
Around the Circus Maximus

The Circus Maximus is a recurring setting in the novel. On sleepless nights Nero remembers his childhood: after his father's death he grew up in the house of his aunt Lepida, sharing a room with a dancer who performed in the Circus Maximus (“Night in Labor”). As emperor, dressed as a charioteer, he roams the booths and street girls around the circus at night with the poet Zodicus (“Literary School”).

Later he races himself: according to the novel four hundred thousand people watch him on the track between the Palatine and the Aventine (“The Charioteer”). After Poppaea's death he wanders around the circus and believes he has found the dead woman in a boy named Sporus (“Alone”).

According to Suetonius, the child Nero grew up at his aunt's under the supervision of a dancer and a barber (Nero 6). Tacitus also writes about the night wanderings (Annales 13.25), and according to Suetonius Nero drove a chariot in the Circus Maximus as well (Nero 22). Pliny the Elder puts the circus's capacity at 250,000 (Nat. hist. 36.102).
Night on the Fabrician bridge

The night excursions grow wilder. Nero brings home a wretched dwarf from the outskirts to keep on a chain for the amusement of his guests. Zodicus and Fannius, the two court poets, throw dogs and cats from the Fabrician bridge into the Tiber every night. They make such a racket that the night watch turns out, suspecting a murder (“Wings Grow”).

Meanwhile in the palace Octavia, Nero's fourteen-year-old wife, waits in vain for her husband to come home and listens to the flute playing from the garden.

According to Tacitus, Nero roamed the streets, taverns and brothels at night disguised as a slave, and with his companions also assaulted passers-by (Annales 13.25). The Fabrician bridge, built in 62 BC, is still in use today.
Nero's garden and the death of Britannicus

At dusk Nero likes to sit in the garden by the fountain. From there he can see the slopes of the Esquiline, where there was once a cemetery for the poor until Maecenas had it turned into a promenade (“Doctors at the Sickbed”). Now he cannot work: the voice of his stepbrother Britannicus will not leave his head.

At dawn he walks out to the outskirts to Locusta, the poisoner, and has her brew fresh poison before his eyes. He gives a festive meal and invites Britannicus too. Britannicus finds the wine too hot and asks for cold water; Zodicus pours his own cup into it. The boy's head falls onto the gold plate, and the feast goes on (“Murder”).

Horace also describes the transformation of the cemetery (Satirae 1.8). Britannicus died at an imperial banquet in AD 55; according to Tacitus too, the drink that was too hot was cooled with the poisoned cold water (Annales 13.15–17); according to Suetonius, Locusta brewed the poison in Nero's bedroom, before his eyes (Nero 33). The novel does not name the garden; the stop is the surviving building of the Gardens of Maecenas.
A woman in the audience

Nero goes to the Theater of Marcellus with Epaphroditus, his secretary, and the actor Paris. From a side box he watches the farces and pantomimes, which the people now like better than tragedies (“A Woman in the Audience”).

He is bored, so he watches the audience instead. Down in the stalls, in the rows of the knights, he notices a woman who seems to be looking toward the imperial box. Paris whispers to him that she is Poppaea Sabina, who is there every evening.

According to the sources, Nero met Poppaea through Otho, whose wife she then was (Tacitus, Annales 13.45–46); the meeting at the theater is the novel's invention.
Nero on stage

Poppaea wants Nero to perform before a large audience. They go through the theaters one by one: Balbus's is small, Marcellus's is pretty, Pompey's is very large; according to the novel it holds forty thousand spectators (“Applause”). Seneca and Burrus organize the paid applauders.

Nero first performs at the youth festival, the Juvenalia; he trembles with stage fright all day (“The Divine Actor”). Afterward the companies of the theaters of Pompey, Marcellus and Balbus all send delegations to congratulate him (“Triumph”). Later he also performs in the Theater of Pompey (the chapter “Society of Roman Citharists”).

According to Tacitus, the Juvenalia performance took place in Nero's private theater, and a special troop was organized from the applauders (Annales 14.15). According to Pliny the Elder, Nero had the Theater of Pompey gilded for a single day for the visit of the Armenian king Tiridates (Nat. hist. 33.54). The 4th-century register gives the theater 17,580 places.
Poppaea on the Campus Martius

Poppaea deliberately draws away from Nero so as to bind him more closely to her. She throws him away from her the way a circus juggler throws a hoop: so that it rolls back on its own (“The Hoop That Rolls Back”).

She has herself carried through the Campus Martius, under the Porticus of Octavia, the promenade of high society. In front of the Theater of Marcellus she meets Menecrates, the lyre player, who invites her to his villa. She looks up the actors and writers she has neglected for a while and hears the latest literary gossip.

Menecrates is a real person: according to Suetonius, Nero presented him with the property and houses of generals who had celebrated triumphs (Nero 30).
The Society of Roman Citharists

The Society of Roman Citharists is housed on the Via Appia, in two rooms on an upper floor. It was once a meeting place for musicians; now it is a dicing den for poets and actors who have fallen out of the emperor's favor (the chapter “Society of Roman Citharists”).

Zodicus and Fannius gather here, and here they run down Nero, who these days sings almost every evening in the circus and the theater. Zodicus says the emperor is performing in the Theater of Pompey that day, but that he did not even go.

The society is the novel's invention; the novel does not give the exact location of the house along the Via Appia. The stop is the road's stretch within the city.
Conspiracy at the harbor

At night ships are loading in the Tiber harbor, and the sailors of the fleet at Misenum arrive too. That same night the conspirators led by Piso meet, among them Zodicus and Fannius, who point to the sailors' discontent. The conspirators plan that at the festival of Ceres, when Nero is at the circus, the consul Lateranus will hand him a petition and the others will stab him, as Caesar was once stabbed (“Revolution”).

The conspiracy is uncovered. Seneca is drawn into it too; the emperor condemns him to death. Seneca dies in the bath water, in the presence of a centurion, in the arms of his wife Paulina (“Seneca”).

This is one of the most historical parts of the novel. According to Tacitus, Epicharis tried to win over an officer of the fleet at Misenum, and the assassination was planned for the circus games of the festival of Ceres (Annales 15.51, 15.53). Seneca died at his villa four miles from the city (15.60–64). The novel does not name the harbor; the stop is the Emporium, Rome's main river port.
The colossus in front of the palace

In the first half of the novel, after Corbulo's victory in the East, Nero has the statues of the old emperors removed and sets up his own hundred-foot bronze statue in front of the palace colonnade (“To Forget”). Toward the end of the novel, in the days of the revolt, someone hangs a leather sack on the colossus. Matricides were sewn into such sacks. From this Nero understands that it is the end (“In Phaon's Garden”).

Nero had Agrippina killed years before; the novel tells of it in the chapters “Storm” and “The Best Mother,” beyond the edge of the map, on the seacoast.

According to Suetonius, the 120-foot statue stood in the vestibule of Nero's Golden House, and during the revolt a sack was tied to one of his statues with the inscription: “What could I do? But you deserved the sack” (Nero 31, 45). The colossus was built only after the fire of 64; the novel places it earlier. Hadrian later had it moved next to the Colosseum; the site of its base is shown separately on the map.
Flight from the city

At night Epaphroditus wakes Nero: the soldiers have deserted him, and people are speaking of Galba as emperor. Nero puts on a charioteer's clothes, takes Britannicus's old lyre, and flees the palace with Sporus and his secretary through a gap broken in a wall (“In Phaon's Garden”).

They come out onto the Palatine, then walk in the dark along the bank of the Tiber, stumbling over corpses. Fires flare up on the Pincian and the Vatican. Until dawn they meet no one on the olive-lined road.

The novel names no gate. The Via Salaria started at the Porta Collina of the Servian wall; according to Suetonius, Nero fled on horseback, barefoot, his face covered, with four companions, and passed the camp of the guard (Nero 48).
In Phaon's garden

On the Via Salaria, not far from the city, lives Phaon, a freedman who once worked in the imperial treasury and has retired to farming. At his gate a fugitive in charioteer's clothes, with a stubbly chin, asks to be let in: the emperor (“In Phaon's Garden”).

By evening the soldiers arrive. In a shed Nero tries to kill himself with his stage sword but cannot; in the end Epaphroditus, out of pity, presses his head onto it. After his death his old nurse, Ecloge, arrives from Rome, washes him, laments him in Greek, and puts an obol for Charon in his mouth (“Lament”).

According to Suetonius, Phaon's villa lay between the Via Salaria and the Via Nomentana, around the fourth milestone, beyond the edge of the map. As he died, Nero said: “What an artist perishes with me!” His nurses Egloge and Alexandria, together with Acte, buried him in the tomb of the Domitii on the Pincian Hill (Nero 48–50).
Fabiola (Nicholas Wiseman, 1854)

Cardinal Wiseman's novel is set in the Rome of Diocletian and Maximian, during the great persecution of the Christians that began in 303, and ends with the victory of Constantine. Its heroine is Fabiola, a rich pagan Roman girl who is baptized by the end of the novel. Beside her, the Roman martyrs of Christian tradition are the main characters: Pancratius, Sebastian and Agnes.

This is a literary walk: it follows the plot of the novel, not a historical account. The novel takes the martyrs' stories from late antique acts of the martyrs and from legend; their historical value is limited. Wiseman was also an archaeologist, and he often gives the places precisely, citing the excavations of his own day. The novel has three parts; references give the part and chapter number. The text follows the English edition on Project Gutenberg.
Lucina's house

The novel opens on a September afternoon in the Campus Martius. According to the novel, the house of Lucina, the Christian widow, stood exactly opposite the east side of the Saepta Iulia: the church of San Marcello stands on its grounds today, and it reached back to the foot of the Quirinal (Part I, chapter 1).

Here Lucina talks with her fourteen-year-old son Pancratius. That day at school the oldest pupil, Corvinus, challenged Pancratius to a fight; he refused to fight, so Corvinus struck him in the face. Lucina therefore decides the time has come: she gives her son the little purse she wears around her neck, holding a sponge stained with the blood of his martyred father (Part I, chapters 2–3).

San Marcello is one of Rome's titular churches. According to the Liber Pontificalis, Pope Marcellus was condemned, as a punishment, to serve as a stable hand in his church, which stood in the house of a woman named Lucina; the novel's Lucina alludes to this tradition.
The Vicus Patricius: Agnes's house and the pope's church

According to the novel, Agnes, Fabiola's Christian cousin, twelve or thirteen years old, lived with her parents on the Vicus Patricius. On the same street stood the house of the senator Pudens, where according to tradition the Apostle Peter also lived, and which in the time of the novel was the church and residence of the popes (Part II, chapter 10). Here the pope consecrates Agnes and Syra, Fabiola's slave, as brides of Christ. The blind Caecilia joins them as a third, bringing a crown woven of thorns instead of flowers (Part II, chapter 11).

According to the novel, Fabiola's family lived in the house of Fabius, a knight, in the valley between the Quirinal and the Esquiline (Part I, chapter 4); it gives no more precise location.

The novel itself identifies the Vicus Patricius by the church of Santa Pudenziana; the church stands on the site of the titulus Pudentis, and its apse mosaic was made around 400. The tradition of the house of Pudens and of Peter's stay there is legendary.
Sebastian's apartment on the Palatine

Sebastian, a Christian officer of the imperial guard, lives on the Palatine. The novel describes the place precisely: in the rooms named after Mammaea, built by Alexander Severus, at the corner of the hill that looks toward the Caelian, above the later Arch of Constantine and the Meta Sudans fountain (Part I, chapter 9).

On a moonlit autumn evening Sebastian and Pancratius look out from here at the Flavian amphitheater, the Septizodium and the Baths of Caracalla. Pancratius points to the arches of the amphitheater: their triumphal arch is there. Then a lion's roar is heard from below the Caelian; wild beasts have been brought to the amphitheater's vivarium.

The Historia Augusta does mention rooms on the Palatine named after Mammaea (Alexander Severus 26); their location is unknown. The stop is the Meta Sudans fountain, which the novel also names.
The cemetery of Callistus on the Via Appia

Diogenes, the old gravedigger, lives with his sons in the Subura and is the chief gravedigger of the cemetery of Callistus (Part II, chapters 1–2). The faithful set out in pairs along the Via Appia, and nearly two miles from the gate, behind the tombs, they go down through different entrances of a villa. Diogenes leads the young people through the galleries with a lamp; Torquatus secretly draws marks in the sand so that he can find his way back later (Part II, chapters 2–4).

The apostate Torquatus, recruited by Fulvius, the informer, betrays the cemetery. After the edict is proclaimed, soldiers break in. They capture Caecilia, the blind Christian girl, who dies quietly, without violence, before the prefect's tribunal (Part II, chapters 16–17).

The catacomb of Callistus lies along the Via Appia Antica, beyond the edge of the map; the stop is the Porta Appia. The crypt of the 3rd-century popes was uncovered by Giovanni Battista de Rossi around 1854; he is the novel's “young antiquarian.”
The Baths of Caracalla

The Baths of Caracalla are one of the main meeting places of the novel's pagan Rome. In the gaming hall of the baths Torquatus, the dubious Christian, loses his money. Fulvius, the informer, keeps him in his power by threatening to denounce him if he returns to the Christians (Part II, chapter 9).

The baths' cloakroom keeper, the Christian Cucumio, and his wife Victoria watch the meetings of the three. Victoria overhears the plan to raid the cemetery of Callistus on the day after the proclamation, and warns the Christians in time (Part II, chapters 15–16).

The Baths of Caracalla were dedicated in 216. The novel also alludes to Cucumio's epitaph.
The edict in the Forum

Corvinus nails up the imperial edict on the extermination of the Christians in the Forum, on a board fixed to a pillar near the Puteal Libonis, the magistrate's seat. At night Dacian guards watch the square (Part II, chapter 13).

Pancratius and the centurion Quadratus nevertheless tear it down and burn the pieces in Diogenes's house in the Subura. In the morning Corvinus finds only the empty board, and on the ground a knife he had seen in the hands of a schoolmate (Part II, chapters 13–14).

The story repeats in Rome an event at Nicomedia involving Diocletian's first edict of 303: according to Lactantius, a Christian tore it down and ripped it up there (De mortibus persecutorum 13). The exact location of the Puteal Libonis is disputed; the stop is the Rostra.
The building of the Baths of Diocletian

Early in the novel, at Fabius's banquet, there is talk that the emperor wants his baths finished within three years and is having convicts brought here from the mines of the empire (Part I, chapter 6). After the edict the work grows even crueler: the baths are built by Christian prisoners (Part II, chapter 20).

Corvinus picks fighters from among them for the games. The superintendent of the convicts leads him around the building site; according to the novel, the round vestibule lit from above is like that of the Pantheon.

The Baths of Diocletian were completed around 305. The tradition that they were built by Christian convicts comes from late antique acts of the martyrs and medieval legends; no contemporary source confirms it.

Pancratius, with twenty companions, is driven in chains through the streets to the Mamertine prison, beaten along the way, and thrust down into the lower chamber. The novel describes the two underground chambers one above the other, connected only by a round opening in the middle of the vault (Part II, chapter 21). The sentence: they are to be thrown to the wild beasts in the Flavian amphitheater.

Later Agnes too is locked in this prison, in the novel's word the “Tullianum,” on Fulvius's accusation. Fabiola learns of it from a guard, goes in to her, and speaks with her for the last time before the execution (Part II, chapters 28–29).

This is the map's real Carcer: its lower, round chamber is the Tullianum.
The death of Pancratius in the amphitheater

On a frosty morning the crowd streams into the Flavian amphitheater; the emperor sits in the imperial box on the east side (Part II, chapter 23). Pancratius stands motionless, facing the emperor. A panther is let loose on him and with one spring tears open his throat. Pancratius's blood mingles with his father's in the purse he wears around his neck.

At the end of the novel Corvinus, who betrayed Pancratius, wanders drunk to the wild-beast cages beside the amphitheater, and a panther kills him the same way, through the bars (Part III, chapter 2).

According to tradition, the real Pancratius was not killed by wild beasts but beheaded on the Via Aurelia.
The tomb of Pancratius on the Via Aurelia

Pancratius's body is buried along the Via Aurelia in the cemetery that later took his name, and that passed the name on to the neighboring gate (Part II, chapter 24). The novel adds that in times of peace a basilica was built over his tomb, which still stands.

The basilica and catacomb of San Pancrazio are indeed behind the Janiculum, along the Via Aurelia. The Porta Aurelia is known today as Porta San Pancrazio.
The martyrdom of Sebastian on the Palatine

Sebastian is betrayed. On the orders of the emperor Maximian, the palace's Mauritanian archers shoot him with arrows one dawn. According to the novel, an old chapel among the ruins of the Palatine marks the spot where he fell (Part II, chapter 25).

But Sebastian survives: he is carried to the apartment of Irene, a Christian lady living on the Palatine, where Dionysius, priest and physician, tends him. After his recovery he confronts the emperor on the palace's great staircase, and the emperor has him clubbed to death before his eyes and his body thrown into the Cloaca Maxima. Lucina finds it and buries it where Sebastian's basilica now stands on the Via Appia (Part II, chapters 26–27).

The novel follows Sebastian's late antique acts. The chapel is San Sebastiano al Palatino, in the Vigna Barberini; the stop is the excavated temple next to it, believed to be Elagabalus's.
The martyrdom of Agnes

Fulvius, the informer, whom Agnes had once turned down, denounces her as a Christian, and the prefect condemns her. Of the first part of her sentence the novel says nothing, except that her angel protected her and her presence turned the “den of infamy” into a sanctuary. According to the footnote, this place is marked by the church of Sant'Agnese on the Piazza Navona (Part II, chapter 29).

Early the next morning she is brought before the prefect again in the Forum. The manacles slip from her thin wrists. Agnes kneels, draws her hair forward, and the executioner beheads her with a single stroke of the sword.

Sant'Agnese in Agone stands above the arches of the Stadium of Domitian; today's Piazza Navona preserves the shape of the stadium's arena. Ambrose and Pope Damasus already wrote of Agnes's martyrdom; the details come from legend.
The baptism of Fabiola

After Agnes's death Fabiola becomes a Christian. At Easter a small party goes around the city wall to the far side, turns off the Via Portuensis into a vineyard near Caesar's gardens, and goes down into the cemetery of Pontianus, where the two Persian martyrs Abdon and Sennen rest (Part II, chapter 34).

Deep in the catacomb, Fabiola is baptized in a square basin, four to five feet deep, filled from an underground spring. The novel notes that the baptistery still exists, with a painting of the Baptism of Christ above it, added a century or two later.

The catacomb of Pontianus is on the slope of Monteverde; its baptistery and wall paintings can still be seen.
The tomb of Agnes on the Via Nomentana

Agnes's villa lay along the Via Nomentana, a mile and a half from the city; here the novel shows Agnes among her gentle animals. Here Fulvius asks for her hand, and Agnes answers that she is already betrothed (Part II, chapter 12). Agnes is buried in the cemetery beneath the villa. As heir to the villa, Fabiola moves here with the sick Miriam, her former slave Syra, who dies here (Part II, chapter 34).

At the end of the novel, after Constantine's victory, building is already under way in the villa's garden: Constantia, the emperor's daughter, is having a basilica built over Agnes's tomb. Fabiola keeps a hospital in her town house and lives at her villa; Torquatus, now converted, becomes the gravedigger of the villa's cemetery (Part III, chapters 1–3).

Sant'Agnese fuori le Mura and the round Santa Costanza beside it stand beyond the Porta Pia, outside the edge of the map. The old basilica was built in the mid-4th century by Constantina, Constantine's daughter; the novel calls her Constantia.
The First Man in Rome (Colleen McCullough, 1990)

Colleen McCullough's novel is set between 110 and 100 BC. It follows the rise of two men: Gaius Marius, the provincial “new man” who would be consul seven times, and Lucius Cornelius Sulla, the impoverished patrician. In the background are the war against Jugurtha, the Germanic invasions and the fall of the tribune Saturninus. On the novel's first pages Marius is still hopelessly waiting for the consulship; on the last he is the first man in Rome.

This is a literary walk: it follows the plot of the novel, not a historical account. McCullough drew on many sources, but the characters' private lives, much of the dialogue and several minor figures (Lucius Decumius, for example) are the novel's invention. Where an ancient source also records an event, this is noted separately. References give the volume and page of the Hungarian edition (Árkádia, 1991): I. 12 = volume one, page 12.
New Year on the Palatine: the area Flacciana

The novel opens at a rainy dawn on 1 January 110 BC. The senator Gaius Julius Caesar, grandfather of the later dictator, lives on the Palatine, in a narrow alley that opens onto the Clivus Victoriae (I. 12). His wife Marcia and their two daughters, Julia and Julilla, do not join the procession: they go along the Clivus Victoriae to a grassy, empty plot with a view over the whole Forum and the Capitol. This is the area Flacciana, the site of the demolished house of Flaccus; from here they watch the new consuls' inauguration (I. 12–14, 32).

The house next door belongs to Clitumna, Sulla's stepmother. Sulla, now thirty, was born a patrician but is so poor that he cannot enter the senate; his stepmother and his mistress Nicopolis keep him (I. 28–30). That morning he goes up to the hillside, needles two noble ladies whose lover he has been, and here sees Caesar's younger daughter, Julilla, close up for the first time (I. 32–33). From the hill the marks of the summer fire are still visible: it burned the Viminal and part of the Esquiline (I. 31–32).

Beyond the novel: the house of Marcus Fulvius Flaccus, ally of Gaius Gracchus, was demolished in 121 BC, and the site was afterwards called the area Flacciana (Cicero, De domo sua 102). Its exact location is unknown; the marker stands on the Forum side of the Palatine, on the site of the later Domus Tiberiana, beside which the Clivus Victoriae ran.
The consuls' inauguration on the Capitol

The processions of the two new consuls, Marcus Minucius Rufus and Spurius Postumius Albinus, merge in the Forum and climb the Clivus Capitolinus with the knights at their head. At the first bend the priests wait with the two white sacrificial bulls; the procession reaches the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus (I. 14–15). Gaius Marius stands in the crowd: he was praetor five years ago, has waited three years for the consulship, and feels that because he is not of noble birth he will never get it (I. 15).
