Sulla goes down the Stairs of Vesta to the Forum and joins the back of the crowd in front of the temple. The sacrifice goes badly, the bull dies hard, and Sulla looks with foreboding at the mediocre nobles. Then he notices a former praetor with great eyebrows and a scarred face who reminds him of an eagle: Marius (I. 34–35). Meanwhile Jugurtha, king of Numidia, sits in his rented villa on the slope of the Pincian, because as a king he may not cross the city's sacred boundary, the pomerium (I. 35–36).
The Subura: the crossroads tavern

Jugurtha wants to have his cousin Massiva, a rival claimant to the Numidian throne, killed in Rome, but the killer must be a Roman. His confidant Bomilcar goes into the Subura in plain clothes: from the Argiletum through the Fauces Suburae to the Subura Maior, and from there onto the Vicus Patricius, which leads towards the Viminal. Where the Subura Minor runs into it, on a triangular open space, he finds a tavern beside the crossroads shrine and fountain (I. 104–105).

It is the tavern of the crossroads college (collegium); its custodian is Lucius Decumius, a scrawny little man who always smells of onions. Bomilcar finds his assassin here: Decumius himself (I. 106–113, 119). Decumius remains an important character to the end of the novel. Aurelia's apartment block will later stand in the same triangle (see stop 7).

The line of the Vicus Patricius survives in today's Via Urbana.
The murder of Massiva before the temple of Castor

In the second week of January Marcus Livius Drusus celebrates a triumph. Massiva watches it in the Circus Maximus as the guest of the consul Albinus, then hurries ahead with the consular guests up the Stairs of Cacus, over the Palatine and down the Stairs of Vesta to the Forum, to watch the procession enter along the Via Sacra beside the consuls in front of the temple of Castor and Pollux (I. 113). In the crush he falls behind his escort. Decumius stabs him and vanishes into the white-togaed crowd towards the Argiletum (I. 113–114).

Bomilcar is arrested and locked up in the Lautumiae, the prison in the old quarry on the side of the Capitol (I. 118).

Beyond the novel: the murder of Massiva is historical. According to Sallust, Bomilcar hired the assassins; the killer was caught, Bomilcar fled, and it was then that Jugurtha called Rome a city for sale (Jugurthine War 35). The killer's name and the setting on the day of a triumph are the novel's invention.
Marius elected consul (108 BC)

Marius is fighting in Africa as Metellus's legate and has difficulty getting leave for the consular elections. After a swift crossing he rides into the Forum and, still without the white candidate's toga, registers as a candidate at the table of the consul presiding over the election; the crowd cheers him (I. 276).

The assembly of the centuries meets on the Campus Martius, at the voting ground called the saepta. Lucius Cassius Longinus is elected first consul; for the second place the race between Marius and Quintus Lutatius Catulus Caesar is so close that it is decided only when the third class votes: Marius wins (I. 278). That evening they celebrate at the house of his father-in-law Caesar, where Marius meets the household's other future son-in-law, Sulla (I. 279).

Beyond the novel: Marius won the consulship for the following year in 108 BC (Sallust, Jugurthine War 73). The republican voting ground lay in the same part of the Campus Martius where Caesar and Augustus later built the marble Saepta Iulia; the marker stands on it.
The army of the poor (107 BC)

As consul, Marius announces in the senate, in the Curia Hostilia, that he will also recruit soldiers from the propertyless citizens (capite censi). The senators shout in outrage (I. 317). Marius walks out with his quaestor Sulla and the tribune Manlius Mancinus, and turns to the people from the speakers' platform of the Comitium, the rostra. He asks for an army equipped, trained and paid by the state; the crowd cheers, and the other nine tribunes dare not veto (I. 318–319). After the law is passed, Scaurus, the leader of the senate, speaks against Marius in the senate (I. 320).

Beyond the novel: according to Sallust, Marius did recruit from the capite censi (Jugurthine War 86). The African command was given to him by the popular assembly on the proposal of the tribune Titus Manlius Mancinus (Jugurthine War 73).
Aurelia's apartment block in the Subura (105–100 BC)

Aurelia, niece of Marcus Aurelius Cotta, marries the younger Gaius Julius Caesar. An apartment block (insula) is bought with Aurelia's money; Cotta finds one in the middle of the Subura. It is a well-built nine-storey house with eight shops, and it fills the whole triangle where the Subura Minor runs into the Vicus Patricius. It stands over a main sewer, so it even has a bathroom and a latrine (I. 445–448). They pay ninety-five talents for it; after the April wedding the wedding party walks through the Subura, and the whole neighbourhood cheers the bride (I. 448–450).

Aurelia lives in the ground-floor apartment and manages the building herself. She may not charge rent for the crossroads tavern in the house; its custodian is Lucius Decumius, who adores Aurelia and regularly sends her flowers (II. 273–274). Here, on the 13th of Quinctilis (July) 100 BC, their son is born: Gaius Julius Caesar, the later dictator (II. 287).

Beyond the novel: according to Suetonius, Caesar lived in his youth in a modest house in the Subura (Divus Iulius 46). The apartment block and the tavern are the novel's invention. The sources give Caesar's birthday as 12 or 13 July.
Jugurtha's end in the Tullianum (104 BC)

On 1 January 104 BC Marius celebrates his triumph and on the same day enters his second consulship. The evening before, Jugurtha was the guest of Metellus Numidicus and dined on snails. At dawn on the Campus Martius, by the Villa Publica, Sulla, who is staging the triumph, tells him that he will not be strangled: he will be thrown alive into the pit of the Tullianum (II. 14–15). The procession passes along the Vicus Tuscus, through the Forum Boarium and the Circus Maximus, behind the Palatine, then over the Velia and down the Via Sacra into the Forum. Jugurtha is disappointed: the buildings are small and old (II. 17–18).

At the lower end of the Forum his walk ends. At the foot of the Capitol, below the Gemonian Stairs, stands the Tullianum, a single small building of great stones. He is stripped and led to the round opening gaping in the floor. Jugurtha does not wait for the ladder: without a sound he steps into the pit himself (II. 19–20).

Marius reaches the temple of Jupiter by noon. Afterwards he is about to go to the senate's inaugural meeting in his triumphal dress, his face still painted, but Sulla stops him and sends him home to change (II. 20–21).

Beyond the novel: according to Plutarch, Jugurtha was thrown into the prison pit after the triumph and died of starvation six days later (Marius 12).
Caepio's trial in the Comitium (103 BC)

Quintus Servilius Caepio, who embezzled the gold of Tolosa and through whose fault the Roman army was destroyed at Arausio, is brought before the popular assembly. The tribune Gaius Norbanus prosecutes him. Two tribunes, Titus Didius and Lucius Aurelius Cotta, try to veto, but the crowd drags them off the rostra, stones fly, and one stone hits Scaurus, the leader of the senate (II. 94–95).

One after another the tribes find Caepio guilty and vote a heavy penalty. Caepio is taken to the Lautumiae prison; his supporter Antistius announces that he will get him out, since no one condemned to exile has ever been imprisoned, and Norbanus mockingly lets him go (II. 95–97).

Beyond the novel: Cicero also discusses Norbanus's trial and the violence around it (De oratore 2.197–203).
The murder of Nonius in the Carinae (101 BC)

In the tribunician elections Saturninus comes only eleventh, though there are ten places. One of those elected is the rich Picene Quintus Nonius, the elder brother of Sulla's brother-in-law (II. 257). That evening, on his way home, in the first alley of the Carinae, a dozen men with clubs fall on him and kill him together with two friends (II. 258).

Glaucia is presiding over the election. In the empty Forum he announces that Nonius's place goes to the next candidate, Saturninus. Later he tells Saturninus only that if he asks no questions, he will not have to be lied to (II. 258–259).

Beyond the novel: according to Appian, Nonius was killed by the men of Saturninus and Glaucia, and Saturninus was then elected tribune (Civil Wars 1.28).
The oath: the temple of Semo Sancus on the Quirinal (100 BC)

Saturninus's second land law requires every senator to swear an oath to it, not in the usual place, the temple of Saturn, but in the open-air shrine of Semo Sancus Dius Fidius on the lower summit of the Quirinal (II. 274). Anyone who refuses is to be banished from Italy, fined twenty talents and deprived of his citizenship (II. 274–275).

In the senate Marius announces that he will be the first to swear. Scaurus then asks for his private opinion; Marius is forced to admit that in his view the law is probably invalid, and so loses Saturninus's trust (II. 280–281). Metellus Numidicus will not swear. He announces that at dawn the next day he will go into exile on Rhodes, and has the fine brought in, forty sacks of money; his stammering son, the treasury quaestor, has to count it aloud (II. 282–283).

Beyond the novel: Metellus Numidicus refused the oath and went into exile (Plutarch, Marius 29; Appian, Civil Wars 1.29–31). The temple of Semo Sancus stood on the Quirinal, near the Porta Sanqualis; its exact location is unknown. The marker is at the neighbouring temple of Salus.
The murder of Memmius on election day (100 BC)

In late autumn the consular candidates set off for the saepta to present themselves. Gaius Memmius, whom everyone expects to be the next consul, walks from the Palatine with his supporters. Where the road down from the Quirinal meets the Via Lata, he runs into Glaucia, who is wearing the white candidate's toga against Marius's ban. Words lead to blows: Glaucia's men draw clubs, and Glaucia himself beats Memmius to death (II. 324–326).

Saturninus is in the saepta canvassing for his friend's candidacy when he hears the news; among the angry young senators he sees Sulla, and he flees to the Quirinal (II. 326). Marius stands with Sulla beside the body and says that what is natural on the battlefield is horrifying on the Field of Mars, under the walls of the city (II. 332–333).

Beyond the novel: according to Appian, Memmius was clubbed to death at the consular elections by the men of Glaucia and Saturninus (Civil Wars 1.32). The marker is at the saepta; in the novel the murder happens on the way, beside the Via Lata.
The temple of Bellona: the senate's ultimate decree

Marius summons the senate to the temple of Bellona, outside the pomerium. Meanwhile news arrives that Saturninus and the mob have occupied the Forum. On Scaurus's proposal the senate unanimously passes the ultimate decree (senatus consultum de re publica defendenda), empowering the consul to defend the Republic (II. 333–334).

Marius appoints Sulla his deputy and has the weapons stored in the temple's cellar handed out. About a thousand citizens arm themselves, mostly from the first and second property classes. Marius speaks to them from the temple's platform: there must be no bloodshed, because the life of the poorest Roman is sacred too, and they may take orders only from him or from Sulla (II. 335–337).

Here the novel also mentions the war column in front of the temple, over which the fetial priest threw a spear towards enemy territory when war was declared (II. 336).
Saturninus on the Capitol

Marius's small force charges across the Forum in a shield wall and scatters the mob. Saturninus and his companions flee up to the Capitol, to the temple of Jupiter (II. 338–339). From there he shouts down that the temple will be stained with Roman blood. Marius laughs: he will smoke them out without bloodshed. He sends Sulla to the water office to have the Capitol's water supply cut off (II. 339).

The captured rioters are locked in the Lautumiae. The non-Romans are executed at once; the Roman citizens are condemned the next day and thrown from the Tarpeian Rock, while a large crowd watches from the lower Forum (II. 340–341).

Beyond the novel: Appian and Orosius also record that Saturninus's men, who had fled to the Capitol, surrendered because the water was cut off (Civil Wars 1.32; Orosius 5.17).
Death in the Curia Hostilia

Saturninus and his companions surrender on 8 December. As there is no secure prison, on Marius's proposal they are locked in the senate house, the Curia Hostilia: it has no windows, and its doors are the strongest in Rome. Scaurus is shocked but agrees. Meanwhile Sulla is seen talking at suspicious length with the younger Caepio and Metellus Piglet (II. 343–344).

At dawn fifty young nobles climb ladders onto the roof of the curia, tear up the tiles and stone the fifteen prisoners to death through the holes (II. 345). Marius and Scaurus go in alone among the bodies. Marius proclaims an amnesty for the young men, and then from the speakers' platform promises the people nineteen days' grain in his own name (II. 346–349).

At the end of the novel Marius tells Sulla that one day he will be the first man in Rome. Asked who will be first until then, he laughs and answers: no one (II. 352).

Beyond the novel: according to Appian, the crowd killed the prisoners with tiles from the roof of the senate house (Civil Wars 1.32). The Curia Hostilia stood on the north side of the Comitium; the marker is on the Curia Julia, built later beside it.

Historical walks

Walks from novels

Literary walks: each follows on the map the plot of a novel set in Rome. They are not historical sources; the places are named by the novel itself, and the text points out where the novel departs from reality.
The aqueducts of Rome
Supply and distribution according to Frontinus (AD 97)

As water commissioner, Frontinus measured every aqueduct and compared the results with the imperial records (commentarii). He showed that the real supply was much larger, and that most of the difference was lost to unauthorized taps and leakage (De aquaeductu 64–76). He then describes, aqueduct by aqueduct, where the water went (78–86).

The unit is the quinaria: the cross-section of a pipe 1¼ digits in diameter (Frontinus 25–26). It is not a rate of flow, and its modern conversion is disputed, so the figures here are only compared with one another.
according to the imperial records · Frontinus’s measurement (at the intake, or closer to the City where that was not possible)
distributed outside the City · distributed inside the City. The waters of Claudia and Anio Novus were mixed inside the City, so they appear together there.
Source: Frontinus, De aquaeductu 64–86 (AD 97), after the edition of R. H. Rodgers (2003).
A measured flow: the Anio Novus

Frontinus measured only the cross-section of the water, not its velocity, so his figures cannot be turned into a flow rate. The Anio Novus is the only aqueduct whose actual flow has been estimated from modern measurements: the limestone (travertine) deposited on the walls and floor of the channel preserved the level the water reached, and the ripple pattern on its surface how fast it flowed. Measurements were taken at three sites: two near Tivoli, the third just outside Rome.
<thead><tr><th>Site</th><th>State</th><th>Flow from the ripples (m³/s)</th><th>Flow from channel geometry (m³/s)</th><th>Velocity (m/s)</th></tr></thead>
Galleria Egidio (Tivoli Loop, underground)early0.93 ± 0.151.1 ± 0.10.81
Empiglione Bridge (Tivoli Bypass)latest1.6 ± 0.21.90.88
Roma Vecchia (arcade outside the city)latest1.2 (+0.4/−0.5)1.4 ± 0.41.0

“Early” and “latest” are the authors’ labels: the flow belonging to an early and to the last surface of the deposit; they give no dates for them. Uncertainties are two standard deviations; for the geometry-based value at Empiglione Bridge the authors could not give one. Velocity is the cross-sectional mean calculated from the ripples.

Source: Keenan-Jones et al., Scientific Reports 12 (2022) 1239, Supplementary Table S3 (CC BY 4.0); the 1.4 ± 0.4 m³/s at Roma Vecchia first in Keenan-Jones, Motta, Garcia, Fouke, Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports 3 (2015) 1–10.

So the water reaching Rome in the late state of the aqueduct was 1.2–1.4 m³ per second; 1.4 m³/s corresponds to 120,960 ± 34,560 m³ per day. Because of bottlenecks in the channel, more than 2 m³/s could never flow through it (Motta et al., Archaeometry 59, 2017). According to the 2015 study this is less than earlier estimates based on Frontinus's figures, and even a thin deposit reduced the maximum flow by about 25%. The authors place the decline in flow roughly between AD 52 and 250.

Frontinus measured 4,738 quinariae at the intake (De aquaeductu 73). The two figures cannot be converted into each other: he measured a cross-section at the intake, while the travertine records the flow at three later points, so the quinaria is not converted into cubic metres here either. The two sites near Tivoli lie on two parallel branches of the aqueduct and show different periods, so the three rows are not a profile of a single moment.
The total distribution: 14,018 quinariae
outside the City, in Caesar’s name · outside the City, to private parties · inside the City, in Caesar’s name · inside the City, to private parties · inside the City, for public uses

The 9,955 quinariae inside the City were distributed by 247 delivery tanks (castella). Of the 4,401 quinariae for public uses, 279 went to military camps, 2,301 to 95 public works, 386 to 39 displays (munera, such as fountains) and 1,335 to 591 street basins (lacus) (Frontinus 78).

The table shows the distribution inside the City, according to Frontinus 79–86. The sign “…” marks figures missing from the manuscripts. Frontinus’s figures do not always add up: for several aqueducts the subtotals differ from the total, and the per-aqueduct figures do not sum to the totals of chapter 78. Part of this comes from transfers between aqueducts (771 quinariae), part from copying errors. The data follow R. H. Rodgers’s critical edition (2003).

On the map several aqueducts can run on one line of arches, so the line width is proportional to the summed measured supply of the aqueducts running there: Claudia + Anio Novus, Marcia + Tepula + Iulia, Anio Vetus, Virgo.
The eleven aqueducts on the map

Nine aqueducts based on the book De aquaeductu by Frontinus, the superintendent of the water supply (curator aquarum, AD 97), supplemented by the two later ones. Catacombs within the map area

There were no burials inside the city wall: this was already forbidden by the Law of the Twelve Tables (Cicero, De legibus 2.58). The catacombs are therefore all outside the walls, along the roads, and the large ones (Callixtus, Domitilla, Sebastianus, Priscilla, Agnes) lie beyond the edge of the map. There are two exceptions, both in the former suburbs enclosed by the later Aurelian Wall. One is the Tomb of the Aurelii (early 3rd century, from before the wall). The other is a small 4th-century catacomb beside the Via Latina, attached to a tomb building; it can be seen on the SITAR layer (12604–12605).

The figures of the regions are also related. Where there are more apartment blocks there are more baths (rank correlation: 0.70), and where there are more fountains there are more bakeries (0.70). The number of apartment blocks also goes with the number of aqueducts that supplied the region in AD 97 according to Frontinus (0.68). With fourteen regions a value above 0.54 is unlikely to be chance. Caution is needed because the figures of the catalogue are partly schematic (those of the bakeries are mostly 15, 16 or 20) and Frontinus’ data are two and a half centuries earlier.
Feeding Rome

Most of the food for a city of a million came by sea. According to Josephus, Africa fed Rome for eight months of the year and Egypt for four (Jewish War 2.383, 2.386). According to the Epitome de Caesaribus, under Augustus twenty million units of grain came from Egypt every year (1.6); the text does not name the unit, which scholars usually take to be the modius.
Grain

From the law of Gaius Gracchus (123 BC) eligible citizens received grain at a reduced price, and from the law of Clodius (58 BC) free, five modii a head each month, about 33 kg (P. Garnsey – D. Rathbone 1985). Under Augustus a little over 200,000 citizens received public grain (Res gestae 15; see “The population of Rome”). From the end of Augustus’s reign the grain supply was supervised by the praefectus annonae (Tacitus, Annals 1.7).

Transport was in the hands of private shippers, so the emperors encouraged them with privileges. Claudius took on himself the loss of cargoes wrecked in storms and granted privileges to anyone who built a grain ship (Suetonius, Claudius 18–19). According to the jurist Gaius, a man of Latin status who built a ship of at least 10,000 modii and carried grain to Rome with it for six years received Roman citizenship (Institutes 1.32c). In the 2nd century the owner of a 50,000-modius ship was exempted from public duties (Digest 50.5.3).
According to the Historia Augusta, Septimius Severus left at his death a seven years’ store of grain, reckoning a distribution of 75,000 modii a day (Severus 23.2).
Oil: Monte Testaccio

Behind the river harbour, the Emporium, stands Rome’s largest archaeological “database”: an artificial hill made almost entirely of broken olive oil amphorae. Sherds soaked in oil could not be reused. The hill is no haphazard dump: amphorae with their bases removed were filled with sherds and built into stepped retaining walls, the other sherds were tipped in behind them, and the smell of rancid oil was covered with lime (J. A. Lobell 2009, on J. Remesal’s excavation).

The estimates start from the volume of the hill and the density of the excavated sections, which is why they differ so much. A Dressel 20 amphora held about 70 litres of oil (7–8 modii, 61–70 litres according to P. Tyers); empty it weighed about 30 kg, full about 100 kg. By Broekaert’s calculation this means 1.4–1.75 billion litres of oil from Augustus to Aurelian, about 74,000–92,600 amphorae, or 5.2–6.5 million litres, a year, and 100–150 shiploads a year (Broekaert 2011). Ward-Perkins’s higher number of amphorae implies about 6 billion litres.
The inscriptions

Many amphorae carry an inscription painted after firing (titulus pictus); scholars label its lines with Greek letters. Line α is the weight of the empty vessel, β the name of the shipping merchant, γ the weight of the oil, δ the control entry: the checkpoint in Spain, the consular year and the names of the officials. On one amphora, for example, the empty vessel weighs 82 Roman pounds and the oil 216 Roman pounds (Lobell 2009). The stamps pressed into the handles preserve names connected with the pottery workshop or the estate. Thanks to the consular dates the layers of the hill can be dated to the year; Heinrich Dressel began collecting them in 1872, and since the 1980s the excavations of E. Rodríguez Almeida, then of J. M. Blázquez and J. Remesal, have continued the work (CEIPAC, University of Barcelona).

According to the Historia Augusta, Septimius Severus gave the Roman people a free daily distribution of oil for all time (Severus 18.3). Broekaert argues that the stamps and inscriptions show imports peaking already under the Antonines; Severus’s measure was rather a reorganization of transport. It was then that the confiscated Spanish olive estates passed to the emperor: on the stamps the abbreviation AVGGGNNN stands for Severus and his two sons (Broekaert 2011).
Which district did the oil come from? The database of amphora inscriptions

The database of the CEIPAC research group in Barcelona (Roman Open Data) records 48,059 inscribed amphorae from the whole empire; 14,051 of them were found in Rome, 12,120 of these around Monte Testaccio. 88% of the amphorae from Rome are Baetican oil amphorae (Dressel 20). The amphorae from Rome carry 7,459 stamps, 10,938 painted inscriptions and 1,424 scratched marks in the database.
The γ line, the weight of the oil, can be read in full on 348 amphorae from Rome. The most frequent value is 216 Roman pounds (on 157 amphorae) and the median is 215 pounds: roughly 70 kg of oil.

The δ line opens with the place of control: the name of the district of Baetica where the oil was weighed and registered. 2,190 δ inscriptions are known from Rome, but the name of the district can be read on only 424 amphorae; 318 of these can be dated by the names of the consuls or by the excavated layer.

The stamp ties the amphora to the pottery that made it. From which year?

4,714 amphorae from Rome can be dated to a single year: 555 by the consular date written on them, 4,159 by the excavated layer. Most amphorae come from these years: 145 (1,033), 149 (186), 160 (149), 161 (132), 174 (270), 177 (121), 179 (841), 207 (125), 208 (177), 214 (266), 216 (124), 246 (118), 254 (439). This is not a fluctuation of imports: each part of the mound holds the refuse of different years, and the numbers show which years’ layers research has reached (Dressel’s collecting in the 19th century and the Spanish excavation under way since 1989). The database dates one amphora to 256, but the pair of consuls written on it (Valerianus II and Lucillus) belongs to 265; we corrected this.

The weight of the empty amphora: the α line

The α line gives the weight of the empty vessel in Roman pounds. 2,098 α inscriptions are known from Rome, but the number can be read in full on only 503 amphorae. The median is 90 pounds (about 29 kg) and half of them fall between 85 and 96 pounds. On 59 amphorae both the α and the γ line are intact: on these the vessel made up on average 30% of the weight of the full amphora (medians: 88 pounds of vessel, 215 pounds of oil). This confirms the estimate above: a full Dressel 20 weighed roughly 100 kg, 30 kg of it the vessel.
At the end of the 3rd century

By the time of Aurelian (270–275) bread rather than grain was being distributed: according to the Historia Augusta he added an ounce to the weight of the loaves from the revenues of Egypt (Aurelian 47.1), and he also distributed pork (35.2). Besides the free oil, bread and pork he planned free wine as well: he wanted vineyards planted in Etruria, but this was not carried out; the imperial wine was sold in the porticoes of the temple of Sol (48.1–4).

The open data set of the Epigraphic Database Roma (EDR) contains 44,796 inscriptions found in Rome. For 30,124 of them the findspot is known (as a text description), and 37,209 are dated. By type: 37,275 epitaphs, 1,884 religious, 1,685 honorific and 1,027 building inscriptions; the rest are other or unknown (graffiti, seat inscriptions, fragments).

More than four-fifths of the inscriptions are epitaphs, and these are densest in the first half of the 1st century AD. Occupations in the inscriptions

Of the 44,796 inscriptions from Rome in EDR, 42,722 have a readable text in the data set. Using a dictionary of 127 Latin occupational titles we found an occupation in 2,338 inscriptions: physicians, cooks, goldsmiths, accountants. The inscriptions of soldiers (2,171) are left out of this summary, as are priesthoods and senatorial and equestrian offices. Every hit was checked by reading, and those where the word is not the person’s occupation were dropped: for example the emperors’ victory title “Medicus”, the names Mercator, Sutorius or Fullonius, the divine name “Bona Dea Nutrix”, and the texts of laws and decrees. EDR does not yet contain all the inscriptions of Rome, so the figures show proportions, not complete head counts.

Administration and domestic service account for 59% of the inscriptions that name an occupation. They also have the highest share of the imperial household (administration: 28%, domestic service: 24%). Not a single imperial slave or freedman appears among the traders. Among craftsmen and traders, where a status is stated it is mostly “freed” (crafts: 72 of 102, trade: 20 of 25).

Legal status is looked for in the name that belongs to the occupational title, back to the boundary of the entry or sentence, and directly after the title. Only a marker that agrees in grammatical case with the title is accepted (libertus, servus, verna, vicarius, or the father’s name: “Marci filius”); a “servus” supplied by the editors also counts. A person is imperial when the marker is preceded by the emperor or empress (Augusti libertus, Caesaris servus), or when a single-named person has only this: “Felix Caesaris dispensator”. In inscriptions listing several people a wrong assignment can still occur. “Not stated” does not mean freeborn: for people with a single name (for example “Blandus structor”) the inscription simply does not give the status.

Legal status and imperial names over time

Of the 42,791 inscriptions from Rome with a readable text in EDR, 8,445 carry a freed-status marker (libertus, liberta), 1,997 a slave marker (servus, serva, verna), and 2,718 a father’s name (“Marci filius”), the sign of free birth. An imperial freedman or freedwoman (Augusti libertus) appears in 1,445 inscriptions, an imperial slave (Caesaris servus) in 577. The curves show on what percentage of the dated inscriptions of each period a given marker or name appears.

The freed-status marker appears on 38% of inscriptions in the first half of the 1st century AD, on 13% in the first half of the 2nd century and on 3.4% in the second half of the 3rd. The father’s name becomes rare even earlier: still 28% in the first half of the 1st century BC, 7.3% in the 1st century AD. This shows the habit of writing the marker out; it does not allow conclusions about how many freed people or slaves lived in the city. The share of imperial freedmen is steady from the mid-1st to the end of the 2nd century AD (5.9%).
Imperial family names
Anyone who received Roman citizenship, or was freed by the emperor, took the emperor’s family name, and the name was inherited. So after each dynasty the number of people bearing its name grows.
Iulius · Claudius · Flavius · Ulpius · Aelius · Aurelius
Hover over the curve.

The waves follow one another: the name Claudius is most frequent in the second half of the 1st century AD (10%), Ulpius and Aelius in the 2nd century. Aurelius grows from the end of the 2nd century and is the most frequent in the 3rd (16%). The Constitutio Antoniniana played a part in this: in AD 212 Caracalla (officially Marcus Aurelius Antoninus) gave citizenship to almost every free inhabitant of the empire. In the 4th–5th centuries the name Flavius rises again; by then it is no longer a family name but a status name of officials and soldiers, after the dynasty of Constantine.

An important limit: the dating of the inscriptions is partly based on these very names (the editors place the inscription of an Aurelius after the reign of Marcus Aurelius), so the start of each wave partly follows from the dating method. The emperors’ own names, the names of legions and buildings (legio VII Claudia, basilica Iulia) and the voting tribes were not counted.

Age and family in the epitaphs

Of the 36,341 epitaphs from Rome with a readable text in EDR, 8,412 give the age of the deceased (8,941 ages in all), and 12,968 say for whom the tomb was set up: a spouse, a child, a patron. An epitaph shows who was commemorated and how; it cannot be used as mortality data.
Age in the epitaphs
male · female · not clear from the text
Hover over a bar.

The median of the ages given is 20 years; 28% are under 10, and only 5.8% over 60. Infants under one year appear 113 times. Age was written out more often for those who died young, while infants and the old less often received such an inscription; so the curve shows the habit of commemoration, not the ages at which Romans died. The sex of the deceased is shown by “qui vixit” or “quae vixit”, by “cum quo” or “cum qua”, by the ending of the name in the dative and by the term used (filiae, marito); where these can be checked against “qui/quae”, they agree with it in 96–99% of cases. Fragmentary numerals (for example “XX[- - -]”) and the second copies of inscriptions repeated under several EDR numbers are not counted.

The horse guard was picked from the cavalry units of the Danube and Rhine frontiers (Pannonians, Noricans, Raetians, Batavians); the German bodyguard of the early emperors were Batavians and Ubians; among the fleet soldiers there are Egyptians, Sardinians and Thracian Bessi. Praetorians rarely give an ethnic name; they mostly name their home town.

Limits: only epitaphs are counted, not votive inscriptions or rosters. The unit named in an inscription may be that of the dedicator (the heir or a comrade). Other legions are not included, because in Rome their names mostly occur in lists of officers’ careers.
Christian inscriptions (3rd–8th century)

The database of the University of Bari, the Epigraphic Database Bari (EDB), collects the inscriptions of the Christians of Rome. The open data set contains 40,760 inscriptions, almost all from the catacombs and cemeteries outside the city walls; a number of inscriptions appear in two or three records (the same stone in an older and a newer volume of the corpus); without these second copies (585) we counted 40,175. Of these 27,387 are dated, 3,423 are in Greek (8.5%) and 520 bilingual. 13% of the inscriptions were not carved but scratched into, or painted on, the plaster closing the tomb; 540 are in verse.

In Rome the median of the ages recorded in epitaphs is 20 years, and 29% of them belong to children under ten; in North Africa the median is 45 years and 38% of the ages are over sixty. This is a difference not of mortality but of custom: in Rome it was mainly the ages of those who died young that were carved in stone, in Africa those of the old as well, and more often rounded. The Whipple index measures the heaping of round ages (ending in 5 or 0): 100 if there is no rounding, 500 if every age is round.

A check with two independent databases: for the epitaphs of Rome we obtained here (from EDCS texts, Christian inscriptions included) a median of 20 years, 29% under ten and 6.1% over sixty; the card “Age and family in the epitaphs” gives 20 years, 28% and 5.8% from the texts of EDR. For age we also counted the form “annorum XXX” here, because it is the more common one in the provinces; truncated numerals and lengths of marriage or military service are not ages. An inscription with an identical text of at least 40 letters was counted only once per province.
Coin hoards: when money was hidden

The Oxford database Coin Hoards of the Roman Empire (CHRE) collects the hoards of coins in circulation between 30 BC and AD 400 from the whole empire (it also records later, 5th-century finds). The downloaded file contains 19,189 entries: 13,349 of them are hoards, the rest single gold coins or stray finds. 865 hoards are known from Italy, and from Rome and its 10-kilometre surroundings only 18 with a reliable date.

A hoard is dated by its latest coin. This is the earliest possible time of concealment, not the actual one: the money may have been hidden later. It also matters that we know only those hoards whose owners never came back for them.
The empire, Italy and Rome
the empire · Italy · one hoard from Rome each · sieges of Rome: 410, 455, 472
Source: Coin Hoards of the Roman Empire (CHRE), our own summary.

The curve shows what percentage of the dated hoards close in each 25-year span. In the empire 20% of the hoards close in the quarter-century between 250 and 275: the time of the 3rd-century crisis, of civil wars, invasions and debasement. Italy has the same peak (17%), but its largest is in the 1st century: this is the money of the Campanian towns buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79 (327 of the Italian hoards are from Campania). There it was not the owners’ decision but the catastrophe that preserved the money.

The quarter-century between 250 and 275 is a low point in the map’s other data series as well. In Rome only 17 dated construction phases from excavations are known from this time (119 at the peak of AD 75–100), and the number of inscriptions in EDR falls to a third of the 2nd-century average (919 instead of 2,892). Three independent data series point to the same period; this proves no cause, because each series has its own long-term trend.

Does concealment coincide with the sieges? In the 5th century it does: for five of the six hoards the latest coin falls in the year of a siege or in the few years before it. The latest piece of the 69 solidi recovered from the Tiber is of about 410; that of the 397 solidi found in the House of the Vestals on the Palatine is of 467–472, the time of Ricimer’s siege. In the 3rd century four hoards from Rome close between 253 and 268, at the same time as most hoards in the empire.

But these are 18 hoards, not statistics. The “contemporary event” column shows coincidence in time, not a proven cause; 5th-century Rome was attacked so often that almost any hoard falls near one of the attacks. The peaks of the empire have no counterpart in Rome: from the second half of the 2nd century, when many hoards close in the empire, only two gold hoards are known from the city. We left out two entries: one contains coins up to the 5th century according to its description, yet is dated 161, the other two aurei, not certain that they were found together. Within 25 kilometres of the city there are a further 9 hoards (for example three from Ostia, with latest coins of 260–282).

In peacetime one or two hoards a year stayed in the ground, during the civil wars several times as many: 8.4 a year in 81–71 BC, 12.4 a year in 49–42. A hoard is hidden by someone who is afraid and left by someone who does not come back for it, so the peaks show the losses of war, not wealth. The most frequent closing years are 74 BC (32), 42 (28) and 46 (23).

What to watch for. The closing year is the year the latest coin was struck; the hoard may have been hidden later. If much money was struck in one year, more hoards “close” with that year, so the chart shows five-year bands, not years. The 129 hoards found in the territory of Dacia consist of denarii that had left the empire; their peaks do not necessarily reflect the Roman civil wars. From Rome itself the database knows four hoards; two have a closing year: one of 121 denarii and 2 victoriati (147 BC), the other of 16 denarii from Largo di Torre Argentina (97 BC).

The peak of 80–71 BC falls in the same decade in which, according to the Greenland ice, lead emissions, that is, silver mining, sank to their Republican minimum (see “Shipwrecks and lead pollution”). This is the decade of the war of Sertorius in Spain and of the revolt of Spartacus; from Spain there is not a single hoard from the preceding ten years, and 18 from this decade.
Where did the Romans come from?

For the size of the city's population there are only estimates (see “The population of Rome”), but two scientific studies give direct data on its make-up from bones in cemeteries around Rome. Both rest on small samples, so the proportions cannot be projected onto the whole population of the city.

From this the authors conclude that many more people came to imperial Rome from the eastern half of the Mediterranean than from the western provinces. They mention the cause only as a possibility: the eastern part of the empire was more densely populated, with large cities. Of the nine individuals from the Isola Sacra cemetery at Portus, four belong to the Near Eastern, four to the eastern Mediterranean and one to the European group, while their oxygen isotopes are compatible with growing up locally: this points to a long-settled community of mixed origin. The groups express statistical similarity, not ethnic names; the authors themselves write that the source populations should not be taken literally.
Isotopes: who grew up elsewhere?

The strontium and oxygen isotopes of tooth enamel preserve the trace of childhood drinking water and food. Anyone whose values fall outside the range around Rome spent their childhood elsewhere. A total of 105 individuals from two suburban cemeteries of the 1st–3rd centuries AD were analysed.

Source: K. Killgrove, J. Montgomery, “All Roads Lead to Rome: Exploring Human Migration to the Eternal City through Biochemistry of Skeletons from Two Imperial-Era Cemeteries (1st–3rd c AD)”, PLOS ONE 11(2) (2016) e0147585, Tables 1–2 and text (CC BY 4.0).

The four individuals are three adult men and one adolescent aged 11–15. The strontium values of two point to a region of older rock, such as the Alps or one of the islands of the Tyrrhenian Sea; one to a cooler, wetter landscape such as the Apennines; one to a hotter, drier one such as North Africa. Four further individuals also deviate, but this is not statistically conclusive. In the more expensive mausoleum nobody was detectably foreign; in the simple graves some were.

The 4 out of 105 (3.8%) is a lower bound, not the share of immigrants: anyone who came from a region with rock and climate similar to Rome's is invisible to the method, and many slaves were also born here. So the two studies do not contradict each other: DNA also shows origins several generations back, while isotopes show only where the individual grew up.
Shipwrecks and lead pollution

There are no statistics for the Roman economy as a whole, so research relies on indirect measures. Two of them can be followed over centuries: the number of known shipwrecks in the Mediterranean tells of maritime trade, and the lead trapped in Greenland ice of silver mining and coinage. Neither is about Rome directly, but both measure the empire that supplied the city.
Shipwrecks per fifty years
all dated wrecks (1,751) · only those dated to within 100 years (1,116). Each wreck is spread across the bars in proportion to the years of its date range, so the counts are fractional.
Source: J. Strauss, A. I. Wilson, M. Flohr, OxREP Shipwrecks Database, version 2.1 (2017), oxrep.web.ox.ac.uk/shipwrecks-database; 1,818 wrecks, 1,751 of them dated; own calculation.

The peak is the 1st century AD: 342 wrecks fall in it, but only 156 in the 2nd century, less than half. The more strictly dated wrecks show the same, so the drop is not an artefact of imprecise dating. The decline begins already in the first half of the 2nd century, decades before the Antonine Plague broke out in 165.

What the curve does not mean. A wreck is made visible and datable by its cargo: divers find amphorae and stone, but not grain, textiles or wooden barrels. During the imperial period the barrel gradually displaced the amphora, so some later ships simply do not show. Most wrecks were found in the shallow waters off the French and Italian coasts; the North African coast has hardly been surveyed. Andrew Wilson, one of the authors of the database, therefore judges the true scale of the 2nd-century drop to be uncertain: ceramic finds on land show no downturn at that time, and a certain collapse of trade comes only in the 7th–8th centuries.

Stone-carrying ships do not follow the general curve: they peak in the 3rd century (19.1), when the total number of wrecks is already well below its maximum, and they do not decline in the 2nd century either. Wilson likewise places the peak of stone transport in the 2nd–3rd centuries (cf. “Building activity over time”).

The oil amphora of Monte Testaccio, the Dressel 20, has been identified on 22 wrecks: 15 off the French coasts (three of them off Corsica), six off Italy (two each off Sardinia and Sicily, one each off Apulia and Tuscany), one off Spain. More than half fall in the 1st century AD, whereas the dated inscriptions of the Testaccio come from the 2nd–3rd centuries (see “Feeding Rome”): so the two sources show two different phases of the oil trade, not the same one.

At the harbours of Rome. The database records 12 ships at Fiumicino, the site of ancient Portus (dating the earliest three to AD 42–66 and the latest to the 4th century), one at Ostia, and four in Lake Nemi (AD 35–50). Along the coast from Anzio to Civitavecchia a further 11 wrecks are listed; of these Ladispoli B carried nine marble columns, and Ladispoli A, according to the database, may have been adapted to carry large storage jars (dolia). The coordinates in the database are deliberately imprecise, so the wrecks are not on the map.
Lead in Greenland ice

Silver was extracted from lead-bearing ore, and the wind carried the lead fumes of the smelters as far as Greenland, where they settled in the snow year by year. A 2018 study estimated European lead emissions from the ice core at annual resolution between 1235 BC and AD 800. As the denarius was made of silver, the curve tracks mining and coinage.

The imperial-period mean (0.91) is one and a half times that of the crisis of the Republic and nearly three times the minimum of 80–61 BC; according to the authors, emissions also dropped suddenly in 64, at the first debasement of the denarius. The third-century minimum, around 260, is 0.14 thousand tonnes: the lowest value of the imperial period, and it falls in the period when most coin hoards were hidden in the empire (250–275; see “Coin hoards: when money was hidden”). After 900 BC similarly low values occur in the series only around 356 BC and AD 489 (0.12).

According to the authors the absolute size of the emissions is uncertain within a factor of two; the direction and timing of the changes are more reliable than the tonnes. The two measures agree in placing the peak in the 1st century AD, but put the turning point at different times: the number of wrecks falls already at the start of the 2nd century, that of lead only with the plague of 165. In fifty-year bands (500 BC – AD 700) the rank correlation of the two series is 0.52: they move together, but not closely.
Disasters in Rome: fire, flood, earthquake

Ancient authors recorded three recurring calamities of the city: fires, the floods of the Tiber and earthquakes. The card puts the data of three modern collections on one timeline: 30 individually described fires, 33 floods and 25 earthquakes located at Rome. For the fires, the names of the burnt buildings jump to the map.

Sixty per cent of the regional mentions (31 of 51) fall in the centre of the city: in Regions VIII (Forum Romanum, imperial fora, Capitoline), IX (Circus Flaminius and Campus Martius) and X (Palatium). From the two outermost regions, I (Porta Capena) and XIV (Transtiberim), no major fire is recorded at all. This is partly a source effect: authors recorded the destruction of great public buildings, rarely that of outlying residential quarters. The temple of Vesta burned five times, the Regia and the theatre of Pompey at least four times.

Floods of the Tiber

Between 414 BC and AD 398 we know of 33 floods. BC: 414, 363, 241, 215, 203, 202, 193, 192, 189, 181, 156, 60, 54, 44, 32, 27, 23, 22, 13. AD: 5, 12, 15, 36, 69, 147, 162, 217, 253, 371, 398; in addition one each under Nerva (96–98), Trajan (98–117) and Hadrian (117–138), without an exact year.

Source: the list of G. S. Aldrete, Floods of the Tiber in Ancient Rome, Baltimore 2007; ancient sources: Livy, Cassius Dio, Tacitus, Plutarch, Horace, Pliny the Younger, Historia Augusta, Aurelius Victor, Ammianus Marcellinus, Claudian.

The floods reached the low-lying parts of the city: the Campus Martius, the area of the Forum Boarium and the Velabrum, the valley of the Circus Maximus. The “Present-day relief” layer shows on the map which parts lie low, but in the valleys the present surface is 5–15 metres higher than the ancient one, so the flooded area cannot be drawn from it precisely.
Earthquakes

The Italian earthquake catalogue places 25 earthquakes at Rome between 461 BC and AD 618; they rest on the reports of ancient authors. Six reached intensity VII–VIII, at which buildings are damaged: 83 BC (7.5), 72 BC (7.5), AD 15 (7.5), AD 51 (8), AD 443 (8), AD 484 (7.5). The rest, where the intensity is known, are of IV–VI: felt, but causing hardly any damage. In 5 cases the catalogue itself marks as doubtful whether the earthquake was at Rome.

Source: E. Guidoboni, G. Ferrari, D. Mariotti, A. Comastri, G. Tarabusi, G. Sgattoni, G. Valensise, CFTI5Med, Catalogo dei Forti Terremoti in Italia (461 a.C.–1997), INGV 2018, doi:10.6092/ingv.it-cfti5 (CC BY 4.0); earthquakes with epicentre “Roma”. Intensity is epicentral intensity (Io) on the Mercalli–Cancani–Sieberg scale.

The three rows sometimes coincide: in 192 BC all three calamities struck the city, in AD 5, 15 and 217 there was a flood and an earthquake in the same year, in 191 an earthquake and a great fire. One reason is that Roman historians listed bad omens together, at the end of a year, so where one survives the other often does too. According to Canter, after the great fires the city was regularly rebuilt to a better standard (cf. “Building activity over time”).
Prices and wages in 301: Diocletian’s Price Edict

At the end of AD 301 Diocletian and his co-emperors fixed by edict the maximum price of more than 1,200 goods, kinds of work and services. It is the only ancient source that shows at once how much a day labourer could earn and what he got for it. Prices are given in denarii communes: by then a unit of account, not a coin in circulation.

What to watch for. The figures are maximum permitted prices, not market prices, and they apply to the whole empire, not to Rome: in the city part of the food was distributed by the state (see “Feeding Rome”). All but one of the inscribed fragments of the edict come from the eastern half of the empire, and we do not know how far it was observed in the west; according to Lactantius goods vanished from the market and the edict had to be withdrawn.

The maximum price of a modius of wheat was 100 denarii, that of shipping it from Alexandria to Rome 16: so the sea voyage made up at most a sixth of the price of wheat. How far was Rome? Travel time and transport cost

The ORBIS model of Stanford University joins the road network, navigable rivers and sea routes of the Roman world into a single network and calculates how much time and money it took to get from one place to another. It approximates conditions around AD 200 with 632 sites, some 85,000 km of roads, 28,000 km of rivers and 1,026 sea routes. The card shows what the model gives when the destination is Rome.

Distance was measured in money and time, not in kilometres. Alexandria is 1,952 km away in a straight line, yet a kilo of wheat could be brought from there to Rome for 2.2 denarii; from Savaria, 678 km away, the same cost 11.8 denarii, that is, more than five times as much from a third of the distance. From Carthage (591 km) Rome could be reached in 4.9 days, from Sirmium at a similar distance (669 km) in 21.6 days. This is one reason why Rome lived on the grain of Egypt and Africa and not on that of the Danube lands.

Time is that of the fastest route with departure in July, on foot by land (30 km a day), under sail at sea. What to watch for. These are the results of a model, not recorded journeys: they assume average wind and wave conditions, take no account of individual storms or waiting in port, and in reality sailing largely stopped in winter. The cost in denarii is to be understood within the model’s own price system, so it is the ratios that matter here, not the sums. For the sea freight rates of the Price Edict see the “Prices and wages in 301” card, for the grain supply the “Feeding Rome” card.
What did the Romans eat? Diet from the bones

Bone collagen preserves the carbon and nitrogen isotopes of the food eaten in the last years of life. δ13C shows which plants the food chain was built on (wheat, barley, pulses: C3; millet: C4) and whether marine protein was part of it; δ15N marks the position in the food chain: the more meat, dairy or fish, the higher it is. It does not show dishes, only the source of the protein.

For comparison the authors also measured 17 contemporary animal bones (Castel Malnome, Via Padre Semeria, the Colosseum area): δ15N is 3.8–6.7‰ for the 9 herbivores (deer, cattle, sheep, goat, hare), 4.6–6.8‰ for the 3 pigs and 9.1–10.6‰ for the 3 dogs. The human mean is 10‰ or above in all six cemeteries, i.e. similar to or higher than the dogs and well above the herbivores.

The authors’ conclusions. The diet was basically terrestrial, with C3 plants (cereals, pulses) as the plant base; consumption of C4 plants such as millet is detectable but was not widespread. There is no evidence of an exclusively marine diet; occasional fish eating cannot be ruled out, though, since up to 20% of the protein could come from the sea without showing in the collagen values. The authors explain the differences between cemeteries by what people could get in the neighbourhood where they lived. Quarto Cappello del Prete near Gabii has the lowest mean and the widest spread; most of the dead there were children.

Six of the seven communities have means of 8.2–8.8‰, i.e. 1–3‰ lower than the imperial cemeteries (10.0–11.4‰). The authors read this as a dietary transition: with the collapse of the Empire the crisis of the trade system narrowed the range of foods available to the Romans, and less high-protein food was eaten. They see the same at Gabii (imperial 10.7‰, medieval 8.7‰). The exception is the San Pancrazio community (11.5‰), the only one where consumption of aquatic resources was detected.

Points to bear in mind. The imperial cemeteries lie outside the walls and, according to the authors, belong to the lower classes, tied to production sites or rural villas; these data say nothing about the city’s elite. δ15N can be raised by things other than diet (breastfed infants, starvation, manured fields), so a difference of a few tenths of a ‰ between cemeteries means little by itself. Some medieval samples are small (Amba Aradam 4, Piazzale Ostiense 8 individuals). A direct download from the IsoArcH database did not work; I used the published tables of the two open-access studies.
Climate from tree rings: summers north of the Alps

This is not the weather of Rome. The width of tree rings allows early-summer rainfall and summer temperature to be reconstructed year by year, but a series this long and annually resolved comes from Central Europe: 7284 oak samples from north-eastern France and Germany (April–June precipitation) and 1546 stone pine and larch samples from the Austrian Alps and adjacent areas (June–August temperature). It describes the climate of the Empire’s north-western provinces (Gaul, Germania, Raetia); rainfall patterns around the Mediterranean may differ.

What the authors read from it. From the Late Iron Age to about AD 250 early-summer rainfall was mostly above average and fluctuated within narrow margins; temperature shows two depressions, around 350 BC and 50 BC. The 3rd century brought distinct drying, at the same time as the crisis of the provinces of Gaul, Germania and Raetia. In the 4th century rainfall increased while summers stayed below average; in the 5th century rainfall even surpassed early imperial levels, then dropped sharply in the first half of the 6th. Between about 250 and 550 the authors see exceptional variability. The paper speaks of coincidences, not of proven cause and effect.

Extreme years in the dataset (300 BC – AD 600). The five driest early summers all fall in the mid-6th century: 551 (47 mm), 566, 564, 565 and 546. The coldest summers: 545 (−3.1 °C), 549, year −44 of the dataset (−2.8 °C), 543 and 562. Between 537 and 545, eight summers out of nine are at least 2 °C colder than the 20th-century mean.

Points to bear in mind. Individual years are very uncertain: the calibration error (RMSE) is ± 39 mm for precipitation and ± 0.7 °C for temperature. The oak samples come from archaeological finds, subfossil trunks, historical timber and living trees, and their number varies strongly by period (according to the authors 286 series per year on average, most in Roman times, 550, fewest around AD 400, 44), so long-term levels are less certain than year-to-year change. On the shipwrecks and lead pollution card the third-century low falls in the same period, but that alone does not show that climate caused it.
Who ran the Republic? A database of office-holders

The Digital Prosopography of the Roman Republic (DPRR) gathers the known elite of the Republic into one database: 4,876 persons (341 of them women) and 9,807 records of office-holding for 171 kinds of office, from 509 BC to the year of Actium (31 BC), with a few later records. Almost four fifths of the records come from Broughton’s The Magistrates of the Roman Republic. The figures below are my own aggregates of data downloaded from the database’s public query endpoint.

Building activity over time

When did Rome build the most? There is no exact record, but the map’s two own data sets give an approximate picture. Neither is complete: they show only what has been excavated, or what we have put on the map.
1. Construction phases from excavations

Within the map area, Rome’s archaeological register (SITAR) records 1329 construction phases dated by the excavators (walls, foundations, floors; modern layers excluded); 1225 of them fall between 800 BC and AD 800. The date is usually a period, for example “1st century AD”. In that case the unit’s weight is spread evenly over the 25-year bands of the period, so each unit counts as one in total (aoristic method). The “more precisely dated” view shows only phases whose dating spans at most 100 years.

In both data sets the period AD 50–125 is the strongest: in the excavation data the band AD 75–100 is the highest, among the map’s buildings AD 100–125, followed immediately by 75–100. The second peak in both is the age of Augustus (50 BC – AD 1). In the excavation data the 2nd century is also strong, and from the mid-3rd century the figures fall sharply. Among the map’s buildings smaller peaks mark the Severan age (AD 200–225) and the turn of the 3rd and 4th centuries (the Aurelian Wall, the Baths of Diocletian, Constantine’s buildings).

Limits. The excavation data are dense where much has been dug (the Forum, the Palatine, the sites of modern construction), and the dating of layers is often accurate only to a century. The foundations of the great imperial buildings often destroyed earlier layers, so the early periods are under-represented. The map’s features were selected by us: about half of them are named buildings mentioned in ancient sources, which favours public buildings. The figures therefore show proportions and peaks, not all building activity.
The population of Rome

No census figure for the population of Rome survives. Ancient sources count only certain groups, mainly the adult male citizens entitled to free grain or cash gifts. Modern scholars estimate the total population from these and other indirect evidence, so the figures below are estimates, not data. Even for the same period they differ by as much as a factor of two.

Why do the estimates differ?

The grain-dole multiplier. The number of recipients (c. 200,000 under Augustus) counts only adult male citizens. For the total population one must add women, children, slaves, non-citizen foreigners, soldiers and the elite. There is no ancient figure for their share, so the choice of multiplier alone produces differences of hundreds of thousands. This is the route to the often-quoted figure of about one million.

Density. According to Storey (1997), one million inhabitants on the 13.86 km² of the ancient city would mean 72,150 people per square kilometre, similar to the densest parts of modern Hong Kong. The density of the excavated blocks of Pompeii and Ostia gives a much smaller population, about 450,000.

The number of buildings. The 4th-century regionary catalogue lists 46,602 apartment blocks (insulae) and 1,790 houses (domus) (see “The 14 regions in numbers”). If insula means a whole building, this points to a large population; if only a flat or a plot unit, a much smaller one. The meaning of the word is disputed, so no population can be calculated from the figure.

Late antiquity. The spread between estimates is largest for the sieges of the 5th century (410, 455, 472) and the Gothic War of the 6th: scholars interpret the same few pieces of evidence (the recipients of the meat and bread distribution, Procopius’s account) in different ways.

The Notitia catalog: Region III (Isis et Serapis)

The location of the sanctuary of Isis and Serapis, which gave the region its name, is disputed. The most frequently cited proposal (M. de Vos; Lanciani; Häuber–Schütz, FORTVNA) looks for it at the eastern foot of the Oppius, between the present-day Via Labicana and Via Merulana; on the map it appears marked “location uncertain” (Isis et Serapis?). Other suggestions place it in the area of Santi Pietro e Marcellino or on the summit of the Caelian. The nearby ruins in Piazza Iside are often called the Temple of Isis, but this is not proven. How to read the map

Sources. There is no single Pausanias-like description of Rome. The history of the buildings is given by Livy, Varro, Dionysius, Cicero, the Res Gestae of Augustus, Suetonius, Cassius Dio and the inscriptions; the 4th-century regionary catalogues, in turn, list what stood in each region.

Excavations. In the 16th–19th centuries the Forum was known as a stone quarry and under the name “Campo Vaccino” (cow pasture). Systematic excavation began after 1803; between 1898 and 1905 Giacomo Boni dug down to the Republican-era and Archaic layers (Lapis Niger, Spring of Juturna, Regia, Iron Age cemetery). Today the Parco archeologico del Colosseo conducts the research; in 2020 an underground shrine linked to the cult of Romulus was presented beneath the steps of the Curia.

Lanciani layer. Rodolfo Lanciani’s 1:1000 atlas Forma Urbis Romae (1893–1901) over the whole area of the map: plates 1–4, 6–11 and 13–46, fitted into a uniform grid (for details see the Sources). Ancient remains in black, the city of the time (around 1900) in red, aqueducts and sewers in blue. At the control points the deviation is 1–8 m.

The imperial forums come from plate 22. Here the difference is especially clear: Lanciani drew the Forum of Caesar before the excavations of the 1930s, in a conjectured position, about 35 m further southeast than the real one, while the Forum and Markets of Trajan already largely agree with the modern survey.

The map was made largely before Boni’s excavations, begun in 1898, so it shows clearly what has come to light since then: on the site of the Basilica Aemilia Lanciani could only write the legend “locus basilicae Aemiliae”, the Lacus Curtius, the Lapis Niger and the Iron Age cemetery are still missing, and he drew the Regia according to the pre-excavation hypothesis, as a smaller rectangle. He gives the Temple of Divus Iulius as a reconstruction ringed by columns, and he took the large hall behind the Temple of Castor to be the Temple of Augustus.

Excavation data (SITAR). More than 6,000 excavated or reconstructed units from the open archaeological database of the Soprintendenza Speciale di Roma: walls, building phases, drains, roads, houses. They appear according to the year slider, so that, for example, the six Archaic building phases of the Regia (625–510 BC), the four phases of the Temple of Castor or the two phases of the Forum of Caesar can be viewed one after another. Their color shows their character (red: place of worship, brown: residential building, blue: water, gray: road, tan: other); the dashed line is the excavators’ reconstruction. Clicking any of them, the information panel shows the identification, the dating, the investigation and the description in English; the original Italian text can be expanded.

Marble Plan fragments. Those fragments of the marble plan of the city made between AD 203 and 211 (Forma Urbis Severiana) whose location has been identified, fitted to their real position in SITAR: the yellow patches are the fragments, with the lines of the ancient drawing inside them. The inscriptions of the Basilica Iulia and the Basilica Ulpia can also be read on them.
Scale. The bar at the bottom left shows 50 m, 100 Roman feet (29.6 m) and one actus (120 feet, 35.5 m).

<footer>Ground plan made for study purposes. The outlines follow the survey of the ruins visible today (OpenStreetMap), so they mostly show the final, imperial-period state; the monuments of the Forum burned down and were rebuilt several times.</footer>

The Forum Romanum was a marshy valley between the Capitol, the Palatium and the Velia. In the 10th–8th centuries BC people were still being buried here; the valley was drained by the Cloaca Maxima, and in the late 7th century BC it was first paved as a public square. For the next thousand years the heart of the Roman state stood here: the Senate, the popular assembly, the courts, the oldest sanctuaries.

With the year slider you can follow how the sanctuaries of the regal period become a Republican square, then an imperial ceremonial court, and how the buildings are turned into churches in late antiquity. With the “By function” row you can narrow the map down to temples, baths, gates or tombs, and the “What is visible today?” button shows what still stands of them.
